10937952.case_name: In Re APPLICATION OF ENBRIDGE ENERGY TO REPLACE AND RELOCATE LINE 5
10937952.holding_quote: the PSC erred by (1) failing to consider whether the tunnel project will factually and proximately cause the extension of Line 5's operational life, potentially resulting in additional environmental harm; (2) comparing alternatives in an inconsistent manner; and (3) failing to consider the project's impact on public trust resources.
10937952.situation:
This file concerns the Line 5 pipeline Replacement Project and the Michigan Public Service Commission's (PSC) approval of Enbridge's application to construct it. The matter arrives following the PSC's decision approving the application and its affirmance by the Court of Appeals.

SUBJECT MATTER AND GEOGRAPHY

The Great Lakes constitute the largest freshwater system on Earth and have been described in Michigan case law as Michigan's great natural resource. The Straits of Mackinac connect Lake Michigan and Lake Huron and are a critical point in this ecosystem. They are spanned by the Mackinac Bridge and are a significant natural and commercial resource for the state. Multiple Indian Tribes are involved in this litigation and point out that the Great Lakes and the Straits of Mackinac have nourished life in the region for thousands of years, referencing the historical importance of fishing to native inhabitants of Michigan and treaty fishing rights.

THE LINE 5 PIPELINE AND ITS HISTORY

The Line 5 pipeline is operated by Enbridge. It is 645 miles long and carries oil and liquid natural gas (LNG) from Superior, Wisconsin, to Sarnia, Ontario. It is part of a larger network of Enbridge pipelines stretching across the United States and Canada. Although Line 5 mostly transports hydrocarbons across Michigan to eastern Canada, the line provides crude oil to a few smaller facilities in Michigan, provides most of the Upper Peninsula's propane supply, and provides jet fuel to the Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport.

In 1953, Enbridge's predecessor, Lakehead Pipe Line Company, Inc. (Lakehead), received approval from the PSC to construct the pipeline presently known as Line 5. The Michigan Conservation Commission, predecessor to the Natural Resources Commission, granted Lakehead an easement to construct two 20-inch pipes (the dual pipelines) located on or suspended above the lakebed across the Mackinac Straits.

A collateral attack on the PSC's 1953 decision was rejected in Lakehead Pipe Line Co, Inc v Dehn, 340 Mich 25 (1954). In that case, landowners challenging the condemnation of their land along the pipeline's path argued that the construction and operation of the pipeline was not a purpose for which the State may grant the power of eminent domain, contending that Lakehead primarily contemplated transporting oil from Canadian oil fields to refineries in Canada. The Court rejected that argument, noting that Lakehead proposed to deliver oil to Michigan refineries and other purchasers in the State, and holding that the construction, maintenance, and operation of the pipeline would benefit the people of Michigan. The pipeline's approval, construction, and attendant litigation all preceded the 1963 adoption of Michigan Constitution, Article 4, Section 52, which requires the Legislature to provide for the protection of the air, water, and other natural resources of the state, and preceded the 1970 enactment of the Michigan Environmental Protection Act (MEPA), 1970 PA 127. MEPA was originally enacted as a standalone statute and later recodified in essentially the same form as part of NREPA, 1994 PA 451.

CONDITION OF THE DUAL PIPELINES

The dual pipelines have a daily carrying capacity of up to 540,000 barrels and are elevated above the lakebed by supports. Appellants allege that the pipelines are vulnerable to damage. Anchor strikes are a particular concern. In April 2018 a strike dented, but did not rupture, the dual pipelines. Given the fast-moving currents and the connection of both Lake Michigan and Lake Huron to the Straits, appellants allege that if one of the pipes were to rupture, the resulting spill would be environmentally and economically catastrophic.

THE REPLACEMENT PROJECT

The Replacement Project emerged from a series of agreements negotiated between Enbridge and Governor Rick Snyder on behalf of the state of Michigan from 2017 through 2018. The project involves drilling and constructing a new, concrete-lined tunnel through the bedrock approximately 60 feet to 250 feet under the Straits' lakebed, and running a new 30-inch pipe through that tunnel. Under the terms of Enbridge's agreement with the state, this would allow the dual pipelines to be decommissioned and, per the agreement, would essentially eliminate the risk of adverse impacts that may result from a potential oil spill in the Straits. The project would not change Line 5's current carrying capacity or the service it provides.

Initially, the project contemplated that the tunnel could be used for other utilities, such as electric and broadband lines. The PSC declined to approve this aspect of the project, concluding that Enbridge failed to demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that co-locating third-party utilities in the tunnel with the Straits Line 5 replacement segment is reasonable or safe.

STATUTORY AND CONTRACTUAL FRAMEWORK

In 2018, the Legislature created the Mackinac Straits Corridor Authority (MSCA) and authorized it to enter into an agreement to build a utility tunnel under the Straits, 2018 PA 359. Enbridge agreed to construct and maintain the tunnel and the replacement pipeline and to deactivate the existing dual pipelines once the Replacement Project becomes operational. The MSCA agreed to obtain the necessary property rights for Enbridge to construct the Replacement Project. Consistent with this goal, in December 2018, the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) granted the MSCA an easement to construct a tunnel under the Straits. Once Enbridge completes the tunnel, the MSCA will take ownership of the tunnel and provide Enbridge with a 99-year lease.

PROCEDURAL POSTURE

Enbridge filed an application with the PSC to move forward with the construction. The PSC approved the application. The Court of Appeals affirmed that decision. Appellants, including multiple Indian Tribes, challenge the approval.

seed.consideration: Whether the Replacement Project will factually and proximately cause the extension of Line 5's operational life, potentially resulting in additional environmental harm.
seed.why_material: Without determining whether the tunnel project proximately causes Line 5's continued operation and attendant harms, the PSC could not properly assess the project's full environmental impact or compare alternatives under MEPA.

10938477.court: Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
10938477.holding_quote: We conclude that the Board was required to adjudicate Mr. Hepler’s pre-PACT Act claim for service-connected benefits on a direct basis, and the Veterans Court erred by failing to order the Board to do so.
10938477.situation:
This case file concerns Edward Hepler's claim for service-connected disability benefits for hypertension against the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).

SERVICE HISTORY
Mr. Hepler served honorably in the United States Army from August 1970 to September 1973 and from December 2003 to February 2005, attaining the rank of Command Sergeant Major. During his first period of active-duty service, Mr. Hepler served in the Republic of Vietnam. During his second period of active-duty service, he served in Kuwait during Operation Iraqi Freedom. In addition to his Army service, Mr. Hepler served honorably in the Georgia Army National Guard from August 1986 to November 2011.

THE CLAIM AND ITS SUPPORTING EVIDENCE
On December 12, 2011, Mr. Hepler applied for disability benefits from the VA, including benefits for hypertension. He supplemented his application with a statement in support of his claim, writing, "I believe the hypertension . . . is associated with my military service as with each progression in rank and the [ensuing] responsibility and stress [it has] continued to elevate." Along with this statement, Mr. Hepler submitted a letter from a flight surgeon who served alongside him, which stated that hypertension was one of Mr. Hepler's illnesses and injuries that occurred while deployed between 2004 and 2005.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY BEFORE THE VA
The VA Regional Office (RO) denied Mr. Hepler entitlement to disability benefits for hypertension in a rating decision dated September 26, 2013. On December 17, 2013, Mr. Hepler filed a notice of disagreement with the September 2013 rating decision. More than four years later, on April 5, 2018, the VA issued a statement of the case, again denying that Mr. Hepler was entitled to disability benefits for hypertension. On May 8, 2018, Mr. Hepler appealed to the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) and requested a hearing, which was conducted on October 1, 2021. While the appeal was pending before the Board, Mr. Hepler submitted additional medical records reflecting treatment for hypertension. Mr. Hepler also personally testified at the Board hearing as to why he believed his hypertension was directly connected to his active-duty service. More than 11 years passed between when Mr. Hepler filed his claim for benefits and when the Board issued a decision on his appeal.

THE PACT ACT
After the Board hearing but before the Board issued a decision on Mr. Hepler's appeal, on August 10, 2022, Congress enacted the Sergeant First Class Heath Robinson Honoring our Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxics Act of 2022, Pub. L. No. 117–168, 136 Stat. 1759 (2022) (the PACT Act). The PACT Act presumptively entitles veterans who served in the Republic of Vietnam during a specified period to service-connected benefits for certain conditions, including hypertension, due to exposure to the herbicide Agent Orange. 38 U.S.C. § 1116. Eligible veterans may receive disability benefits based on this presumption effective August 10, 2022, but cannot receive an earlier effective date for these presumptively service-connected benefits. Benefits derived from the PACT Act may not be awarded for time prior to the enactment of the PACT Act. 38 U.S.C. § 5110(g); 38 C.F.R. § 3.114(a).

THE BOARD DECISION UNDER REVIEW
On April 28, 2023, the Board granted Mr. Hepler entitlement to benefits for hypertension on a presumptive basis pursuant to the PACT Act. In its decision, the Board did not directly address the direct service-connection claim. The Board "inform[ed] the RO that the evidence of record provides some indication that a relationship between the Veteran's hypertension and service may exist on a direct basis. The RO should consider such evidence when assigning an effective date."

THE PARTIES' POSITIONS AT THE VETERANS COURT
Mr. Hepler timely appealed the Board's decision to the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (Veterans Court), arguing that the Board erroneously failed to grant, deny, or remand his claim for service-connected benefits for hypertension on a direct basis. Mr. Hepler argued that had the Board addressed his claim for service-connected benefits for hypertension on a direct basis, he could have been entitled to an earlier effective date for such benefits, beginning when the VA received his December 2011 application for benefits. He further argued that a grant of such benefits would result in an award of benefits for a period before the enactment of the PACT Act because he filed his direct service-connection claim in 2011.

THE VETERANS COURT DECISION
On July 24, 2024, the Veterans Court dismissed Mr. Hepler's appeal as moot. The Veterans Court reasoned that because the Board granted service-connected benefits for hypertension under the PACT Act, "any concern with the effective date assigned for hypertension is a downstream issue and requires a separate appeal," and so Mr. Hepler's challenge was "best suited for a decision that assigns [an effective date]."

ON August 14, 2024, Mr. Hepler filed a motion for reconsideration or panel opinion. The Veterans Court denied Mr. Hepler's motion. Judge Bartley dissented, urging that the majority was incorrect and noting that "the Board now routinely cites the . . . [Veterans Court's decision in this case] . . . to support its determination that [the] VA is not obligated to adjudicate all reasonably raised theories of service connection in contention as to an earlier period even given service connection grants under new PACT Act provisions."

RELIEF SOUGHT
Mr. Hepler seeks a determination that the Board was required to grant, deny, or remand his claim for service-connected benefits for hypertension on a direct basis, so as to preserve the potential for an earlier effective date tied to his December 2011 application.

seed.consideration: The direct service-connection claim was a separate and distinct claim from the PACT Act presumptive claim, based on different events, and could yield an earlier effective date with more than ten years of past-due benefits.
seed.why_material: Because a claim seeking money that remains available cannot be moot, the availability of that earlier-effective-date relief meant the Board's and Veterans Court's disposition could not treat the direct claim as resolved by the PACT Act grant.

key.label: Mootness after PACT Act grant
key.question: Was Mr. Hepler's appeal moot because he received presumptive service-connected hypertension benefits under the PACT Act?

key.label: Effective date as downstream issue
key.question: Is any concern with the effective date a downstream issue requiring a separate appeal rather than resolution now?

key.label: Forum for effective-date decision
key.question: Is the challenge best suited for a later decision that assigns an effective date?

10940319.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
10940319.holding_quote: Because the district court failed to consider Carter's supervisory liability claim against Clarke under the correct legal standard, we vacate its dismissal of that claim and remand for reconsideration.
10940319.situation:
CASE FILE: Carter v. Cabell (E.D. Va.)

PARTIES
Plaintiff: Benjamin Carter, at all relevant times a prisoner in the Restrictive Housing Unit (RHU) at Sussex State Prison, a facility within the Virginia Department of Corrections (VDOC). Carter proceeds pro se. Carter has since been released from Sussex State Prison but remains incarcerated at a different facility in connection with a separate offense.

Defendants: Joshua Branch, manager of Carter's housing unit; Kevin McCoy and Beth Cabell, two wardens at Sussex; other unnamed Sussex officials; Harold Clarke, then the Director of the VDOC; and the Commonwealth of Virginia.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND
Carter alleges that in the RHU he was subject to conditions of confinement analogous to those found unconstitutional in Porter v. Clarke, 923 F.3d 348 (4th Cir. 2019), a case concerning the conditions death row prisoners at Sussex faced between 2010 and 2015. Carter asserts the conditions he faced were particularly harmful to him because he suffers from numerous serious mental illnesses.

Carter sought better conditions of confinement through the VDOC grievance process. That process generally consists of three steps. First, an inmate must make good-faith efforts to informally resolve his issue through verbal discussion with relevant prison officials and, if needed, an informal written complaint. Second, if informal resolution fails, the inmate must file a regular grievance, which is screened by an intake team who determine whether to accept or reject the grievance based on a set of filing requirements. Third, if a grievance is accepted at intake, it proceeds to a series of more formal reviews.

Carter filed numerous informal complaints and grievances about the conditions he faced in the RHU. Three are relevant here.

First, in June 2022, Carter submitted an informal complaint seeking reclassification into reentry programming, which would have transitioned him out of the RHU. According to Carter, a VDOC policy requires reclassification of inmates who are within two years of their release date; when he filed this informal complaint, his release date was June 2024. The complaint was rejected by Joshua Branch, the manager of Carter's housing unit. Branch did not provide a reason for denying the complaint, and Carter never submitted a regular grievance after Branch's rejection.

Carter alleges that Branch and other Sussex officials retaliated against him for this June 2022 complaint. About two weeks after rejecting the complaint, Branch allegedly told Carter: "Stop writing me up Carter, you[']re really not going to get reentry now." Carter responded by again pleading to be let out of the RHU, but Branch just laughed and said that Kevin McCoy and Beth Cabell, two wardens at Sussex, "weren't having that especially after [Carter] wrote them up about not getting reentry."

Carter then filed two regular grievances relevant here, both in late September 2022. First, Carter submitted a grievance asserting he had been retaliated against for requesting reclassification into reentry programming and transfer out of the RHU. Second, Carter submitted a grievance regarding the conditions of confinement he continued to face in the RHU. Both grievances followed informal complaints Carter had submitted earlier on the same matters.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Shortly after filing these two grievances — and before step two of the grievance process was completed — Carter initiated this action, pro se, by mailing a complaint to the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. That original complaint concerned only his conditions of confinement in the RHU. Carter alleged that those conditions violated the Eighth Amendment and sought damages and injunctive relief under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 against Branch, McCoy, Cabell, and other unnamed Sussex officials; Harold Clarke, then the Director of the VDOC; and the Commonwealth of Virginia. The district court assessed Carter a filing fee and then conditionally granted his motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis. Neither the district court nor the defendants took any other action in response to this complaint.

When Carter filed his first complaint, his two grievances were still at the second, intake stage of the grievance process. Both had been rejected at intake, and Carter's appeals of those rejections were pending. Those appeals were finalized by late October 2022, when both intake rejections were affirmed.

In January 2023, Carter, still proceeding pro se, filed the amended complaint that is now the operative complaint. Carter reasserted his Eighth Amendment conditions of confinement claims. For the first time, he also asserted First Amendment retaliation claims against Branch, McCoy, and Cabell, premised on Branch's comments to Carter following his June 2022 informal complaint. All claims arise under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

DISTRICT COURT ORDERS UNDER REVIEW

First Order (Frivolity Review). The district court reviewed Carter's amended complaint for frivolity under 28 U.S.C. § 1915A. The court dismissed only one claim: Carter's Eighth Amendment claim against Clarke, director of the VDOC, which the court construed as premised on supervisory liability. The court reasoned that Carter failed to state a supervisory liability claim against Clarke because none of his allegations allowed for an inference that Clarke had any knowledge of Carter's specific conditions of confinement. The court then denied Carter's motion for reconsideration, applying the same reasoning: Carter's complaint offered sufficient facts to infer that Clarke had knowledge, in the abstract, of the allegedly unconstitutional conditions of confinement, but exactly zero information to suggest that Clarke had knowledge of the fact that Carter was being held in such conditions.

With Clarke dismissed, the court ordered the remaining defendants — Cabell, McCoy, Branch, and the Commonwealth of Virginia — to respond to Carter's claims. The defendants concurrently filed a joint answer and motion for summary judgment.

Defendants' Positions. The defendants argued that the exhaustion requirement in the Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA), 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), foreclosed all the claims in Carter's amended complaint because Carter failed to exhaust the VDOC grievance process before filing his original complaint. In the alternative, they asserted that Carter's allegations failed to state First Amendment retaliation claims upon which relief could be granted. The defendants did not address the merits of Carter's Eighth Amendment claims.

Summary Judgment Order. Prior to any discovery, the district court granted summary judgment to the defendants and dismissed Carter's case. Carter v. Cabell, 2024 WL 1356670 (E.D. Va. Mar. 29, 2024).

On exhaustion, the court largely agreed with the defendants. It concluded that Carter appeared to have exhausted his grievances before filing his amended complaint, but that it was undisputed he had not yet fully exhausted when he filed his original complaint. Under the unpublished decision in Hardin v. Hunt, 2023 WL 3969989 (4th Cir. June 13, 2023), the court reasoned, a plaintiff cannot cure an initial failure to exhaust by completing a grievance process after commencing a lawsuit and then filing an amended complaint. The court dismissed all of Carter's claims — both the Eighth Amendment claims raised in his initial complaint and the First Amendment claims raised for the first time in his amended complaint — for failure to exhaust.

The court also addressed the defendants' alternative argument that Carter's First Amendment claims should be dismissed for failure to state a claim. Analyzing those claims under Rule 12(b)(6), the court found that Carter's amended complaint stated a plausible First Amendment retaliation claim against Branch but failed to state such claims against McCoy and Cabell. The court reasoned that Branch's alleged statements to Carter about Carter's June 2022 informal complaint were sufficient to support an inference that Branch denied the informal complaint, and thus kept Carter confined in the RHU, in retaliation for "writing [Branch] up," which constituted protected First Amendment activity. The court found Branch's alleged references to McCoy and Cabell insufficient to implicate those officials.

RELIEF SOUGHT
Carter seeks damages and injunctive relief under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for the alleged Eighth Amendment conditions-of-confinement violations and the First Amendment retaliation.

GOVERNING STANDARDS INVOKED
28 U.S.C. § 1915A (frivolity review); 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a) (PLRA exhaustion requirement); 42 U.S.C. § 1983; Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6); summary judgment standard.

seed.consideration: Whether the VDOC grievance process was genuinely 'available' to Carter within the meaning of Ross v. Blake, such that he was actually required to exhaust his Eighth Amendment claims.
seed.why_material: If administrative remedies were not meaningfully available—for instance because officials thwarted the process through retaliatory threats—Carter would be deemed to have satisfied the exhaustion requirement without completing the grievance process.

key.label: Exhaustion timing of First Amendment claims
key.question: Does the filing date of the original complaint or the amended complaint control PLRA exhaustion for claims first raised in the amended complaint?

key.label: Amendment curing exhaustion defect
key.question: Can a prisoner who exhausted after filing an original complaint proceed on newly exhausted claims via an amended complaint?

key.label: Supervisory liability knowledge standard
key.question: Must a plaintiff allege the supervisor knew of his specific conditions, or suffices knowledge of pervasive unconstitutional conditions risking injury to prisoners like him?

key.label: First Amendment retaliation against Branch
key.question: Did Carter plausibly allege protected activity, adverse action, and causation against Branch?

key.label: First Amendment retaliation against McCoy/Cabell
key.question: Did Branch's alleged statements sufficiently implicate McCoy and Cabell in retaliatory denial of transfer?

key.label: Eleventh Amendment bar against Commonwealth
key.question: Are Carter's claims against the Commonwealth of Virginia barred by sovereign immunity and impermissible respondeat superior?

10940926.case_name: Sussex County Planning & Zoning Commission v. Smokey Hollow, LLC
10940926.holding_quote: The court failed to consider, however, the Commission’s primary stated reason for Condition A – environmental concerns unique to the lot.
10940926.situation:
CASE FILE — Smokey Hollow, LLC Subdivision Application (Sussex County)

PARTIES AND POSTURE

Applicant/Developer: Smokey Hollow, LLC. Regulatory body: County Planning and Zoning Commission of Sussex County ("the Commission"). The matter is presently before the Superior Court on Smokey Hollow's petition for a writ of certiorari challenging two conditions the Commission attached to its approval of Smokey Hollow's residential subdivision application.

GOVERNING AUTHORITY AND FRAMEWORK

Under Article II, Section 25 of the Delaware Constitution, the General Assembly may enact laws under which municipalities and the Counties of Sussex, Kent, and New Castle may adopt zoning ordinances limiting and restricting land, buildings, and structures to specified districts and regulating their construction, use, and the use of land for non-agricultural purposes, as an exercise of the police power of the State.

The General Assembly delegated authority to Sussex County Council to regulate land use and development (9 Del. C. § 6902) and established the County Planning and Zoning Commission of Sussex County (9 Del. C. § 6802). The Commission was created to address land use development in a way that promotes "the health, safety, prosperity and general welfare," "secur[es] coordinated plans for land use, transportation, public facilities and utilities and public works expenditures," and "prevent[s] the unnecessary duplication of facilities or utilities." The Commission advises County Council on zoning changes and conditional use requests, but itself approves or denies subdivision applications (Sussex Cnty. C. §§ 115-173, 115-216, 99-6, 99-9).

Under the Sussex County Zoning Code, all unincorporated Sussex County land and certain incorporated municipalities without zoning provisions fall within zoning districts defined by the Sussex County Zoning Map (§§ 115-2, 115-5, 115-7). Where a proposed development cannot be undertaken as of right under the existing zoning classification, the landowner must apply to rezone the property (Ch. 115). Where the parcel's current zoning allows the proposed development but the property must be subdivided, the property owner follows the Sussex County subdivision approval process (Ch. 99). A major subdivision is any subdivision of six or more lots (§ 99-5). A minor subdivision is any subdivision creating five or fewer lots and not adversely affecting the development of the remainder of the parcel or adjoining property and not in conflict with the County Comprehensive Plan, Official Map, Zoning Ordinance, or Chapter 99.

Under the major subdivision approval process, after the developer completes the State of Delaware Planning Office for Preliminary Land Use Service ("PLUS") review process, the developer meets with the Sussex County Planning and Zoning Office ("Zoning Office") to review the proposed project and submits a preliminary plan (29 Del. C. Ch. 92; Sussex Cnty. C. §§ 99-7, 99-8). If the subdivision has 50 or more dwelling units and is in a Coastal Area, the developer must also provide an environmental assessment (§ 115-194.3). After Zoning Office review, the Commission holds a public hearing on the preliminary plan (§ 99-9). The Commission must "either tentatively approve or disapprove or conditionally approve the plat subject to specific changes or modifications" (§ 99-9(A)).

If the applicant disagrees with the Commission's decision, it may appeal to County Council within 30 days after the Commission's official action (§ 99-39(A)). The applicant may also request in writing that the Commission reconsider a condition it imposed, but there is no appeal from the Commission's decision on such a request (§ 99-39(H)).

FACTS

Smokey Hollow owns a 66-acre parcel in unincorporated Sussex County on which it seeks to build an 82-lot residential subdivision. The property is zoned GR (General Residential), meaning the developer can build a residential subdivision as of right and does not need to rezone the property. The property is located in a Coastal Area. Because Smokey Hollow sought to subdivide the parcel into over 50 lots, the Zoning Code required major subdivision approval from the Commission.

Smokey Hollow completed PLUS review, conferred with the Zoning Office on technical requirements, filed a subdivision application with the Office, and submitted a preliminary plan.

At the public hearing, homeowners in the contiguous Fox Haven residential subdivision raised a number of concerns, including that lot 64 posed flooding and runoff risks to their neighborhood. They also spoke about how the proposed development could displace wildlife, destroy trees, increase summer traffic, encroach on private property, and change the area's natural character.

The Commission unanimously approved the preliminary plan subject to 19 conditions. Smokey Hollow accepted all but two:

- Condition A, which eliminated lot 64. Regarding Condition A, the Commission explained that lot 64 was an isolated lot, access was dependent on crossing wetlands, and the lot and surrounding area were subject to frequent flooding.

- Condition O, which required a 25-foot fixed (as opposed to an average) minimum buffer from non-tidal wetlands. The Commission did not explain why it imposed Condition O. It stated that "there shall be a buffer that is at least 25 feet wide from all non-tidal wetlands."

Smokey Hollow contends that imposing the 25-foot fixed buffer from non-tidal wetlands results in the loss of 8 lots (10% of the project), while maintaining an average 30-foot buffer would not eliminate any additional lots.

Smokey Hollow asked the Commission to reconsider the two conditions. It argued that the Commission could not eliminate a lot that complied with the subdivision regulations. It also pointed out that a newly adopted ordinance exempted pending applications from the buffer requirement. As a compromise, Smokey Hollow proposed a 100-foot forested or landscaped buffer for lot 64 and an average (not a fixed) 30-foot buffer from all non-tidal wetlands around certain lots.

The Commission stuck by its determination that lot 64 encroached on wetlands and that developing it could increase flooding in the area. During the public hearing addressing the request to amend the conditions, the Commission stated that lot 64 "was surrounded by the wetlands," was subject to flooding, and that a lot owner would have to "cross[] the wetlands to get to the lot." The Commission also held firm on the fixed buffer requirement. It explained that it imposed "these conditions based on public testimony and site conditions" and that it "didn't just take that lot away from [Smokey Hollow]" but required the conditions "to uphold the code."

REGULATORY BACKGROUND ON WETLAND SETBACKS AND BUFFERS

When Smokey Hollow submitted its application, the Sussex County Code provided that "[a] minimum of 25 feet of permanent setback must be maintained around the outer boundaries of all wetlands . . . No buildings or paving shall be placed within these setbacks" (former Sussex Cnty. C. § 115-25F(3)(a)(4)). A building setback is "[t]he minimum distance that a building must be set back from a street or lot line as required by a building setback line so designated on a plat of a subdivision" (§ 99-5). A resource buffer for wetlands is "a managed area between residential land uses and resources that is not subdividable once established" which protects the environment against land-use impacts (§ 99-5). Ordinance 2852, effective November 17, 2022, required an average 30-foot buffer from non-tidal wetlands under certain circumstances (Sussex Cnty. Ord. No. 2852 §§ 9, 13).

RELIEF SOUGHT / SUPERIOR COURT PROCEEDINGS

Smokey Hollow filed a petition for a writ of certiorari in the Superior Court seeking to strike the two conditions. It claimed that Conditions A and O were unreasonable and contrary to the County Code.

The court granted certiorari, found that the Commission made errors of law, and declared the two conditions unreasonable.

On Condition A, the court held that, consistent with Supreme Court precedent, the Commission must approve a subdivision plan that complies with the County Code, subject only to reasonable conditions that "minimize any adverse impact on nearby landowners and residents." The court concluded that the Commission imposed Condition A in response to neighborhood opposition rather than to minimize adverse impacts on the Fox Haven neighborhood. It also found that Condition A conflicted with Council's legislative determination that a 30-foot subdivision perimeter setback was sufficient.

On Condition O, the court held that the Zoning Code's cluster development standards did not apply to Smokey Hollow's property. It found that the prior version of the Code regulated setbacks from wetlands, not wetland buffers. It held that County Council's later-adopted Ordinance 2852, which requires an average (not fixed) 30-foot non-tidal wetlands buffer, expressly exempted pending applications. The court held that Condition O imposed a buffer that exceeded the Zoning Code and therefore was an unreasonable condition. The court struck both conditions.

The Commission's position is that the Superior Court failed to recognize the Commission's authority to impose reasonable conditions on a subdivision application, even if the application complies with the County Code, and that the court did not fully consider what makes a condition "reasonable."

STANDARD OF REVIEW

Review of an administrative agency's decision determines whether the agency exceeded its discretion. On the Commission's decision on subdivision plan approval, review is whether the decision is supported by substantial evidence and free from legal error. Substantial evidence is "such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion." Questions of law are reviewed de novo.

seed.consideration: Whether the Commission's environmental and flooding concerns specific to lot 64 were supported by substantial evidence, such as a professional environmental assessment or Zoning Office review, rather than only neighbors' anecdotal observations.
seed.why_material: Because the Commission's primary stated reason for eliminating lot 64 was environmental, not community opposition, and a condition eliminating a compliant lot must rest on substantial evidence of a genuine land-use impact.

10941690.situation:
CASE FILE — In the Matter of Salaruddin Eqbal, Respondent

Parties and posture: Salaruddin Eqbal is the respondent in removal proceedings before the Immigration Judge (IJ). The Department of Homeland Security placed him in removal proceedings after his entry into the United States. The IJ has denied all relief and ordered removal. The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) has dismissed Eqbal's appeal from the IJ's decision. This file is drawn to the record before the IJ and the BIA.

Respondent's background: Eqbal is a native and citizen of Afghanistan, born in 1974 in Afghanistan's Panjshir province, an area that historically resisted the Taliban. He belongs to the Tajik ethnic group, a group the Taliban perceived as an enemy. He served as security personnel for high-ranking officials in the Afghan government.

Employment history as recounted by Eqbal: In 1993, Eqbal began working as a bodyguard for Mohammad Qasim Fahim, a prominent opponent of the Taliban's first rise to power in the 1990s. In 1997 or 1998, while working for Fahim, the Taliban arrested and imprisoned Eqbal for one month, during which they beat and tortured him, permanently injuring his back. He was released when Fahim arranged a prisoner exchange. Following the events of September 11, 2001, a new government backed by the United States formed in Afghanistan. Fahim became vice president of Afghanistan, and Eqbal continued his security-related employment with Fahim from 2001 until Fahim's death in 2014. After Fahim's death, Eqbal continued working in the Afghan government in security roles from 2014 until the fall of the government in 2021, first for the president of Afghanistan and then for the deputy director of national security.

Events leading to flight: When the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan in 2021, it began killing and imprisoning individuals who had worked for the former government, including some of Eqbal's colleagues. The Taliban issued warrants for Eqbal's arrest, citing his former employment, and began actively searching for him. Eqbal and his family were forced into hiding and relocated within Afghanistan multiple times to evade the Taliban. In one instance, Taliban agents went to Eqbal's home, found his mother there alone, and interrogated and assaulted her in an attempt to locate Eqbal. In 2023, fearing for his life and unable to escape the Taliban's search, Eqbal fled Afghanistan. At the airport attempting to leave the country, Taliban agents stopped him. With the help of an airport employee who recognized him, Eqbal convinced the Taliban personnel that he was leaving to seek medical treatment and would return. Since his departure, Eqbal's family remains in hiding and has faced inquiry from the Taliban as to his location.

Entry and proceedings: Eqbal entered the United States in June 2024 and was detained and placed in removal proceedings. The IJ found Eqbal removable for lacking a valid entry document at the time he sought admission to the United States. See 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(7)(A)(i). Eqbal filed a Form I-589 Application for Asylum and Withholding of Removal, seeking asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT). He asserts fear of harm by the Taliban due to his work in the former Afghan government and his Tajik ethnicity, and alleges that returning to Afghanistan would be tantamount to a death sentence.

The hearing and the IJ's decision: Eqbal proceeded pro se at the hearing. The IJ denied all relief and ordered him removed to Afghanistan. The IJ determined that Eqbal's testimony was not credible and that he offered no other evidence establishing his eligibility for relief. The IJ's adverse credibility determination was based in large part on what it determined to be discrepancies in the positions Eqbal held in the Afghan government and the dates he held those positions. The IJ's determination that Eqbal did not credibly testify to his employment history impacted the weight the IJ gave Eqbal's non-testimonial evidence, the corroborative evidence it required Eqbal to produce, and its analysis of the merits of Eqbal's claims. The IJ found that Eqbal was not credible, that he failed to provide evidence corroborating his claims, and that the non-testimonial evidence did not independently establish his eligibility for relief.

BIA decision: The Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with the IJ and dismissed Eqbal's appeal.

Relief sought: Asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under CAT.

seed.consideration: The decision-maker should consider whether apparent date discrepancies in an applicant's account stem from interpreter error translating between the Afghan and Gregorian calendars before treating them as inconsistencies.
seed.why_material: Because the impossible dates (predating the applicant's birth and the Taliban's existence) revealed the discrepancies as mistranslation, undermining the entire adverse credibility finding that infected the whole decision.

10945635.situation:
This is an employer intentional tort action brought by plaintiff Camara against defendant Gill Dairy LLC, currently postured at the trial court's denial of Gill Dairy's motion for summary judgment on the tort claim, and the subsequent jury trial and verdict on that claim.

PARTIES AND CLAIMS
Camara filed suit in June 2020. In an amended complaint, he asserted two claims against Gill Dairy: (1) employer intentional tort under R.C. 2745.01, and (2) spoliation of evidence. The employer intentional tort claim is the claim addressed here.

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
Camara alleges that he was working as a farm laborer for Gill Dairy on April 22, 2019, when he suffered severe injuries while operating a piece of machinery called a sand spreader. The sand spreader was connected to a tractor by a power take-off shaft ("PTO shaft"), which was equipped with a hydraulic motor that caused the PTO shaft to rotate while in use. Camara alleges the rotation of the PTO shaft created a hazard for anyone nearby. To protect the user and bystanders from that hazard, the PTO shaft was supposed to have safety guards on it, but it did not have any safety guards on it on April 22, 2019.

On that day, Camara observed an oil leak in the sand spreader. He turned the sand spreader off to look for the source of the leak, but when he could not identify the source, he turned the sand spreader on to investigate the matter further. As he looked for the leak, a piece of clothing on his left leg got caught in the unguarded, rotating PTO shaft. The rotation of the PTO shaft pulled Camara toward the machine, then threw him over the shaft to the other side of the tractor. Camara suffered severe and permanent injuries to both legs and his left shoulder, requiring skin grafts and multiple surgeries.

GOVERNING STATUTE
R.C. 2745.01(A) provides that in an action brought against an employer by an employee for damages resulting from an intentional tort committed by the employer during the course of employment, the employer shall not be liable unless the plaintiff proves that the employer committed the tortious act with the intent to injure another or with the belief that the injury was substantially certain to occur. R.C. 2745.01(B) provides that "substantially certain" means that an employer acts with deliberate intent to cause an employee to suffer an injury, a disease, a condition, or death. R.C. 2745.01(C) provides that deliberate removal by an employer of an equipment safety guard creates a rebuttable presumption that the removal was committed with intent to injure another if an injury or an occupational disease or condition occurs as a direct result.

In his amended complaint, Camara alleges that he is entitled to the rebuttable presumption under R.C. 2745.01(C) because Gill Dairy intentionally removed the safety guards from the rotating PTO shaft and the absence of those safety guards caused his injuries.

SUMMARY-JUDGMENT MOTION
Gill Dairy moved for summary judgment, arguing that Camara had not produced any evidence that Gill Dairy had intended to cause Camara or anyone else injury. With respect to the R.C. 2745.01(C) presumption, Gill Dairy contended that the evidence showed only that it had failed to repair or replace the safety guards that may have become detached from the PTO shaft during normal, routine use, and that such an act or omission was insufficient to establish a "deliberate removal" of an equipment safety guard under the statute. In support, Gill Dairy pointed to deposition testimony from Camara, as well as deposition testimony and affidavits from the owners of Gill Dairy, Tony Gill and Frank Van Genugten. Gill and Van Genugten both attested in affidavits that they did not remove or authorize the removal of either the PTO shaft guard or the PTO coupling guard. Camara submitted an affidavit averring that Gill had frequently serviced and repaired the sand spreader before Camara's injury and had always returned the equipment to service without the safety guards.

TRIAL COURT'S RULING ON SUMMARY JUDGMENT
The trial court denied the motion. It concluded that in resolving doubts and construing evidence against the moving party, Gill Dairy, there was a genuine issue of material fact that should be presented to the jury, namely whether Gill Dairy intentionally removed the safety guards from the subject spreader. Madison C.P. No. CVH 20200107 (Dec. 29, 2021).

TRIAL EVIDENCE
The case proceeded to a jury trial. The following evidence was presented:

Gill Dairy purchased the sand spreader in 2011. The PTO shaft connected the sand spreader to a tractor. When in use, the PTO shaft would rotate at 540 revolutions per minute. The manufacturer included two safety guards designed to protect against hazards created by the rotating PTO shaft: one guard covered the shaft itself ("the PTO shaft guard"); the other covered the point at which the PTO shaft connected to the sand spreader's gearbox ("the PTO coupling guard"). The manufacturer also placed warnings on the sand spreader near the PTO shaft stating "DANGER, ENTANGLEMENT HAZARD" and "Keep Guards in Place."

First, the jury heard that Gill Dairy had hired a company to replace the sand spreader's hydraulic pump in April 2016. Because the pump was located near the PTO coupling guard, replacing the pump would have required the company to remove the guard and then put it back in place once the new pump was installed.

Second, the jury was presented with an image from a video that Camara had taken of the sand spreader in March 2018; the image shows that the PTO coupling guard was missing, as was half the PTO shaft guard, leaving half the PTO shaft exposed. Camara testified that the image reflected the condition of the sand spreader from the time he began working at Gill Dairy in October 2017 until his injury in April 2019. Camara further testified that in 2017 he expressed concerns to Van Genugten about the rotating PTO shaft's lacking proper guards, and that Van Genugten told him not to worry about it and to keep working.

Third, the jury was presented with a report from an investigator with the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration ("OSHA"). The OSHA investigator found that on April 22, 2019, the PTO coupling guard was not present on the sand spreader, which resulted in Camara's injuries. The investigator recounted a conversation with Van Genugten. With respect to the missing PTO coupling guard, the investigator asked Van Genugten when the guard was removed or what had happened to require the pump mounting to be repaired. Van Genugten responded that he did not know, that he was not involved in the repair, and that Gill had performed the repair. The investigator asked how long ago Gill made that repair, and Van Genugten responded that he did not recall but that the PTO shaft had been without a guard for as long as he could remember.

Fourth, the jury was presented with a quote that Gill Dairy had obtained in January 2019, two months before Camara was injured, for a new PTO shaft assembly for the sand spreader. The jury was also presented with a report prepared by an investigator with the Ohio Bureau of Workers' Compensation ("BWC"), which showed that when the investigator asked for a copy of an invoice showing Gill Dairy's purchase of a new PTO shaft assembly in 2019, the investigator was given a copy of the January 2019 quote with the word "quote" removed. When Camara's counsel confronted Gill at trial with the quote and the document given to the BWC investigator that appeared to have been altered, Gill testified that everything Gill Dairy had concerning the sand spreader was given to its lawyer and that no one with Gill Dairy had contacted the investigator to inform him that the document was a quote and not an invoice.

JURY INSTRUCTIONS
After the parties presented their evidence and gave closing arguments, the trial court instructed the jury. On Camara's tort claim, the court instructed that the plaintiff claims his injury was caused by the intentional or deliberate conduct of the defendant, and that before finding for the plaintiff the jury must find by the greater weight of the evidence that: (A) the plaintiff was an employee of the defendant acting in the course of his employment; (B) the plaintiff's injury was proximately caused by the defendant's conduct; and (C) the defendant committed an act or omission with the intent to harm the plaintiff. The court further instructed that if the jury finds the defendant deliberately removed an equipment safety guard, it may but is not required to find that the removal was committed with the intent to injure if the injury occurred as a direct result of the deliberate removal. The court defined "deliberate removal of an equipment safety guard" as meaning that the defendant made a deliberate decision to remove, lift, push aside, take off, or otherwise eliminate an equipment safety guard. The court also instructed that deliberate removal by an employer of an equipment safety guard creates a rebuttable presumption that the removal was committed with intent to injure another if an injury occurs as a direct result.

The trial court gave the jury interrogatories, including: (A) Did the defendant, Gill Dairy LLC, deliberately remove an equipment safety guard from the spreader/sand wagon? (B) Did defendant's removal of an equipment safety guard proximately cause an injury to the plaintiff? (C) Has the defendant, Gill Dairy LLC, rebutted the presumption of intent to injure the plaintiff by proving by equal or greater weight of the evidence that the defendant did not intend to injure plaintiff?

VERDICT
The jury reached a verdict in favor of Camara on his tort claim. A majority of jurors answered yes to interrogatories (A) and (B) and answered no to interrogatory (C). The jury awarded Camara a total of $1,934,000 in compensatory damages. On the spoliation claim, a majority of the jury found that Gill Dairy had willfully destroyed evidence for the purpose of disrupting Camara's ability to prove a claim in a pending or probable lawsuit, but concluded that the destruction of evidence had not actually disrupted Camara's ability to prove his claim in that lawsuit; for that reason the jury entered a verdict in favor of Gill Dairy on the spoliation claim.

RELIEF SOUGHT AND POSTURE
The matter is postured on the trial court's denial of Gill Dairy's motion for summary judgment on the employer intentional tort claim and the jury's verdict following trial. The central legal question raised by Gill Dairy's motion is whether proof of an employer's failure to repair or replace an existing equipment safety guard can establish the employer's "deliberate removal" of an equipment safety guard under R.C. 2745.01(C), and whether the summary-judgment record establishes who removed the PTO coupling guard and whether any removal was deliberate.

seed.consideration: When reviewing a summary-judgment denial that rested on a genuine issue of material fact after a trial has occurred, the appellate court should consider the full record developed at trial, not only the record as it existed at the summary-judgment stage.
seed.why_material: Confining review to the pretrial record led the court to overturn a jury verdict without accounting for trial evidence that could reasonably support the jury's finding of deliberate removal.

10946077.situation:
CASE FILE — Judicial Review of General Conservation Plan and Master Permits for the Utah Prairie Dog

I. SUBJECT MATTER

This matter concerns regulatory measures adopted to protect the Utah prairie dog, a species inhabiting Utah grasslands. During the twentieth century, the species suffered a substantial decline in population attributable to disease, poisoning, and destruction of habitat. In response, the Fish and Wildlife Service ("the Service") listed the species as endangered and subsequently reclassified it as threatened.

Under the Endangered Species Act, an endangered species is a species, other than insects considered pests, "which is in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range," 16 U.S.C. § 1532(6). A species is threatened when it "is likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of its range," 16 U.S.C. § 1532(20).

II. GOVERNING STATUTORY AND REGULATORY FRAMEWORK

The listings triggered the Endangered Species Act and accompanying regulations, which ordinarily bar the taking of endangered or threatened species within the United States. See 16 U.S.C. § 1538(a)(1)(B) (prohibiting the taking of endangered species); 16 U.S.C. § 1533(d) (allowing the Secretary of the Interior to prohibit the taking of threatened species); 50 C.F.R. § 17.31 (establishing a default prohibition against the taking of threatened species). "Take" is defined as "to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct." 16 U.S.C. § 1532(19).

Despite this general bar, the Service can issue permits allowing takes incidental to conduct that is otherwise legal. 16 U.S.C. § 1539(a)(1)(B). For example, a developer may obtain a permit to build a school or hospital on land occupied by prairie dogs.

A permit can be issued only if a developer submits a conservation plan and the Service finds that: (1) the developer would minimize and mitigate the impact of the taking to the maximum extent practicable; (2) the developer would ensure enough funding to minimize and mitigate the impact; (3) the taking would not appreciably reduce the likelihood of the survival and recovery of the species; and (4) the developer would take any other measures necessary or appropriate to implement the plan. 16 U.S.C. § 1539(a)(2)(A)–(B).

III. THE GENERAL CONSERVATION PLAN

In 2018, the Service issued a General Conservation Plan ("the Plan") covering land in seven counties in southwest Utah. The Plan included three "recovery units"—areas that were geographically identifiable and "essential to the conservation and recovery of the entire population of Utah prairie dogs."

The Plan was designed to streamline the issuance of permits over a ten-year period. During that period, regulators expected construction on habitats containing large colonies of Utah prairie dogs.

The Service recognized that developers would focus on just a few counties. For those counties, the Plan would relieve developers of the need to obtain individual permits. Instead, the Plan would allow the Service to issue a "master permit" to a county. The county could then allow developers to use the master permit by issuing "certificates of inclusion." A certificate of inclusion would allow developers to take prairie dogs under conditions specified by the Plan and the county. In places without master permits, the Service could authorize the take of prairie dogs by issuing individual permits to developers.

IV. DEVELOPMENT AREA DESIGNATIONS

To predict the potential impact on prairie dogs, the Plan designated two types of areas: major development areas and minor development areas.

Major development areas are lands that are owned by someone other than the federal government and that are "built out or adjacent to built out areas." Minor development areas are lands that are owned by someone other than the federal government and less likely to experience significant development over the ten-year period. Minor development areas sometimes contain low-quality habitats, which are areas lacking the required biological, ecological, or functional requirements to sustain the species' life cycle.

V. PROJECTIONS OF HABITAT LOSS

The Service used historical averages to project the loss of habitat in major and minor development areas. The Service recognized that future development could exceed the historic averages, acknowledging that "it is possible that future development would be higher than historical averages, at least in some years, with changes in the economy or human population growth." The Service also predicted the impact on prairie dogs if the destruction of their habitats were to increase fivefold.

VI. MITIGATION MEASURES

The Plan supplied two primary approaches for mitigation.

The first approach would be used in major development areas and small colonies on low-quality habitats in the minor development areas. For these areas, the Plan required the movement of prairie dogs from development sites and the establishment of new colonies on federal or protected lands. This movement is called translocation.

For minor development areas with medium- or high-quality habitats, the Plan required protection of habitats through conservation banks, land acquisitions, and conservation easements. Conservation banks are permanently protected and managed lands, and conservation easements are restrictions in deeds.

The mitigation measures would be funded by Utah and by fees paid by developers. To allow adjustments, the Plan required the permittees to monitor the success of mitigation and required the Service to annually review compliance.

VII. THE SERVICE'S FINDINGS AND ISSUANCE OF PERMITS

The Service projected that future development (such as construction of schools and hospitals) would destroy habitats, leading to the take of up to 7,152 prairie dogs over ten years. The Service concluded that the mitigation measures would fully offset the impact. In support of these conclusions, the Service found:

• that the Plan and the proposed permits would not likely jeopardize the continued existence of the Utah prairie dog;
• that the minimization and mitigation measures would fully offset the take of the prairie dogs;
• that funding was assured; and
• that the Plan would not significantly impact the environment.

Based on these findings, the Service issued master permits to three Utah counties—Iron, Garfield, and Beaver—authorizing incidental takes through development.

VIII. PROCEDURAL POSTURE

Friends of Animals petitioned for judicial review of the Plan and the master permits, claiming violations of the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act. The district court denied Friends of Animals' petition for review.

seed.consideration: Before approving the Plan, the Service should have compared the biological value of the habitats to be lost against the habitats where prairie dogs would be translocated or conserved, to ensure new sites had equivalent biological value.
seed.why_material: Because the Endangered Species Act permits a take only if impacts are mitigated to fully offset losses to the maximum extent practicable, and without comparing biological values the Service could not rationally conclude the losses would be offset.

10947182.situation:
CASE FILE

Parties: Defendant Kenneth M. Davis, charged with multiple offenses arising from a shooting; the prosecution is the United States (District of Columbia). Complaining witness Shadonna Nance and her two children, A.S. (age five) and P.N., are victims, along with another victim located in a car behind the shooter's vehicle.

I. THE INCIDENT

On the sunny afternoon of May 19, 2021, Shadonna Nance was driving with her two children on Eastern Avenue in Northeast Washington, D.C. As she approached the intersection of Eastern and Kenilworth Avenues, she attempted to merge into the right lane. She got very close to a car in the right lane, a gray Maserati, which she thought was letting her merge. The cars did not touch.

The driver of the second vehicle exited his vehicle, walked toward Ms. Nance's car until he was adjacent to its rear driver's side door, and fired a gun at Ms. Nance's car. As Ms. Nance attempted to drive away, she hit another car and then crashed into a light pole. After firing around seven shots at Ms. Nance's car, the shooter turned and fired more shots in the direction of the cars behind him. He then got back in his car, made a U-turn, and left the scene, driving off in the opposite direction. All of this was captured on a nearby surveillance camera.

One of the bullets injured Ms. Nance's left arm, and she had bullet fragments removed from her body at the hospital. A.S., age five, seated in the back of the car, sustained injuries to his hand from broken glass. P.N., seated in the front passenger seat, was not injured.

When Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) officers arrived, Ms. Nance told them the gunman was driving a gray two-door Maserati and was an older Black male, approximately six feet tall, weighing roughly 200 pounds, with a muscular build and a gray beard.

II. THE INVESTIGATION

The next day, as part of its initial investigation, MPD contacted a local Maserati dealership. A detective spoke by phone and then met in person with Anthony Johnson, a service director at the dealership. Mr. Johnson knew Mr. Davis from various service appointments Mr. Davis had made for his Maserati GranTurismo. Beginning around 2018, Mr. Davis dropped his Maserati off for service one to two times a year. Mr. Johnson identified dealership records indicating that Mr. Davis's Maserati was serviced and ready to be picked up on May 18, the day before the shooting. Mr. Johnson could not confirm that Mr. Davis picked up the car that day, but testified that Mr. Davis usually picked up his own car and that the car was gone from the dealership on May 19, the day of the shooting.

After viewing a video of the shooting with the detective, Mr. Johnson identified the gunman's Maserati as belonging to Mr. Davis. He noted multiple features of the Maserati in the video, including wheel rims that were "color matched" with the body of the car and the customized fixture of the license plate on the front of the car by a "tow hook" on the passenger side, which enabled him to identify it as Mr. Davis's car. Mr. Johnson did not identify Mr. Davis as the gunman in the video, but noted that the shooter had the same physical build as Mr. Davis.

Mr. Johnson also testified, though he did not tell the detective this, that he had interacted with Mr. Davis earlier in the day following the shooting when Mr. Davis came to the dealership. Mr. Davis came alone, but not in his GranTurismo. Mr. Davis asked how quickly the color of the wheels, or rims, on his GranTurismo could be changed. Although he did not specify a color, Mr. Davis was adamant that he needed the wheel color changed as quickly as possible. Mr. Johnson could not accommodate the request that day because it required making an appointment with a third-party vendor.

Eight days after the shooting, Ms. Nance selected Mr. Davis's picture from a police photo array and identified him as the gunman. She noted that "it was him," that she was "positive," and that her "heart [was] pounding." She later confirmed she got a "good look at the suspect's face," remembered the gunman's nose, and was "one hundred percent sure" Mr. Davis was the gunman.

Historical cell site location information (CSLI) indicated that Mr. Davis's cell phone connected with two cell towers near the crime scene around the time of the shooting.

The MPD issued a press release on June 2, 2021, identifying Mr. Davis as the suspected gunman. Officers began searching for Mr. Davis but, despite checking addresses associated with him and his family members, were unable to locate him. At the address of a woman who identified herself as Mr. Davis's mother, police found a Maserati in the garage covered with a tarp. Mr. Davis was eventually located in Costa Rica and returned to the United States on August 8, 2021.

III. CHARGES AND TRIAL

Mr. Davis was charged with multiple crimes related to the incident and tried before a jury.

The jury found Mr. Davis guilty of eight offenses:
(1) assault with intent to kill while armed (AWIKWA) with respect to Ms. Nance (D.C. Code §§ 22-401 & -4502);
(2) two counts of assault with a dangerous weapon (ADW) with respect to Ms. Nance's children, P.N. and A.S. (D.C. Code § 22-402);
(3) one count of ADW against another victim located in one of the cars behind Mr. Davis's; and
(4) four counts of possession of a firearm during a crime of violence (PFCOV) (D.C. Code § 22-4504(b)) in connection with the other four convictions.

IV. SENTENCING

The trial court sentenced Mr. Davis to 138 months for the AWIKWA conviction and 84 months for each ADW conviction, with all four convictions to run consecutively to each other, for a total of 390 months (32.5 years) of imprisonment. The court merged Mr. Davis's four PFCOV convictions and sentenced him to an additional 84 months, to run concurrently with the other sentences.

V. POSITIONS ON REVIEW

Mr. Davis contends that the trial court made several evidentiary errors; that there was insufficient evidence to convict him of one of the ADW counts; and that the court erred when sentencing him. The prosecution maintains the convictions and sentence.

seed.consideration: Whether the court retained discretion to impose concurrent rather than consecutive sentences and to depart from the voluntary guidelines, given that those guidelines are not binding on judges.
