10951893.situation:
CASE FILE

PARTIES AND SETTING

This matter concerns a residency dispute between a public school district (the District) and Mother, who enrolled her three Children in the District at Andrew W. Mellon Middle School (Middle School) for the 2024-25 school year. Mother is the co-owner of a three-bedroom house in Pittsburgh (Pittsburgh House), which she owns jointly with the Children's father, from whom she is estranged. The dispute centers on whether Mother resides at a one-bedroom apartment located within the District (Mt. Lebanon Apartment) such that the Children are entitled to attend District schools without payment of non-residency tuition.

GOVERNING STANDARDS

The District's Board Policy No. 200, Administrative Regulation No. 200-AR-0, and 200-AR Grievance Procedures require that a student's district of residence be the school district in which the student's parent(s)/guardian(s) reside. This requirement is stated to be consistent with Section 1302(a) of the Public School Code of 1949 (School Code), Act of March 10, 1949, P.L. 30, as amended, 24 P.S. § 13-1302(a). Mother's Residency/Enrollment Policy is also referenced as containing a notice provision.

ENROLLMENT AND SUPPORTING DOCUMENTS

In August 2024, Mother began the process to enroll the Children in the District. She used the address of the Mt. Lebanon Apartment as her home address (District Address) on the enrollment forms. At the time she applied for enrollment, Mother submitted the first page of a lease for the Mt. Lebanon Apartment, later followed by a full copy, and a renter's insurance policy to establish residency. Some correspondence between Mother and the District also references an apartment on Bower Hill Road as Mother's intended residence before she identified the Mt. Lebanon Apartment as her residence.

Certain enrollment documents listed a home address in Pittsburgh (Pittsburgh Address), corresponding to the Pittsburgh House, which Mother co-owns with the Children's father and has been unable to sell. Mother's Pennsylvania driver's license listed the Pittsburgh House as her home address. Enrollment paperwork submitted for each of the Children included proof of residency in the form of the driver's license, the renter's insurance policy, and the residential lease for the Mt. Lebanon Apartment.

RETURNED MAIL AND INVESTIGATION

On November 11, 2024, the District received a return envelope for mail sent to Mother at the District Address. The return envelope bore a label marked "RETURN TO SENDER," "ATTEMPTED – NOT KNOWN," and "UNABLE TO FORWARD," and contained a handwritten notation labeling the District Address as a "Vacant Apartment." The return of mail prompted the District to notify Mother of its intention to commence an investigation of her residency.

In furtherance of the investigation, School Principal Dr. Chris Wolfson (Principal Wolfson) and District Superintendent Melissa Friez (Superintendent Friez) surveilled Mother on November 14 and November 15, 2024. They observed Mother and Children using the Pittsburgh House to drive to and from the Middle School, but observed no entry to or from the Mt. Lebanon Apartment on these dates. Based on the investigation, the District concluded that Mother and Children did not reside in the District, and on November 18, 2024, sent Mother notice of a residency hearing.

Upon notice of the investigation, Mother responded with additional proof of residency documents, including an electric bill, invoices for furniture delivery to the District Address, and a photograph of the Children at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment. The electric bill was for electricity at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment but listed the Pittsburgh House as the mailing address.

RESIDENCY HEARING

A residency hearing was held on November 26, 2024, before an independent Hearing Officer. The District offered the testimony of Principal Wolfson and Superintendent Friez. Mother offered the testimony of a private service provider who assists her with the Children (Service Provider) and her own testimony.

Testimony of Principal Wolfson: In August 2024, Mother began the process to enroll the Children in the District. Mother submitted enrollment paperwork for each of the Children, which included proof of residency in the form of a Pennsylvania driver's license, a renter's insurance policy, and a residential lease for the Mt. Lebanon Apartment. District policy typically accepts a lease or home purchasing agreement as proof of residency. In this case, the District had the lease on file and was able to proceed with enrollment based on the information provided. Principal Wolfson received notice of the letter to Mother returned from the District Address, which prompted the investigation. Mother responded with additional documents, including an electric bill, invoices for furniture delivery to the District Address, and a photograph of the Children at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment. The electric bill for September and October 2024 was entered into the record and reflects minimal kWh usage of zero and 2.42 kilowatt hours for these dates, through October 13, 2024.

On the morning of November 14, 2024, Principal Wolfson waited across the street from the Mt. Lebanon Apartment until the general time that school started and did not observe Mother or Children come or go. He returned at the end of the school day on November 14 and observed no one. He had a view of the front of the building and a backdoor exiting into an alley. He repeated this surveillance in the same general time frame on the morning of the hearing, November 26, 2024, and did not observe Mother or Children come or go, but they arrived at the Middle School that morning. He undertook no other surveillance. Principal Wolfson also introduced the statement of a behavioral health therapist who works with the Children, which stated that she has delivered services at the Pittsburgh House but never at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment.

Testimony of Superintendent Friez: On November 14, 2024, Superintendent Friez surveilled Mother, observing and following from her own car as Mother drove the Children from after-school pick-up at the Middle School to the Pittsburgh House. She observed Mother and the Children exit the vehicle and enter the Pittsburgh House and stayed to observe for approximately 10 more minutes before leaving. The next morning, on November 15, 2024, she returned to the Pittsburgh House to observe Mother from her car. She observed Mother and the Children exit the Pittsburgh House at approximately 7:24 a.m., enter Mother's car, and arrive at the Middle School at 7:55 a.m. She took notes and photographs of the observations on November 14 and November 15, 2024, which were admitted at the hearing. These were the only two dates on which she observed Mother go in and out of the Pittsburgh House. Superintendent Friez never went inside the Mt. Lebanon Apartment.

Testimony of the Service Provider: The Service Provider has provided services to the Children for six years, including both in-home and at-school services. The Service Provider typically sees the Children monthly and communicates via phone calls, text, and email weekly, acting as a liaison between home, school, and any other services provided. The Service Provider had discussions with Mother about her desire to move into the District for six years, with Mother expressing that she likes the area and has family in the District. Mother informed the Service Provider that she leased the Mt. Lebanon Apartment but that the landlord needed to make changes that delayed move-in. The Service Provider met the Children at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment but could not recall whether the date of that visit was September or October 2024, guessing the date was probably September. The Service Provider did not spend much time in the Mt. Lebanon Apartment on that visit because it was still being worked on, and the apartment did not have all of the furniture or beds at that time.

Testimony of Mother: Mother signed the lease for the Mt. Lebanon Apartment on August 23, 2024. Although she signed the lease and paid rent beginning in August 2024, Mother and the Children faced complications with the move-in process, as the landlord continued to perform ongoing construction work, including replacement of flooring, addressing an electrical problem, ceiling work, and plumbing work. Mother ultimately did not receive the keys to the Mt. Lebanon Apartment until approximately October 20, 2024. Notwithstanding, Mother and the Children camped in the Mt. Lebanon Apartment before the arrival of furniture, pitching a tent and using sleeping bags.

Mother testified that she took the following steps to live in the Mt. Lebanon Apartment: (1) turned on the electricity and paid electric bills; (2) received Amazon packages; (3) obtained a rental insurance policy; (4) communicated with the landlord regarding renovations; (5) went to the post office and filled out a card listing the District Address for herself and her Children; (6) put the mailbox in the name of herself and the Children; (7) changed the garage where her car resides and updated her auto insurance with the District Address; (8) put together beds, benches, couches, and other furniture; and (9) installed security cameras. She explained that the mail was returned to the District because she had not yet properly updated the post office or put her mailbox in her name at the time of that mailing.

Mother initially estimated that she and the Children stayed overnight at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment three to four school nights a week, but clarified that this number is variable given circumstances in certain weeks. When asked to estimate the number of overnight stays since she obtained the keys on or about October 20, 2024, she could not offer an exact number, but when prompted to estimate within given ranges, she agreed the number of nights was greater than 10 but fewer than 20. She ultimately narrowed this number to probably around 10 nights so far, while recounting the timeline of circumstances that caused her and the Children to sleep elsewhere. She recalled that they did not stay in the Mt. Lebanon Apartment for a few days the week they received the keys because one of the Children had pneumonia. They also did not stay the following week because the refrigerator was down for one week. Mother admitted to staying overnight at the Pittsburgh House on November 14 and 15, the dates of Superintendent Friez's surveillance, as her son was sick and not in school. She also admitted to staying at the Pittsburgh House on the night before the hearing, as her son had oral surgery the day before the hearing, necessitating babysitters and help, and the Mt. Lebanon Apartment did not have gas on the day before the hearing. Mother explained that she and the Children have frequent reason to return to the Pittsburgh House, as she does not yet have sitters in Mt. Lebanon.

Mother testified that she has intended to move to the District for years, visiting open houses and communicating with realtors. She attempted to purchase a house in the District the prior summer but was outbid. She co-owns the Pittsburgh House with an estranged spouse, with whom she was in a domestic violence situation resulting in court filings. Her estranged spouse will not agree to sell the Pittsburgh House or sign off on paperwork regarding it. Mother's goal is to live in the District and eventually buy a house or larger apartment there. She has had difficulty with the Children's prior school district accommodating their special needs, further motivating her to move into the District.

ADJUDICATION

Following the hearing, the Hearing Officer issued a recommendation ruling in favor of the District, which the Board adopted as its own Adjudication by resolution on January 27, 2025. The Adjudication ruled that the initial determination of Mother's non-residency be sustained and ordered that Mother be responsible for the non-residency tuition charges for the 2024-25 school year.

The Adjudication concluded that the District had the burden of establishing that Mother did not reside in the Mt. Lebanon Apartment and that it met this difficult burden in large part due to the admissions of Mother. The Adjudication found that Mother admitted to staying only 10 nights in the Mt. Lebanon Apartment, and concluded that this admission, together with several other facts, established Mother's non-residency.

The Adjudication found that the evidence shows Mother did not reside in the Mt. Lebanon Apartment because she did not have access to the apartment between August 23 and October 20, 2024, and once she had a key she stayed only an estimated 10 nights between October 20 and November 26, 2024. It further found that the difficulties in transitioning the Children from the Pittsburgh House to the Mt. Lebanon Apartment, the presence of only one bedroom for Mother and three Children in the apartment, Mother's stated desire to leave the School District of Pittsburgh due to dissatisfaction, the electric bills showing minimal utility usage, and Mother's admissions regarding her inability to establish residency support the conclusion that Mother did not establish residency in the District between August 23, 2024, and the hearing on November 26, 2024.

As to credibility, the Adjudication concluded that Mother's testimony that she established residency at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment is not credible. It found that although Mother expressed a strong desire to establish residency, she confuses a desire with actually establishing a residence, and her evasiveness regarding how many nights she and the Children slept at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment made her not credible. The Adjudication found the Service Provider's recollection of having met the Children at the Mt. Lebanon Apartment in September 2024 not credible because Mother testified she did not receive the key until October 20, 2024. The Adjudication found Principal Wolfson and Superintendent Friez's testimony regarding their observations of the Mt. Lebanon Apartment and the Pittsburgh House credible.

The Board found that this case does not involve separated parents.

COMMON PLEAS PROCEEDINGS

Mother timely appealed the Adjudication to common pleas on February 27, 2025. On June 5, 2025, the District filed a Motion for a Hearing to Present After-Discovered Evidence (Motion for Hearing) related to video surveillance evidence allegedly unavailable at the time of the hearing. Mother filed a Brief in Opposition to the Motion for Hearing. Following a conference on May 22, 2025, common pleas ordered that the parties submit briefing on the merits of the appeal, denied the hearing request, and ordered that evidence is limited to what is already of record. The parties each submitted briefs, after which common pleas granted Mother's appeal by Order dated August 14, 2025.

The Order found that Mother admits the family was not living in the Mt. Lebanon Apartment until October 20, 2024. The Order stated that the hearing addressed the residency of the family for the period of October 20, 2024, through November 26, 2024, only. The Order noted that the Adjudication found Mother and Children stayed at the District Address on 10 nights out of 36 nights between October 20, 2024, and November 26, 2024, finding that this represented almost one-third of the time. Common pleas concluded that Mother's time spent overnight at the District Address was sufficient to establish a physical presence in the apartment.

POSTURE

The matter is before the reviewing court on the District's timely appeal from the common pleas Order granting Mother's appeal. The decision presently under review is the Adjudication of the Board sustaining the initial determination of non-residency and imposing non-residency tuition for the 2024-25 school year.

PARTIES' POSITIONS

The District argues that the burden of proof never shifted from Mother to the District, as Mother never met her initial burden of establishing residency. The District contends that common pleas' conclusion that Mother and Children established a sufficient physical presence in the District fails as a matter of law, where they stayed overnight at the District Address only approximately one-third of the relevant period. The District asserts that common pleas erred in finding Mother established residency in the face of substantial evidence of non-residency, such as the returned mail flagging the apartment as vacant and the electricity bill showing low usage. The District argues that common pleas erred in interpreting Section 1302 of the School Code in a manner that would permit a parent to be a resident of two or more school districts. The District further posits that common pleas rejected the credibility determinations of the Board, accepting Mother's testimony that she resides in the District as fact and crediting the Service Provider's testimony that the Board found incredible. Last, the District contends that common pleas erred by accepting a supplemental reproduced record from Mother and Children after having already ruled that the certified record was complete.

Mother responds that the District has waived certain arguments by raising them for the first time on appeal, including its arguments related to the burden of proof and whether common pleas' interpretation permits children to be enrolled in multiple school districts at once. Mother argues that the Adjudication concluded she should be responsible for tuition for the entire 2024-25 school year without regard to any change in her residency status between the date of the hearing and the end of the school year, and that this ruling was unsupported by the evidence. Mother asserts that common pleas correctly concluded that the District failed to produce substantial evidence that Mother and Children were not residents, as case law requires only a physical presence to establish residency, not a finding of domicile or primary residence. Mother also argues that the District violated its own Residency/Enrollment Policy by not giving her 60 school days' notice to establish residency before acting, and that this evidence is reviewable as a public record subject to judicial notice, even though common pleas did not consider it. Mother asserts that the District's factual and legal arguments did not establish non-residency, as the days she and the Children were observed outside the apartment resulted from unlivable apartment conditions, and none of the District's other proffered evidence negated her evidence of a physical presence at the District Address. Mother contends that the District's arguments that common pleas ignored credibility determinations or failed to consider all the evidence are unsupported.

RELIEF SOUGHT

The District seeks reinstatement of the Adjudication sustaining the determination of non-residency and holding Mother responsible for non-residency tuition charges for the 2024-25 school year. Mother seeks affirmance of the common pleas Order granting her appeal.

10953555.holding_quote: Bax argues that the district court erred by failing to consider whether Plaintiffs have an adequate remedy at law. We agree.
10953555.situation:
CASE FILE

Parties

Plaintiffs are three individual Missouri residents—Mary Holmes, Denise Davis, and Andrew Dallas—together with Empower Missouri, a nonprofit organization that describes itself as seeking to ensure that all Missourians "have access to adequate nutrition, quality healthcare, decent housing, and appropriate education."

The defendant is Jessica Bax, sued in her official capacity as Director of the Missouri Department of Social Services (DSS). The suit was initially filed against Robert Knodell, the Acting Director of DSS, who has since been replaced by Bax. DSS is solely responsible for administering the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in Missouri.

Statutory and Program Framework

Congress established SNAP "to safeguard the health and well-being of the Nation's population by raising levels of nutrition among low-income households." 7 U.S.C. § 2011. SNAP is federally funded and state administered. It provides eligible households a monthly benefit for food purchases. See 7 U.S.C. § 2014(a).

To receive SNAP benefits, an individual must submit an initial application and complete an interview. Once DSS registers an application, it instructs the applicant to contact its call center within five days to interview. Applicants are also permitted to interview in-person; once requested, the interview must be scheduled within five days. If an applicant does not interview within five days after applying, DSS notifies the applicant that an interview must be completed within 30 days or the application will be denied. DSS automatically denies an application if an individual does not complete an interview within 30 days of submission, regardless of the applicant's efforts to schedule an interview.

To maintain SNAP benefits, individuals must recertify their eligibility, typically on an annual basis. Recertification requires individuals to complete an application, an interview, and further verification if they report certain changes. Bax contends that DSS has a waiver from the federal government allowing it to "automatically forgo the interview requirement at recertification for households with no earned income in which all adult members are elderly or disabled." This waiver is not part of the record in this case.

DSS operates resource centers throughout Missouri where applicants are supposed to be able to "submit applications and supporting documentation, ask questions about their applications and benefits, and be interviewed as part of the application process."

Facts as to the Individual Plaintiffs

Mary Holmes: In January 2022, Holmes called DSS three times to request a SNAP application, but no one answered the phone. She then paid a family member to drive her to a resource center, submitted her application in-person, and asked to be interviewed that day. DSS refused her request and told her someone would call her in the next few days. She answered a call from DSS the next day but was never connected to a representative. Over the following month she called DSS at least eleven times attempting to interview. Despite enduring numerous holds of over two hours, she was never connected to a staff member. In February 2022, DSS denied her application for failure to interview. After Plaintiffs filed this suit, Holmes received an interview and was approved for SNAP benefits on March 20, 2023.

Andrew Dallas: Dallas has epilepsy, which impacts his daily functioning. He has received SNAP benefits since at least 2021. In December 2021, DSS received a document from Dallas entitled "Food Stamp Change Report," in which he explained that he has epilepsy and that he "cannot understand like normal people do. Please help! . . . I am disabled." DSS understood this note to be a request for a reasonable accommodation, but Dallas did not need to complete any forms at that time to continue receiving SNAP benefits. In January 2023, DSS mailed Dallas SNAP recertification paperwork and did not provide him any assistance. In early February 2023, Dallas called DSS roughly ten times to ask for help completing his recertification paperwork. He never connected with a representative due to long wait times and the main menu language prompts. After joining this lawsuit, Dallas received an interview and was approved for SNAP benefits. His benefits never lapsed.

Denise Davis: In November 2022, Davis applied for SNAP benefits online, but DSS did not register her application. DSS asserts that her application contained an incorrect social security number. In December 2022, she submitted a second SNAP application and called DSS several times a week attempting to interview. She never spoke to a DSS employee because DSS repeatedly deflected and disconnected her calls. More than once she waited on hold for over two hours before DSS's automated system disconnected her call due to high call volume. DSS denied her application for failure to interview. She then submitted a third application. Davis called DSS at least thirteen times and visited a resource center to try to interview, but never reached anyone at DSS. After joining this lawsuit, she received an interview and was approved for SNAP benefits.

Holmes, Davis, and Dallas all now receive SNAP benefits. They anticipate needing this assistance for years to come, which will require dealing with DSS and its benefits administration system.

Facts as to Empower Missouri

Empower Missouri is a nonprofit organization that purports to guarantee access to adequate nutrition. It contends that it devotes significant time and energy to "provide[] resources and information to anti-hunger advocates and communicate[] with DSS regarding agency failures in Missouri's administration of SNAP." From 2021 to 2023, it spent $96,000 on addressing issues that arose from DSS's administration of SNAP.

Claims

Plaintiffs bring four claims against Bax. They assert that her policies, practices, and procedures: (1) wrongfully deny applicants access to SNAP in violation of 7 U.S.C. §§ 2014(a) and 2020(e)(2)(B) and their accompanying regulations; (2) fail to ensure Missourians are able to apply for SNAP benefits on the first day they contact DSS in violation of 7 U.S.C. § 2020(e)(2)(B); (3) deprive Plaintiffs of fair access to SNAP benefits in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause; and (4) fail to provide reasonable accommodations in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

Relief Sought

Plaintiffs seek declaratory and injunctive relief.

Declaratory relief: Plaintiffs request that the court declare unlawful Bax's policies and practices of wrongfully denying initial and recertification SNAP applications; failing or refusing to allow households to apply for SNAP on the first day they contact DSS; subjecting SNAP applicants to arbitrary and inconsistent application processes that result in wrongful denials of benefits; excluding Plaintiffs from participation in the benefits, programs, services, and activities provided by DSS because of their disabilities; utilizing and adopting administrative practices that discriminate against Plaintiffs based on disability; and failing to adopt ADA grievance procedures.

Injunctive relief: Plaintiffs seek an order that Bax provide Holmes with an interview within three days; that the court preliminarily enjoin DSS to maintain in-person DSS resource center operations in compliance with the SNAP Act and the ADA; that Bax be enjoined from making any changes to DSS facility operations—including hours and staffing—until she adopts statewide policies to ensure that such changes do not violate the rights of SNAP applicants; that Bax cease denying SNAP applications for eligible individuals who have not been provided a meaningful opportunity to complete the application process; and that she adopt, implement, and monitor statewide policies and procedures that (1) guarantee all applicants a meaningful opportunity to complete all SNAP application requirements on the first day they contact DSS, (2) ensure that applicants and recipients with disabilities are provided reasonable accommodations, (3) notify SNAP applicants and recipients about the ADA's and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act's nondiscrimination requirements, and (4) provide a grievance procedure for prompt and equitable resolution of ADA and Section 504 complaints. They also request that Bax provide them with reasonable accommodations as appropriate.

Procedural Posture

The parties filed cross motions for summary judgment.

Plaintiffs' position: Plaintiffs argued that Bax violated the SNAP Act by wrongfully denying their applications for failure to interview and by preventing them from applying on the first day they contacted DSS. Holmes and Davis contended that Bax violated their due process rights. Dallas and Holmes contended that Bax violated their rights under the ADA.

Bax's position: Bax countered that no Plaintiff satisfied Article III standing, contending that Empower Missouri did not allege an injury and that the individual plaintiffs' claims are not redressable. She argued that the individual plaintiffs' claims were moot. She asserted that the SNAP Act does not provide a private right of action, and even if it did, DSS's policies and operations do not violate it. She further argued that she did not violate Plaintiffs' due process rights or their rights under the ADA.

Rulings Below

The district court granted Plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment and denied Bax's motion.

Standing and mootness: The district court concluded that Plaintiffs had Article III standing because they each "established an injury 'that is likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision.'" It reasoned that the individual plaintiffs are at substantial risk of losing their SNAP benefits and that Empower Missouri has been forced to divert resources because of DSS's unlawful policies and procedures. Because DSS's practices and policies have not changed, it concluded that Plaintiffs' claims are not moot.

Merits: The district court held that Bax's wrongful denials of Plaintiffs' SNAP applications violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause. It reasoned that Plaintiffs have a protected property interest in SNAP benefits and that DSS's wrongful denial of their applications for failure to interview deprived them of a benefit for which they were otherwise eligible. It further concluded that Bax violated the ADA by denying Dallas and Holmes meaningful access to SNAP because of their respective disabilities.

Remedy: The district court determined that permanent injunctive relief—requiring Bax to enact policies and procedures in compliance with the SNAP Act, the Due Process Clause, and the ADA—was appropriate. It ordered Bax to submit a proposed plan to address the shortcomings in DSS's administration of SNAP within 90 days. It ordered Bax to file with the court monthly statewide statistical reports regarding its application processing, and required that these reports also be filed with Missouri's legislative and executive branch members.

The district court then entered its remedial order and final judgment. It ordered that Bax "take whatever steps were necessary to reduce the average wait time . . . so that 90% of callers have no more than a 20-minute wait time" and "bring the number of applications which are rejected for failure to interview to no more than 20% of all applications." The order also required Bax to implement 26 additional operational requirements.

seed.consideration: Before granting a permanent injunction, whether the plaintiffs have an adequate remedy at law and whether the relief is narrowly tailored to redress only the named plaintiffs' injuries rather than imposing systemic statewide changes.
seed.why_material: Equitable relief is available only when there is no adequate legal remedy, and an injunction broader than necessary to give complete relief to the plaintiffs amounts to an impermissible universal injunction.

key.question: Did Empower Missouri suffer a cognizable injury based on diverted resources spent opposing DSS's SNAP administration?

key.label: Redressability of individual claims
key.question: Would the requested relief redress the individual plaintiffs' injuries despite its breadth?

key.label: Mootness after benefit approval
key.question: Are the individual plaintiffs' claims moot given they now receive SNAP benefits?

key.label: Eleventh Amendment/Ex parte Young
key.question: Does sovereign immunity bar the claims, or does the Ex parte Young exception apply?

key.label: SNAP Act private enforceability
key.question: Do 7 U.S.C. §§ 2014(a) and 2020(e)(2)(B) create rights enforceable under § 1983?

key.label: Due process property interest
key.question: Did wrongful denial of SNAP applications deprive Holmes and Davis of a protected property interest without adequate process?

key.label: ADA failure to accommodate
key.question: Did DSS deny Dallas and Holmes reasonable accommodations because of their disabilities?

key.question: Did plaintiffs establish actual success, irreparable harm, balance of harms, and public interest for injunctive relief?

10954673.situation:
PARTIES: State of Utah v. Connelley. Complaining witness identified as Jessica.

UNDERLYING INCIDENT (per the State's evidence): Jessica encountered Connelley, a stranger to her, while she was walking home late at night through a construction site. Connelley grabbed her by the neck and strangled her. When Jessica tried to fight back, Connelley pulled out a pocketknife and threatened her. He then forced her to perform oral sex on him and anally sodomized her. After he was done, Connelley threatened to take Jessica's phone and wallet. She begged him not to take her wallet and offered him her credit cards instead. He also forced Jessica to give him her car keys.

DEFENSE ACCOUNT (Connelley's trial testimony): Connelley testified that when he asked Jessica what time it was, she laughed at him as if he were 'beneath her.' He followed her and told her she was a 'fuckin' bitch' and that maybe he should 'kick her ass.' He claimed Jessica then suggested that he have sex with her instead. He said she voluntarily performed oral sex on him and allowed him to have anal sex with her. He testified that after a brief conversation following the anal sex, Jessica allowed him to use her phone. The phone case had a pocket for credit cards, and Connelley took one, intending to steal it. He testified that Jessica told him that card did not work and voluntarily gave him two additional cards.

CHARGES: Connelley was charged with two counts of aggravated sexual assault, one count of aggravated assault, one count of aggravated robbery (for the car keys), and three counts of unlawful acquisition of a credit card (one for each credit card).

MERGER ISSUE AT TRIAL: Connelley argued that the three counts of unlawful acquisition of credit cards should merge into the aggravated robbery charge. The district court disagreed with this position.

VERDICT: The jury convicted Connelley of all charges.

SENTENCING HEARING:

PSI corrections. The court asked defense counsel whether any corrections or additions were needed on the PSI. Defense counsel identified errors in several statements in the PSI: (1) that Connelley's two 'prosocial' friends have criminal backgrounds; (2) that he 'doesn't have regular communication with any family members, except his mother' and that 'many in his family are substance abusers or criminals'; and (3) that he had '[a]t least six violations during [his] current incarceration.' After defense counsel identified these concerns, the court asked, 'Okay. Anything else?' Counsel responded, 'No, Your Honor, that's it.' The court did not make any findings regarding the alleged inaccuracies and proceeded with the sentencing hearing.

State's position. The State emphasized Connelley's history of 'victimizing people' over many decades. It stated that Connelley had 'taken no accountability,' that he was someone who had 'done nothing but caused problems to society' and 'victimized people to all sorts of extremes, just constantly.' The State asked the court to impose the maximum sentences on all charges and to run the sentences consecutively.

Victim testimony. Jessica testified about the impact of Connelley's actions. She said she believed she was going to die when he attacked her and that she is now 'afraid to leave [her] house or to go anywhere, especially alone and especially at night.' She said she has experienced insomnia, nightmares, flashbacks, and panic attacks, and that she suffered a lot of physical pain after the assault.

Defense position. Defense counsel asked the court to show leniency based on Connelley's age, pointing out that because Connelley is fifty-two years old, even concurrent sentencing would likely result in an effective 'life sentence without possibility of parole.'

COURT'S SENTENCING DETERMINATIONS: The court observed that Connelley had 'a criminal history that goes back almost three decades' and that the attack 'was especially brutal' and caused serious harm to Jessica. The court found that imposing any sentence less than fifteen years to life on the aggravated sexual assault convictions would 'not be in the interests of justice.' The court imposed sentences of five years to life on the aggravated robbery conviction, zero to five years on the aggravated assault conviction, and zero to five years on each of the unlawful acquisition convictions.

The court ordered that the sentences run consecutively to each other and to the sentences imposed against Connelley in two other criminal cases. The court stated that it had 'considered the gravity and the circumstances of the offenses, the number of victims, [and] the history, character, and rehabilitative needs' of Connelley. The court again pointed to Connelley's lengthy criminal history in both the juvenile and adult criminal system, and noted that Connelley had already had many previous opportunities to rehabilitate himself. The court characterized the incident as 'a violent and disturbing attack . . . on a complete stranger' and stated that the violence inflicted on Jessica was 'horrendous.' The court observed that Connelley's version of events, which he had 'doubled down' on, was 'just not credible,' and found it troubling that Connelley had 'created this narrative that defies credulity' and that he 'believe[d] that that's what happened.' The court expressed the view that if Connelley were out of custody, he would 'attack someone else again,' and stated that Connelley was a danger to the public, had been for almost three decades, and would continue to be. The court explained that Connelley's criminal history and attitude, the violence he inflicted, and the court's concerns about public safety demonstrated that leniency was not appropriate.

10960501.situation:
CASE FILE: Moore v. Moore — Divorce, Property Division, and Child Support

PARTIES
- Plaintiff/Wife: April Moore ("April"), a self-employed attorney who operated her own law firm and later became a W-2 employee. She initiated the divorce.
- Defendant/Husband: Robert Dean Moore ("Robert"), a high-income earner. He counterclaimed for divorce.
- One minor child, born 2014.
- A custodian of two custodial accounts held for the child's benefit was at one point a party to the action and was later dismissed.

I. BACKGROUND: MARRIAGE, CHILD, AND DIVORCE (2013–2016)
April and Robert married in 2013 and had a child in 2014. During the marriage they maintained separate residences: April lived in a home in Dublin, Ohio ("the Dublin home"), and Robert lived in a home in Belmont, Ohio ("the Belmont home"). April owned a home in Vero Beach, Florida prior to the marriage ("April's Vero Beach home"). The parties bought a second Vero Beach home in 2014 ("Robert's Vero Beach home"). In mid-2015 the parties purchased a home in New Albany, Ohio ("the New Albany home"). They soon began steps toward ending the marriage. In January 2016, April sued for divorce and Robert counterclaimed.

II. TEMPORARY SUPPORT (2016 Agreed Order)
Under an agreed temporary support order, Robert was responsible for routine expenses of the parties' Ohio and Florida residences, insurance for the parties' many vehicles, health insurance, and all of the child's routine expenses. April was responsible for her own personal expenses. Robert was to pay April $15,000 per month directly, with $7,500 designated general child support and $7,500 designated reimbursement for the child's nannies.

III. DIVORCE TRIAL AND PRE-DECREE PROCEEDINGS (2016–2021)
In October 2016, April dismissed her divorce complaint and stipulated she would not seek spousal support. The parties agreed to a shared parenting plan, adopted by the court in a shared parenting decree in December 2016. The matter proceeded to trial on Robert's counterclaim over a few dozen days from October 2016 to October 2017. Near the end of trial, in August 2017, April filed a motion for temporary and permanent spousal support.

Post-trial proceedings were protracted, with the parties filing dozens of motions. A portion of the post-trial litigation concerned disestablishing Robert's parentage of April's new baby and cross-accusations of contempt and requests for sanctions.

The parties filed motions to modify the 2016 agreed temporary support order. In January 2020, a magistrate granted each party's motion in part and adjusted Robert's temporary support obligation, with changes focused on mitigating the parties' inability to collaborate on bill payment or reimbursement. The magistrate removed Robert's obligation to reimburse April for the unspecified costs of the child's routine expenses; instead, the magistrate increased Robert's monthly support from $15,000 to $19,000, ordering him to pay $10,000 monthly child support through the Franklin County Child Support Enforcement Agency ("CSEA") and $9,000 monthly directly to April for nannies and other child-related expenses, effective January 1, 2020. The magistrate also removed Robert's obligation to reimburse April for all bills and routine costs of the marital properties; instead, April became responsible for routine costs of the Dublin home and one Vero Beach home, and Robert for the New Albany and Belmont homes and the other Vero Beach home. April filed various motions to set aside the January 2020 order or modify temporary support anew, all eventually mooted by the May 2021 divorce decree.

IV. NEW ALBANY HOME (Pre-Decree)
The parties purchased the New Albany home in May 2015 for $1.65 million in cash from an account later determined to be 95.04 percent marital property and 4.96 percent Robert's separate property. Early in the divorce proceedings in 2016, Robert moved for permission to sell the home, stating it was vacant and April would not allow him access. The parties stipulated Robert would sell the property. It remained on the market from 2017 to 2019, during which April would not agree to reduce the price below $1.65 million. April eventually relented, and in 2020 the house sold for $1.2 million, yielding net proceeds of $1,116,485.03. Robert claimed he spent $223,203.00 toward the sale. The parties stipulated Robert would be reimbursed $35,000.00 for repair expenses related to the sale. The parties had previously stipulated April would pay Robert $30,000.00 in attorney fees related to April's October 2016 attempt to disqualify Robert's attorneys, and the court ruled that $30,000.00 would be subtracted from April's share of sale proceeds. Of the $1,116,485.03, the court awarded $59,520 to Robert for his separate interest and $35,000.00 for repair expenses, divided the remaining $1,021,965.03 equally, and moved $30,000.00 from April's side to Robert's, totaling $480,982.52 to April and $635,502.51 to Robert.

V. THE MAY 4, 2021 DIVORCE DECREE
The divorce decree was filed May 4, 2021. The trial court set a de facto termination date of the marriage as January 30, 2016. The court determined the parties' separate and marital interests in assets including three Ohio residences, additional residential real estate, two Florida residences, millions of dollars in various bank accounts, approximately ten vehicles, personal property, retirement accounts, and Robert's various multi-million dollar bonuses, stock shares, and dividends. It determined separate and marital obligations in debts, including April's 2013 tax liability, debt for private jet services, and debts and expenses related to residential properties.

The court denied April's motion for spousal support, noting she had expressly waived spousal support in October 2016. It denied April's request for Robert to reimburse her for certain bills she paid during the divorce, reasoning that Robert had paid most of the marital property expenses since 2016, and finding April had improperly demanded reimbursement for her own personal expenses and expenses Robert originally paid, which the court described as "a frivolous double dip that demonstrates [April's] lack of respect for this Court's ethics and intelligence."

The court noted it had entered a shared parenting decree in December 2016, and finalized the plan by addressing outstanding financial decisions, including child support. The court determined Robert's annual income for child support was $7,478,043. It found April's reported income from her law firm lacked credibility, citing inconsistencies and improprieties in the firm's bookkeeping and April's efforts to withhold information about alleged expenses. Because April had not provided credible income evidence, the court estimated her income from yearly cash flows in her personal bank statements and determined April's annual income for child support was $359,687 (the court used the term "imputed," which was later characterized as a terminology issue).

The court believed it was required to determine child support by plugging the incomes into its basic child support schedule worksheet, calculating Robert's basic obligation at $37,710.49 per month. It rejected Robert's argument that support should be $0 to $7,500.00 per month, finding he lacked an accurate understanding of the child's needs or lifestyle. It rejected April's argument for $100,000.00 per month, noting she failed to document her "extraordinary" budget, which the court found "more related to how [April] would like to live than how [the child] actually lives." The court noted April's budget included only $2,600 monthly in expenses specific to the child, apart from $10,300.00 per month for nannies.

The court held the worksheet amount was presumed proper under R.C. 3119.03. After considering the child's needs and lifestyle, it concluded the worksheet amount was not inappropriate or unjust and that no deviations were appropriate, save a monthly reduction of $30.77 for cash medical support. It ordered Robert to pay the child's private school tuition and health insurance, and ordered the parties to split the child's other school and extracurricular expenses and any extraordinary medical expenses, with Robert paying 70 percent and April 30 percent. At the beginning of the decision the court indicated the support order would not be retroactive, but by the end held the effective date of the child support order would be January 1, 2020.

VI. FIRST APPEAL RULINGS (Moore II, 2022) — GOVERNING PRIOR MANDATES
Both parties appealed the decree. On the prior appeal, the reviewing court's rulings established the following, which govern the proceedings on remand:
- Robert's Vero Beach property: the trial court mistakenly awarded April half the $2.6 million value of the property instead of half the $1.7 million stipulated marital interest; that discrete portion was reversed and remanded with instructions to correct the award amount. A reversal did not require re-evaluation of the entirety of the marital property.
- Child support: the $37,710.49 monthly calculation was contrary to law because it applied the rubric for combined incomes up to the statutory maximum ($150,000.00, now $336,467.04) under R.C. 3119.021, rather than being determined on the unique facts under R.C. 3119.04 for combined incomes exceeding the maximum. The trial court was to revisit the child support decision on remand using the proper analysis. As to the effective date, the January 1, 2020 retroactive date conflicted with the decree's earlier statement that the order would not be retroactive; the court was to resolve its conflicting statements, without any particular starting date being addressed.
- Debt allocation: the trial court incorrectly made April responsible for 100 percent, rather than 50 percent, of the $435,695.22 jet services debt, the $36,670.36 payment toward April's 2013 tax liability, and April's $20,459.99 withdrawal from a marital account. These were to be corrected on remand.
- New Albany property: the trial court valued it at the time of the 2020 sale rather than at the de facto termination date of January 1, 2016. This discrete portion was reversed and remanded with instructions to "establish a value for the New Albany property as of the de facto termination date and adjust the related allocations as it then finds appropriate."
- Attorney fees: Robert's assignment of error challenging the $775,000.00 attorney fee award to April was overruled.
- April's argument regarding calculation of her income was mooted by the child support reversal. Her remaining assignments were overruled, and her contention that the decree was not a final appealable order was rejected.

VII. PROCEEDINGS ON REMAND (2022–2023)
Before addressing the remand, the trial court handled numerous motions filed during and after the appeal. April filed motions in February 2022 and January 2023 to compel Robert to respond to discovery requests related to child support, Robert's financial information, and other matters. In June 2022, Robert moved to suspend or escrow his monthly child support. Later in June 2022, April moved to modify the temporary child support order and establish a final child support order, arguing the parties' incomes had changed since January 2020 and that the court should hold a hearing.

The magistrate allowed the parties to submit narrative affidavits and exhibits on temporary child support, and held (Nov. 18, 2022 Order) that the "issues that were remanded" would be determined based on the trial record and consistent with the appellate instructions.

April's child support evidence included documentation indicating Robert may have earned over $10 or 11 million per year in 2017, 2019, and 2020, and over $16 million in 2018. She sought to compel discovery to verify Robert's more recent income. April reported her income (per a licensed CPA's tax documentation) as $58,810 in 2019, $38,484 in 2020, and $160,470 in 2021. She became a W-2 employee on October 24, 2022, at an annual salary of $160,000 plus a monthly vehicle stipend. April asserted the child's support and maintenance required $13,400 per month for shelter, $4,200 for a nanny, and $3,000 for food — $20,600 per month total — plus additional amounts at the court's discretion based on lifestyle. She argued additional discovery was needed to assess Robert's lifestyle, noting Robert and the child regularly travel by private jet.

Robert asserted April's 2016-2017 trial evidence showed the child's monthly expenses totaled around $12,500, most for nanny expenses, and argued current income was unnecessary because R.C. 3119.04 for families earning over the statutory maximum focuses on the needs and living standards of the child and parents.

The magistrate (Feb. 21, 2023 decision) set temporary child support at $14,200 per month, effective January 1, 2023. It calculated the statutory baseline from the 2016-2017 trial-record income evidence, noting current income would have only a negligible effect on the baseline. It awarded more than baseline based on current information about the child's expenses and "the substantial disparity in the parties' respective incomes."

April moved to set aside the magistrate's decision and for a full child support hearing. The trial court (June 7, 2023 judgment entry) denied these and other motions, approving the magistrate's temporary support order as "fair and reasonable," while holding the final child support order would be based exclusively on the trial record. It denied April's motions for updated financial information, reasoning that "there has not yet been a final order since the support issue is pending remand from the Court of Appeals" and "[t]here cannot be a change of circumstances for which discovery could be appropriate until a final order is issued."

VIII. JUNE 12, 2023 DECISION UPON REMAND
The court adjusted the May 4, 2021 decree per the appellate instructions. It reduced April's obligations for jet services, tax payments, and account withdrawals to $217,847.61, $18,355.18, and $10,229.99, respectively. It reduced April's award for Robert's Vero Beach property from $1.3 million to $863,448.00. As to the New Albany property, the court determined Robert had a separate property interest of $81,840.00 and was owed $35,000.00 for sale-related improvements and $30,000.00 for attorney fees. It observed that although the property was valued at $1.65 million in 2016, "appraisals are estimates of valuation and not necessarily supported by market conditions," and found it would not be "equitable to blindly shift the burden of any market loss, or to award the benefit of any market gain, to a particular party." Of the $1,116,485.03 net proceeds, it awarded $484,822.52 to April and $631,662.51 to Robert.

The court re-evaluated child support per the appellate guidance. It noted the standard monthly obligation for the statutory maximum combined income level of $150,000.00 was $1,239.00 and for $336,467.04 was $1,926.00. It observed that to award less than those amounts, it would be required under R.C. 3119.04(B) to find such a high amount against the best interest of one or more parties and to include supporting findings. It held there was no reason to award less than the statutory amount and that the facts supported an upward deviation. It considered April's expense lists in Exhibits BB, XXX, and YYY from the 2016-2017 trial, noting Exhibit BB included only $2,600 in monthly child-specific expenses apart from $10,300 for two nannies. Subtracting the cost of one nanny, it found monthly expenses of $7,750 for the child. On cost of living, it held it equally plausible the child would have lived in Franklin County or Belmont County had the parties remained married. The court concluded Robert's child support should be $8,500 per month, plus 100 percent of school tuition and health insurance and 70 percent of school expenses, extracurricular activities, and health care expenses. It maintained the January 1, 2020 effective date and incorporated all remaining portions of the original decree unchanged.

IX. JUNE 21, 2023 ENTRY
In a separate entry, the court modified a portion of the decree relating to a restraining order to allow the custodian of two custodial accounts to withdraw up to $1,005,000 and dismissed him as a party.

X. SUBSEQUENT PROCEEDINGS (2023–2025)
The parties' appeals of the June 2023 entries were dismissed for lack of a final appealable order (Moore III, docketed Aug. 24, 2023): the June 12 entry was not final because the court retained jurisdiction to allow CSEA to recalculate child support and resolve disputes about overpayment; the June 7 entry was interlocutory; and April failed to show the June 21 entry affected a substantial right requiring immediate appeal.

Robert moved to reduce the final property division award to a lump sum judgment. On August 21, 2023, the court granted the motion, holding April owed Robert $261,342, and denied April's request to redesignate a portion of Robert's childcare-related payments as a gift rather than child support. April's appeal was dismissed for lack of a final order (Moore IV) because the child support overpayment issue remained unresolved.

Robert then moved to reduce his child support overpayment to a lump sum judgment, and April moved for a comprehensive de novo valuation and division of marital property. On November 21, 2023, after reviewing CSEA records, the court determined Robert's overpayments totaled $303,470.81. It denied Robert's request for a lump sum judgment, instead ordering that Robert's monthly child support be reduced by $3,000 until the overage was satisfied. It denied April's motion for full reconsideration of the property division, noting its jurisdiction to alter the property division was limited to the matters on remand from Moore II. April's appeal of the November 2023 entry was dismissed for lack of a final order (Moore V) because, although the overpayment was resolved, the court needed to incorporate its piecemeal judgments into one final judgment under Civ.R. 75(F).

On remand, April moved for reconsideration of the June 2023 child support calculation and for an evidentiary hearing on updated finances, needs, and lifestyles of the parents and child. Robert argued consideration of new information was outside the Moore II mandate. The court (Jan. 3, 2025 judgment entry) denied April's motion, holding the June 12, 2023 entry was a final order not subject to reconsideration and that reconsideration was not warranted because "the record on remand was clear that the original trial record would be the factual basis for the decision following remand."

The court asked the parties to propose a solution for creating a final appealable order and to draft a proposed final order jointly or separately. The parties did not agree. April's proposed order stated the May 2021 decree would be vacated in full, the parties would conduct discovery and proceed to an evidentiary hearing on child support, the court would conduct a comprehensive division of marital assets and debts, and would include those and other findings in a future judgment. Robert's proposed order incorporated the June 7, 12, and 21, 2023, August 21 and November 21, 2023, and January 3, 2025 entries, plus all unaffected portions of the May 4, 2021 decree. The court's ultimate order followed Robert's proposal, incorporating the undisturbed portions of the 2021 decree and all subsequent entries by reference.

XI. GOVERNING STANDARDS AND STATUTES INVOKED
- R.C. 3119.021 (basic child support schedule for combined incomes up to the statutory maximum, $150,000.00, now $336,467.04).
- R.C. 3119.03 (worksheet amount presumed proper).
- R.C. 3119.04 and R.C. 3119.04(B) (determination of support for combined incomes exceeding the statutory maximum, based on the needs and standard of living of the child and parents; findings required to award less than the schedule maximum).
- R.C. 3105.171 (division of marital and separate property).
- Civ.R. 75(F) (requirement of a single final judgment resolving all property).
- R.C. 2505.02 (final appealable order).

XII. ISSUES PRESENTED FOR REVIEW OF THE TRIAL COURT'S RULINGS
1. Whether the court erred in failing to consider current income, needs, and lifestyle as required by R.C. 3119 and in failing to hold evidentiary hearings.
2. Whether the court erred in failing to apply the correct version of R.C. 3119.04 and in failing to follow the statute's procedural requirements.
3. Whether the court erred in setting child support at $8,500 per month without considering all requirements of R.C. 3119.04.
4. Whether the court erred in applying its child support decrease backward in time and in granting Robert repayment of more than $300,000 in child support and $153,000 in other support.
5. Whether the court erred in failing to award ownership of the New Albany home to Robert and in failing to establish a de facto date marital value.
6. Whether the court erred in modifying property division awards set out in the decree, and did so while lacking jurisdiction.
7. Whether the court erred in failing to comprehensively divide all property as required by R.C. 3105.171 and in awarding an inequitable property division to April without justification.

10961452.situation:
MATTER: Parada Calderon v. Blanche — Immigration removal proceedings; motion to reopen for CAT protection.

PARTIES: Petitioner is Parada (Parada Calderon), an applicant for protection from removal to El Salvador. The government respondent is the agency (Blanche). Refugees International appeared as amicus curiae in support of Parada; no amicus briefs were submitted advocating for a quantitative evidence requirement.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY:

Parada was placed in removal proceedings in 2023. In February 2024, an Immigration Judge (IJ) denied his application for protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT). Parada appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA). The BIA remanded the record to the IJ for further proceedings, finding that the IJ had erred by (1) refusing to consider certain country conditions evidence and (2) failing to adequately explain why she had afforded reduced weight to an expert report.

On remand, the IJ denied Parada's request to reopen the record and denied his application for CAT protection. Parada appealed that decision to the BIA, which denied the appeal. Parada then filed a petition for review of the BIA's decision.

Parada separately pursued applications for asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under CAT; review of the BIA's denial of those applications was sought in Petition No. 24-7433.

MOTION TO REOPEN:

While his petition was pending, on February 24, 2025, Parada filed a motion to reopen his removal proceedings, seeking to submit additional evidence of torture in El Salvador. The motion was filed two days after the 90-day deadline. The BIA deemed the motion timely after equitably tolling the deadline based on ineffective assistance of Parada's prior lawyer.

BIA'S RULING ON THE MOTION TO REOPEN (decision under review):

The BIA denied the motion to reopen on the merits.

The BIA acknowledged that Parada submitted "new evidence provid[ing] more recent information on the treatment of deportees upon return to El Salvador," and found that Parada "demonstrated a reasonable likelihood that he could be detained in El Salvador under the current state of exception."

The BIA nonetheless dismissed some of the evidence submitted in support of the motion, including an expert report's descriptions of "deplorable conditions of men in prison," on the basis that "anecdotes—no matter how disturbing—can't substitute for quantitative evidence, which is what CAT requires."

The BIA rejected "the majority of the evidence" Parada submitted on the ground that this evidence was "not based on new or previously unavailable evidence but reflect[ed] the continuation of abuse of suspected gang members under the state of exception on March 27, 2022, which was prior to [Parada's] individual hearing."

Based on the evidence it did consider, the BIA concluded that "the evidence does not show a reasonable likelihood that [Parada] would be able to establish that it is more likely than not that he would be tortured if detained," and denied the motion to reopen.

BACKGROUND — STATE OF EXCEPTION:

Parada's individualized risk of torture is set against the backdrop of an extreme crackdown on civil liberties in El Salvador known as the "State of Exception." In March 2022, Nayib Bukele, President of El Salvador, initiated the State of Exception: an emergency state of affairs that "limit[s] constitutional protections and grant[s] vast power to the country's security forces." The State of Exception went into effect March 27, 2022, before Parada's individual hearing.

GOVERNING STANDARDS INVOKED:

- CAT protection standard: whether it is more likely than not that the applicant would be tortured if removed (here, if detained in El Salvador).
- Motion to reopen standard: reopening requires new or previously unavailable evidence; the 90-day filing deadline applies but may be equitably tolled (here, based on ineffective assistance of counsel).
- The BIA applied a requirement that CAT claims be supported by "quantitative evidence" rather than anecdotal accounts.

RELIEF SOUGHT: Parada petitioned for review of the BIA's denial of his motion to reopen his removal proceedings.

seed.consideration: Whether the agency, before deciding, weighed the totality of qualitative evidence—including all three expert reports and country-conditions evidence—rather than demanding statistical or quantitative proof of the likelihood of torture.
seed.why_material: Because CAT's implementing regulations require consideration of all evidence relevant to future torture, imposing a quantitative-evidence requirement imposed a nearly insurmountable and legally erroneous burden on the applicant.

key.label: Reasonable likelihood of detention
key.question: Did Parada show a reasonable likelihood he could be detained in El Salvador under the State of Exception?

key.label: New or previously unavailable evidence
key.question: Was Parada's proffered evidence new and unavailable at the former hearing, as required for reopening?

key.label: Prison conditions as torture
key.question: Do the harsh conditions of confinement in Salvadoran prisons amount to torture rather than lesser mistreatment?

key.label: Governmental intent or acquiescence
key.question: Did Salvadoran officials intend to torture detainees or acquiesce in such abuse?

key.label: Likelihood of individualized torture
key.question: Did the evidence show it is more likely than not that Parada himself would be tortured if detained?

key.label: Prima facie eligibility for reopening
key.question: Did Parada's evidence establish prima facie eligibility for CAT deferral to warrant reopening?

key.label: Weight of expert report
key.question: How much probative weight should be given to Dr. Montgomery's expert report describing prison conditions?

10961455.situation:
CASE FILE

Applicant: Mbueno-Vita (proceeding with his family)
Proceeding type: Application for asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT)
Country of removal at issue: Angola

I. PARTIES AND POSTURE

This matter comes before the Immigration Judge (IJ) on the application of Mbueno-Vita and his family for asylum, withholding of removal, and CAT relief. The application was filed timely with the assistance of pro bono counsel. Mbueno-Vita appeared pro se at both of his merits hearings. He was the only person to testify during the proceeding. His wife, Aniance, was present in the courtroom for both hearings but did not testify.

II. APPLICANT'S ACCOUNT (as recounted in the proceeding)

Mbueno-Vita states that he is a member of UNITA, a national political party in Angola that opposes the current ruling party, the People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola ("MPLA"). He states that on multiple occasions the Angolan police and military harmed him because of his political activism.

June 14, 2019 rally. Mbueno-Vita attended a rally calling for the recognition and legalization of the Angolan Renaissance Party ("PRA-JA") as a national political party. After the rally ended, he boarded a bus with other rally attendees to return home. En route, the bus was stopped by Angolan police. The police began firing their weapons at the rally attendees, killing at least two people. As Mbueno-Vita attempted to exit the bus, a police officer hit him in the back of his right leg with a rifle. Mbueno-Vita sought medical attention for his injury. Following this incident, he continued to engage in political activity and attended two additional rallies in support of PRA-JA and the broader coalition of opposition parties.

May 8, 2021 rally. Mbueno-Vita participated in his fourth rally opposing the Angolan government. He was tear-gassed and arrested by the Angolan military along with approximately twenty other people. He was loaded onto a truck and transported to an unofficial police compound. At this "black site," he states he was tortured for two days. Officers beat him and walked and stomped on him until he had difficulty breathing. One detainee died during this time and others were badly injured. Before releasing Mbueno-Vita, the police warned him and the other detainees that if they told anyone about the death of the man in detention, they would also be killed.

Events after release. Despite this threat, Mbueno-Vita publicly denounced the death of the man at the "black site" shortly after his release. In October 2021, Angolan military personnel came to Mbueno-Vita's home but left when they saw his neighbors outside. Later that night, the military personnel went to the home of another man in the neighborhood whom they believed had also revealed details of the imprisonment and death. The military personnel killed that man and raped his wife.

Flight and departure. When Mbueno-Vita learned of the other man's murder, he went into hiding. He lived in a church, which he would leave only occasionally to see his family. After more than five months in hiding, Mbueno-Vita and his family fled to Kanfufu in the Luanda Norte province of Angola. He remained in hiding in Kanfufu with his family for another four months until they were able to leave Angola in June 2022. They entered the United States in September 2022.

III. THE IJ'S DECISION

The IJ denied Mbueno-Vita's application for asylum, withholding of removal, and CAT protection.

Adverse credibility. The IJ made an adverse credibility determination based on four distinct grounds. The IJ found that Mbueno-Vita's corroborating evidence did not rehabilitate his testimony.

CAT protection. The IJ denied CAT protection because Mbueno-Vita's claim was "primarily based upon testimony" that the IJ found not credible, and because the record did not contain sufficient evidence to establish a particularized risk of torture independent of the testimony found not credible.

Internal relocation. The IJ also determined that Mbueno-Vita could internally relocate to avoid any future harm.

IV. THE BIA'S DECISION

The BIA dismissed Mbueno-Vita's appeal, citing the same rationales as the IJ. The BIA affirmed that Mbueno-Vita did not provide credible testimony and concluded that the IJ's findings were "based on specific and cogent reasons supported by the record." The BIA also concluded that, notwithstanding the adverse credibility determination, the record lacked sufficient evidence that Mbueno-Vita faced a particularized risk of torture, and indicated that internal relocation was possible.

V. RELIEF SOUGHT

Mbueno-Vita seeks asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture.

VI. DUE PROCESS CONTENTIONS

Mbueno-Vita raises due process arguments in connection with the proceeding, including an argument tied to an alleged violation, which the applicable standard measures by whether the "outcome of the proceeding may have been affected by the alleged violation." Certain due process arguments were not raised before the BIA.

10931963.holding_quote: Here, the BCNR ran afoul of § 3301 by failing to explicitly or implicitly identify any duties “reasonably . . . expected” of an Infantry Unit Leader in its 2023 Decision.
10931963.situation:
PARTIES

Plaintiff/Petitioner: William Olas Bee, a former member of the U.S. Marine Corps.

Defendant/Respondent: The United States, represented on behalf of the Marine Corps ("agency") and involving records held by the Department of the Navy and the Department of Veterans Affairs ("VA").

SERVICE HISTORY

Mr. Bee enlisted in the U.S. Marine Corps in 1999. He served until his voluntary discharge on April 1, 2013. His initial "primary military occupation specialty" ("PMOS"), also called a "rate," was "Infantry Rifleman." A PMOS identifies a marine's primary skills within the Marine Corps' career-designation system, the "Military Occupational Specialty" ("MOS").

Mr. Bee deployed to Afghanistan four times during his service. During his third deployment, he suffered a major head injury. Following that deployment, he was diagnosed with a "[p]otential [traumatic brain injury] with persistent symptoms."

During his fourth and final deployment, from December 2009 through June 2010, Mr. Bee was wounded by explosions of multiple improvised explosive devices, which killed two fellow marines. After this deployment, in 2010, he was diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury ("TBI") and post-traumatic stress disorder ("PTSD").

In June 2010, Mr. Bee returned to the United States from Afghanistan and was placed on limited duty effective June 21, 2010. Around September 2010, he was removed from limited duty and subsequently promoted from sergeant to staff sergeant, with his PMOS changing from Infantry Rifleman to "Infantry Unit Leader."

In November 2010, following his promotion, Mr. Bee was transferred to the Marine Corps Field Medical Training Battalion-East, where, until his separation from service, he served as an instructor for Navy chaplains and medics.

SEPARATION

In October 2012, Mr. Bee requested to separate early from the Marine Corps through the Voluntary Separation Program ("VSP").

On April 1, 2013, Mr. Bee was discharged pursuant to his VSP request. On his discharge certification, formally referred to as a "DD Form 214," his discharge was noted as April 1, 2013. In block 28 of the form, titled "Narrative Reason for Separation," the Navy noted "FORCE SHAPING-VSP," referring to the VSP Mr. Bee entered into and which resulted in his voluntary discharge.

Prior to discharge, Mr. Bee was not afforded review by a medical review board to determine whether his PTSD and TBI rendered him unfit for duty and entitled to a medical disability retirement.

VA DISABILITY BENEFITS

In April 2013, after his discharge, Mr. Bee applied for disability benefits from the VA. On October 10, 2013, the VA issued a letter of its proposed VA Rating Decision, noting that Mr. Bee had a TBI and PTSD, that his injuries were "service connect[ed]," and that each condition was rated at 70 percent disability. He was rated for other conditions and received an overall disability rating of 100 percent.

PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE BOARD FOR CORRECTION OF NAVAL RECORDS

In April 2018, Mr. Bee submitted an application to the Board for Correction of Naval Records ("BCNR") requesting a change in the narrative reason for separation noted on his April 1, 2013 DD Form 214 from Force-Shaping VSP to medical disability retirement for his PTSD and TBI. He submitted a supporting brief arguing that he should have qualified for disability retirement at the time of his discharge on April 1, 2013, due to his PTSD and TBI, which he contended were more than 30 percent disabling.

In 2019, the BCNR denied Mr. Bee's petition in a three-page opinion, concluding that the evidence showed Mr. Bee was fit for service at the time of discharge and thus not entitled to a medical disability retirement ("2019 Decision").

FEDERAL CLAIMS COURT COMPLAINT AND REMAND

On October 6, 2021, Mr. Bee filed a complaint before the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, seeking an award of disability retirement pay and challenging the BCNR's 2019 Decision. The challenge resulted in a voluntary remand so that the BCNR could reconsider its decision.

On remand, in a more fulsome decision, the BCNR again denied Mr. Bee's petition ("2023 Decision"). The BCNR concluded that the preponderance of the evidence showed that, at the time of his discharge, Mr. Bee was fit for duty and thus not entitled to a medical disability retirement. The BCNR did not explicitly state in its decision whether it was affording "liberal consideration" to Mr. Bee's petition.

AMENDED COMPLAINT AND POSITIONS OF THE PARTIES

Mr. Bee amended his complaint to challenge the BCNR's 2023 Decision. He argues that the BCNR erred in two respects: (1) it failed to apply the correct legal standard for assessing his fitness for duty, and (2) it failed to afford liberal consideration to his petition, which he argues was required under 10 U.S.C. § 1552(h) and binding military policy.

The government defends the BCNR's determination. The government also argues that Mr. Bee's complaint before the Federal Claims Court is time-barred under 28 U.S.C. § 2501.

RELIEF SOUGHT

Mr. Bee seeks an award of disability retirement pay and correction of his DD Form 214 to reflect a medical disability retirement for his PTSD and TBI in place of the Force-Shaping VSP narrative reason for separation.

DISPOSITION UNDER REVIEW

The Federal Claims Court determined that Mr. Bee's complaint was timely and denied the government's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The Federal Claims Court determined that Mr. Bee's complaint failed on the merits, granted the government's motion for judgment on the administrative record, and denied Mr. Bee's motion for judgment on the administrative record.
