10932184.holding_quote: In focusing its analysis solely on Civ.R. 3(C)(9) and erroneously concluding that subsection was controlling, the trial court failed to consider whether Franklin County is otherwise a proper venue.
10932184.situation:
CASE FILE

Parties and Background

Wendee and Robert were married on November 9, 2010. From 2013 until June 2024, the parties resided in Franklin County. In June 2024, they moved to Perry County. (Aug. 11, 2025 Tr. 3.)

The Franklin County Divorce Complaint

On April 1, 2025, Wendee filed a complaint for divorce in Franklin County. The complaint alleged that Robert conducted activity that gave rise to the claim for relief in Franklin County, that Franklin County is the county in which all or part of the claim for relief arose, and that Robert's principal place of business was in Franklin County. (Compl. at ¶ 2-4.)

Wendee requested service by process server on April 3, 2025, and initiated certified mail service on April 8, 2025.

The Perry County Divorce Complaint

On April 7, 2025, after Wendee filed her complaint in Franklin County, Robert filed his own complaint for divorce in Perry County (Perry C.P. No. 25DR-87).

Proceedings in the Perry County Case

On May 8, 2025, Wendee filed a motion to dismiss the Perry County case. She asserted that the jurisdictional-priority rule deprived the Perry County court of authority to proceed because she had already perfected service in the Franklin County case. Robert admitted that the Franklin County complaint was the first to be filed and the first to have service perfected. (Memo Contra at 6.) Robert nonetheless argued the jurisdictional-priority rule did not apply because Franklin County was not a proper venue. (Memo Contra at 6.)

On May 23, 2025, the Perry County court issued an order denying Wendee's motion to dismiss. The Perry County court did not specifically address the jurisdictional-priority rule. It determined that venue was proper in Perry County and improper in Franklin County under Civ.R. 3(C)(9), because Wendee did not reside in Franklin County for the 90 days prior to filing her complaint in Franklin County.

Wendee filed a motion to set aside the May 23, 2025 order in the Perry County case, followed by a petition for a writ of prohibition in the Fifth District Court of Appeals. The Fifth District dismissed the writ as moot after the Perry County court placed the case on its inactive docket pending the outcome of the appeal, and concluded, alternatively, that Wendee had an adequate remedy at law by way of her appeal. State ex rel. Lester v. Boyer, 2025-Ohio-4430 (5th Dist.).

Robert's Motion to Dismiss the Franklin County Case

On June 4, 2025, Robert filed a motion to dismiss the Franklin County case pursuant to Civ.R. 12(B)(2) and (3). Robert argued that Franklin County was an improper venue under Civ.R. 3(C)(9). Wendee filed a memorandum in opposition. The trial court conducted an oral argument on Robert's motion on August 11, 2025.

The Trial Court's Judgment

On August 12, 2025, the trial court issued a judgment entry granting Robert's motion to dismiss. The trial court determined that Franklin County was not the proper venue for the divorce proceedings, noting that both parties reside in Perry County and had resided there for at least 90 days immediately preceding Robert's filing of the Perry County complaint. The trial court determined:

"This court does not find that Civil Rule 3(C)(9) is an exclusive means to determine venue in all civil cases. However, when it is the basis for competing Complaints for Divorce, and following its directive does not create a scenario that is unfair to one party or the other, Civil Rule 3(C)(9) should be the controlling provision." (Aug. 12, 2025 Jgmt. Entry at 2.)

The trial court granted Robert's motion to dismiss Wendee's Franklin County complaint for divorce and stated "[t]he parties shall proceed with the Complaint for Divorce action filed in Perry County, Ohio." (Aug. 12, 2025 Jgmt. Entry at 2.)

Governing Provisions Invoked

Civ.R. 12(B)(2) and (3); Civ.R. 3(C)(9), including its ninety-day residency provision; and the jurisdictional-priority rule.

Relief Sought

Robert sought dismissal of the Franklin County complaint for improper venue and lack of jurisdiction. Wendee sought denial of that motion, and had earlier sought dismissal of the Perry County complaint on the basis of the jurisdictional-priority rule, contending that her prior filing and perfected service in Franklin County controlled.

seed.consideration: Whether Franklin County was otherwise a proper venue under the other subsections of Civ.R. 3(C)(2), (3), and (6) that Wendee actually invoked, rather than only under Civ.R. 3(C)(9).
seed.why_material: Because the subsections of Civ.R. 3(C) have equal status, venue proper under any invoked subsection would make Franklin County proper and trigger the jurisdictional-priority rule.

10933057.holding_quote: The family court here lost sight of these fundamental principles, failed to consider the broad protective purpose of the DVPA, and exalted expediency over justice when it summarily dismissed Wife's petition for a DVRO based on its own docket management concerns.
10933057.situation:
CASE FILE

PARTIES AND BACKGROUND

This is a domestic violence restraining order (DVRO) proceeding in family court between Wife (petitioner) and Husband (respondent). The parties are natives of Nigeria who later immigrated to the United States. They met in Nigeria in 2011, married in 2013, and had a son, T.I-D. (Child), in 2014. Husband came to the United States in 2016 or 2017. Wife and Child joined him in San Diego in 2021.

THE DVRO REQUEST

On April 21, 2023, Wife filed a pro se DVRO petition seeking protection for herself and Child from Husband. She alleged Husband was verbally and physically abusive throughout the marriage and had become increasingly abusive after she and Child immigrated to the United States. She described multiple examples of abuse, including an instance in which Husband allegedly hit her to the point of unconsciousness. She averred that Husband controlled her finances, prohibited her from having personal friendships with others, and threatened to have her deported to Nigeria.

Husband opposed the DVRO petition and denied the allegations of abuse and improper control.

INITIAL ORDERS

On the same day Wife filed her petition, the family court granted Wife sole legal and physical custody of Child. It also issued a domestic violence temporary restraining order (DVTRO) prohibiting Husband from abusing Wife or Child, ordering Husband to stay at least 100 yards away from Wife and Child, and directing Husband to move out of the family home. The court later modified the DVTRO to grant Husband supervised visitation rights.

COUNSEL AND SCHEDULING

Both parties retained separate counsel. When Wife's counsel substituted into the case, he filed a declaration estimating the evidentiary hearing likely would require two court days.

The family court scheduled an evidentiary hearing and then continued it several times. The continuances resulted from: Wife's request for an extension to retain counsel; the recusal of the originally assigned judge; the unavailability of Wife's counsel on one hearing date; a stipulated continuance; and the illness of Wife's counsel on another hearing date. With each continuance, the court extended the duration of the DVTRO.

Despite the two-day estimate, the then-assigned judge (Hon. Christopher Morris) set the matter for a half-day hearing on April 11, 2024. Prior to that hearing, the case was reassigned to the Honorable Charles E. Bell, Jr. (All further dates are 2024 unless otherwise noted.)

DVRO HEARING — APRIL 11

At the outset, the court expressed doubt that a half day would suffice, stating, "I have a feeling that you're going to need more time than half a day, I would imagine." Wife's counsel replied that the prior judge had set the matter for a half day and agreed it could not be completed in a half day. The court responded, "So I just wanted to plant that seed with both of you. … I am conscious of that."

The court adjudicated the parties' motions in limine, again suggested it "would be difficult to get everything done in a half day," and asked Wife's counsel for a duration estimate. Wife's counsel estimated two full days in total, with a half day for Wife's case in chief. Husband's counsel estimated he would also need half a day. The court said, "Okay."

Wife took the stand during her case in chief. Her direct examination lasted about an hour and a half on April 11 (from 9:36 a.m. to 10:28 a.m., and from 10:47 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.).

Wife testified that Husband did not yell at her or make her fear for her safety in the early stages of their relationship, but began yelling after Child was born. She testified Husband first yelled at her when she told him he was spending too much money and needed to support Child financially; he allegedly dragged her into another room and directed family members there to admonish her that she had no right to talk to him about money. She testified Husband yelled at her and called her a bad wife on several other occasions while they lived in Nigeria.

Wife testified Husband controlled her activities and movements, banning her from leaving home without his permission. On one occasion he allegedly forbade her from attending a family member's funeral until other family members intervened. She testified Husband closely controlled what she bought, and she had to comply or "there [would be] trouble."

Wife described an incident of physical abuse in Nigeria. After Husband lost his job, she again told him he was spending too much money. Husband allegedly took her phone, slapped her face with his open palm, returned the phone, and left. He allegedly returned twenty minutes later and struck her with his fist until she lost consciousness. When she regained consciousness, her eyes were bruised, and Husband would not allow her to go to the hospital.

Husband then immigrated to the United States. Wife did not see him again until she and Child came to live with him in San Diego four or five years later. After a few months of peaceful cohabitation, Husband allegedly began yelling and shouting again. Wife testified Husband once became angry when she did not answer his sister's phone calls; he yelled, cursed, called her disrespectful, and said he had "picked [her] from the gutter." She testified Husband verbally abused her every two or three weeks throughout 2022, and during these episodes threatened to kill her, take Child away, and have her deported to Nigeria.

Wife testified about physical violence Husband allegedly committed against Child. She claimed Husband flogged Child with a belt in January 2022 for behaving poorly at school, which resulted in a report to Child Welfare Services (CWS). According to Wife, Husband coached her and Child to deny the abuse and threatened that she could be jailed or deported if she disclosed it. When CWS interviewed Wife and Child, they denied the abuse. CWS found the allegation of physical abuse against Child not substantiated.

Wife described two additional incidents from March 2023. In the first, Child threw a slipper at someone, and Husband struck Child's head, face, and body with his hand. In the second, Child closed his bedroom door to keep someone out, and Husband hit and threatened to kill Child. Wife claimed Husband also hit Child for poor school reports and threatened to kill Child if Child disclosed Husband's abuse of Wife.

Wife described an incident of physical abuse three days before she filed her petition. On April 18, 2023, the parties disagreed about their income tax returns. Wife claimed Husband left the residence, returned late at night, woke her, yelled at her, pulled her hair and ear, and hit her face and ear with his hand and his phone. Wife made an audio recording of the incident on her own phone, in which persons speak alternately in Igbo (a language primarily spoken in Nigeria) and English.

At this point the court paused Wife's testimony to discuss housekeeping matters. The court asked for an updated estimate. Wife's counsel said he needed another two hours for Wife's case, excluding cross-examination. Husband's counsel said he would require "a full day." The court opined the trial "was really a two day," and both counsel reiterated they had originally asked for a two-day trial. The court replied, "I'll respect that. I'll respect that. I won't hold that against you on that one."

The court set a continued full-day hearing for August 29.

DVRO HEARING — AUGUST 29

At the start, the court admitted into evidence the 16-minute-and-39-second audio recording of the tax-return incident. On the recording, Wife can be heard saying, "Why are you hitting me," "Please don't lay your hands on me anymore," and "Stop hitting me, it's hurting me." Husband says, "And if I lay hands on you, what would happen?" Wife repeats that Husband is hurting her, and he replies, "Do your worst. … Get the phone, call the cops. … I said get the phone and call the cops, silly fool." Husband then says, "You haven't seen any hurt; you will feel the real hurt." Wife repeatedly asks him to stop, and he responds, "[Wife] thinks that I'm a fool, let her do her worst, I brought her to America, I will send her back." Another man can be heard saying, "See how your son is watching you," and "Please don't touch her."

After admission of the recording, Wife continued her testimony. She stated Husband struck her with a closed fist, punched her, squeezed her ear, and pulled her around during the recorded incident, and that Child was present.

Wife testified about abuse allegedly occurring on April 20, 2023, one day before she filed her petition. She testified the parties disagreed about paperwork concerning childcare services, and Husband yelled and told Child that Wife was "going to feel [his] presence," that he was "going to deal with" her, and that she would "regret ever knowing" him. Wife reported the incident to police and obtained a criminal protective order against Husband.

Wife completed her direct examination. It took less than one hour on August 29 (from 9:28 a.m. to 10:23 a.m.), and two and a half hours across both hearing days.

Husband's counsel cross-examined Wife. He elicited testimony that Husband remitted thousands of dollars per year to her while she lived in Nigeria, that she had her own bank account, that Husband introduced her to someone who helped her gain employment in the United States, and that Husband made regular support payments during the DVRO proceedings — all to counter Wife's narrative that Husband curtailed her financial freedom. Counsel also elicited testimony that Wife lied to CWS when she denied that Husband had abused Child in January 2022. The cross-examination was at times combative and mired in objections, many of which were sustained. It lasted about two and a half hours.

Wife's counsel conducted a brief redirect of about 15 minutes. Wife then rested.

Husband's counsel conducted a direct examination of Husband for about 35 minutes, addressing his schooling and employment history, his immigration to the United States, his asylum proceedings, and his financial support of Wife. Counsel did not ask Husband about Wife's allegations of physical or verbal abuse.

The court set a continued half-day hearing for the following day and opined that no further continuances or extensions would be granted.

DVRO HEARING — AUGUST 30

Due to an apparent misunderstanding between counsel about which party would arrange for court reporting services, a court reporter did not arrive for the scheduled start. Counsel belatedly secured a reporter, and the reported portion began after a 90-minute delay.

At the start of the reported portion, Husband's counsel orally moved to dismiss "the underlying restraining order" (presumably the DVTRO) and "the entire action" under Code of Civil Procedure section 533, which permits a court to modify or dissolve an injunction or temporary restraining order when, among other circumstances, the ends of justice would be served.

Husband's counsel argued the ends of justice would be served by dismissal because: (1) Wife's counsel had failed to arrange for the court reporter to appear on August 30; (2) Husband had been subject to the DVTRO throughout the case; (3) Husband had incurred significant costs for supervised visitations with Child; (4) Wife's counsel had, per Husband's counsel, fabricated an illness at a prior hearing, resulting in a continuance; (5) Husband had not violated the DVTRO; (6) Husband was not prosecuted for the April 20, 2023 incident; and (7) Wife's allegations of abuse were not credible.

Wife's counsel argued against the request, asserting that: (1) Code of Civil Procedure section 533 does not apply to DVRO proceedings; (2) there was a genuine misunderstanding between counsel about who would procure the court reporter; (3) DVRO proceedings involving credible allegations of abuse should be decided on the merits; and (4) there was evidence Husband had violated the DVTRO.

RULING

The court provided a tentative ruling to dismiss the DVTRO in the interests of justice. It summarized the "restraints placed upon" Husband since the DVTRO's issuance on April 21, 2023, stated the DVTRO did "what it [was] supposed to do" and had "allowed for a cooling off period between the parties to ensure that there is not a continuation or repeat of [the] conduct." The court observed the parties had taken "a day and a half nearly to do one witness," admonished counsel "[t]here isn't unlimited time," and stated it was "not the court's responsibility to control how practitioners conduct their cases."

The court then conducted a direct examination of Husband consisting of four questions. It asked whether Wife had "reason to fear [him] contacting her in the future outside of any court ordered parenting plan," and Husband replied, "No." It asked whether he was "voluntarily stating on the record that [he] will not, as defined by the Domestic Violence Protection Act, [do] any acts that fall under [the definition of] domestic violence … towards [Wife] in the future," and Husband replied, "I do." It asked how he would conduct himself if he came across Wife at a court-ordered exchange of Child or elsewhere, and Husband replied, "peacefully without any problem." It asked whether he knew Wife had a right to bring a restraining order against him in the future if needed, and Husband said, "I do."

Based on this testimony, the court found there was not a "reasonable probability of future unlawful violence or any act under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act to necessitate the [temporary] restraining order remaining in place." The court dissolved the DVTRO without prejudice. It then clarified that it was dismissing the entire DVRO action "in the interest of justice," and not merely dissolving the DVTRO, because "[n]either [side] ha[d] completed [its] case in the time allotted by the court."

At a subsequent hearing, the court reiterated that it had dismissed the DVRO petition because "the attorneys representing the parties failed to comply with the two-day time estimate for the evidentiary hearing." The court noted its dismissal was "not based on the court finding that [the] 'acts shown at [the] noticed hearing [were] insufficient to support the [domestic violence restraining] order.'"

GOVERNING AUTHORITY

The proceeding arises under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act. The dismissal motion invoked Code of Civil Procedure section 533.

seed.consideration: Before dismissing, the court should have weighed the DVPA's broad protective purpose and the strong policy favoring disposition of domestic violence petitions on the merits against its docket-management concerns.
seed.why_material: Because credible evidence of abuse was presented, dismissing for scheduling reasons closed the courthouse to an alleged victim without any merits determination, defeating the statute's aim of promptly protecting survivors.

10933720.situation:
CASE FILE — Dissolution of Marriage

PARTIES AND FAMILY BACKGROUND
This is a marital dissolution matter involving the Former Husband and the Former Wife. At the time of the petition, the parties had been married for twenty-six years and had one minor child, a son.

EMPLOYMENT HISTORY
During the beginning of the marriage, the Former Wife worked at Chesapeake Capital. Two years into the marriage, the parties moved to Ireland and then to London to further the Former Husband's career. In 2001, the parties returned to Florida. The Former Husband began working at Citigroup in 2002 and remained employed there at the time of trial.

Upon returning to Florida, the Former Wife was employed on an interim basis for four years, and then took a job with UKG, where she remained employed for eighteen years prior to trial. Her employment at UKG was part-time beginning in 2009, after the parties' son was born, until 2021, when she returned to full-time status.

ASSETS AND FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENTS
As of the date of separation, the parties had accumulated over five million dollars in assets. During the marriage, they maintained separate bank accounts and one joint bank account. Each contributed a proportionate share of income to the joint account to pay household expenses. The Former Husband contributed $5,000 per month, and the Former Wife contributed $2,000 per month.

The parties present differing accounts of the sufficiency of these contributions. The Former Wife testified that the $7,000 in monthly contributions was not always sufficient to cover the parties' joint expenses and that this resulted in the parties making additional contributions. The Former Husband testified that the parties' expenses were always covered by the $7,000 joint contribution.

INCOME AND TAX HISTORY
In 2021, the parties' taxable income was $367,070. They owed $15,869 in taxes on that amount (after withholds and credits), which they paid from their joint account.

The parties separated on June 20, 2022, and thereafter filed separate tax returns. In 2022, the Former Husband had a gross income of $191,738, and the Former Wife's gross income was a little over half of that amount—$87,233. In 2023, the parties' W-2s reflected the Former Husband's income as $224,355 and the Former Wife's income as $119,512.

The parties' financial affidavits and testimony indicated that, at the time of trial, the Former Wife had a monthly gross taxable income of $10,640, while the Former Husband's monthly gross income was $20,998.

CONTRIBUTIONS AND EXPENSES AT SEPARATION
The Former Wife testified that the Former Husband stopped contributing to the household in February 2022, though he remained living in the marital home until June 2022. According to the Former Wife's testimony, the Former Husband did not contribute any monies to the health care expenses of the child or to the health savings account (HSA), which benefited the Former Wife, the child, and the Former Husband. The Former Wife expended $13,000 for the child's extracurricular and medical expenses.

PROCEDURAL POSTURE AND RULINGS
In November 2023, the trial court ordered the Former Husband to pay temporary child support and arrears at $1,500 per month.

Pursuant to the amended final judgment, the trial court:
- Awarded child support at $1,344, a lesser amount, retroactive to the date of separation, taking into account an overage paid by the Former Husband, with child support to continue until the child reaches the age of majority;
- Awarded the Former Wife lump sum durational alimony; and
- Granted the Former Wife ultimate decision-making authority.

PRESERVATION
The Former Husband did not file a motion for rehearing in the trial court directed at the final judgment's factual findings.

10934255.holding_quote: We find the trial court's failure to consider the factors set forth in R.C. 2929.19(B)(1)(b) renders Appellant's sentence clearly and convincingly contrary to law.
10934255.situation:
This is a criminal matter in the General Division of the Stark County Court of Common Pleas involving defendant Elijah Arrington, following the transfer of his case from the Juvenile Division.

ORIGIN AND JUVENILE PROCEEDINGS

On August 29, 2024, a complaint was filed in the Stark County Court of Common Pleas, Juvenile Division, alleging that Arrington appeared to be a delinquent child for committing acts constituting the offense of felonious assault, in violation of R.C. 2903.11(A)(1), a felony of the second degree if committed by an adult. The complaint was filed after Arrington, then 17 years old, assaulted a female corrections officer at the Ohio Department of Youth Services ("DYS"), Indian River Juvenile Correction Facility ("Indian River"), located in Massillon, Stark County, Ohio.

On October 3, 2024, the State filed a motion to transfer jurisdiction to the adult criminal division pursuant to R.C. 2152.10(B) and 2151.12(B).

The juvenile court conducted a probable cause hearing on December 18, 2024. After discussion with his counsel and his Guardian ad Litem, Arrington waived his rights and stipulated to a finding of probable cause. The juvenile court found probable cause that Arrington committed felonious assault and that the commission of that offense would constitute a felony of the second degree if committed by an adult. The juvenile court ordered Arrington to undergo a psychological evaluation for purposes of the amenability hearing.

The juvenile court held an amenability hearing on February 19, 2025. Dr. Aimee Thomas with Lighthouse Family Center, who completed the psychological evaluation of Arrington, testified regarding Arrington's history of delinquent activity, repeated removal from his home, early and ongoing drug abuse, gang involvement, and mental health issues. Based upon her interview with Arrington, the results of his psychological testing, and her review of collateral information, Dr. Thomas concluded that Arrington was not amenable to the juvenile justice system.

The juvenile court issued Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law on February 25, 2025. The juvenile court found Arrington was not amenable to care or rehabilitation within a juvenile facility and that "community safety may require restraint that possibly exceeds beyond [Arrington's] obtaining the age of 21." The juvenile court further found there were no relevant factors weighing against transfer. The juvenile court granted the State's motion to transfer and ordered Arrington's case be transferred to the General Division of the Stark County Court of Common Pleas.

PROCEEDINGS IN THE GENERAL DIVISION

On March 20, 2025, the Stark County Grand Jury indicted Arrington on one count of felonious assault, in violation of R.C. 2903.11(A)(1)(D)(1)(a), a felony of the second degree. Arrington was transferred from Indian River to the Stark County Jail for the pendency of the case. At his arraignment on March 28, 2025, Arrington entered a plea of not guilty to the Indictment.

On April 28, 2025, Arrington advised the trial court he wished to withdraw his former plea of not guilty and enter a plea of guilty to the charged offense. Following a Crim.R. 11 colloquy, the trial court accepted Arrington's plea and convicted him of one count of felonious assault. The trial court immediately proceeded to sentencing. The trial court ordered Arrington to serve an indefinite minimum prison term of 7 years to a maximum prison term of 10 1/2 years. The trial court memorialized Arrington's conviction and sentence via Judgment Entry filed May 12, 2025.

RELIEF SOUGHT AND CONTENTIONS

Arrington appeals from the May 12, 2025 Judgment Entry. He raises two assignments of error.

First, Arrington contends his adult prison sentence is unauthorized by and contrary to law because the trial court failed to comply with the mandatory sentencing provisions of R.C. 2929.19(B)(1)(b), which require trial courts to consider a child's youth and all of its attendant characteristics before sentencing them to adult prison. He cites Ohio Const. Art. I, § 9; Crim.R. 52; R.C. 2929.19(B)(1)(b); R.C. 2953.08(A)(4) and (G); and State v. Patrick, 2020-Ohio-6803.

Second, Arrington contends he was deprived of his constitutional right to the effective assistance of counsel when counsel failed to introduce any mitigating youth factors at the sentencing hearing. He cites Crim.R. 52; R.C. 2929.19(B)(1)(b); and the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution, referencing the April 28, 2025 transcript at pages 9-13 and the February 3, 2025 evaluation.

seed.consideration: Whether the trial court should weigh youth and its attendant mitigating characteristics under R.C. 2929.19(B)(1)(b) before sentencing an offender who committed the offense while under 18 to adult prison.
seed.why_material: Because the offender was under 18 at the time of the offense, the statute mandates consideration of these youth-mitigating factors, and failure to do so renders the sentence contrary to law.

10936117.court: Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
10936117.holding_quote: Nevertheless, the district court erred when it decertified the class for declaratory relief based on factors that are not relevant to the Rule 23(b)(2) analysis.
10936117.situation:
This is a class-action and habeas matter arising from immigration bond-hearing procedures under section 1226(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. The case is before the district court on remand following prior appellate proceedings, on cross-motions: the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment seeking class-wide declaratory relief, and the government's cross-motion to decertify the class and to dismiss.

STATUTORY AND REGULATORY FRAMEWORK

Section 1226(a) of the INA generally governs the arrest and detention of noncitizens pending their removal. Under that provision, an alien may be arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States. The discretionary decision whether to detain such noncitizens lies with the Attorney General and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

If DHS determines that a noncitizen should be detained during the pendency of removal proceedings, the noncitizen may request a custody redetermination hearing (also known as a bond hearing) before an immigration judge (IJ), pursuant to 8 C.F.R. sections 236.1(d)(1), 1003.19, and 1236.1(d). During the bond hearing, the IJ decides whether the noncitizen poses a danger to the community or a flight risk. If the noncitizen does not, the noncitizen may be released. Under Matter of Guerra, 24 I. & N. Dec. 37 (BIA 2006), the burden of proof in those proceedings rests on the noncitizen, not the government, to establish to the satisfaction of the IJ and the Board of Immigration Appeals that he or she does not present a danger to persons or property, is not a threat to national security, and does not pose a risk of flight. Under Matter of Barreiros, 10 I. & N. Dec. 536 (BIA 1964), this standard is akin to the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard.

FACTS

Junior Onosamba-Ohindo is a native and citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He entered the United States without inspection and was placed in removal proceedings. Pending those proceedings, DHS detained him at the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in New York. He requested review of DHS's custody determination from an IJ and, after a bond hearing, was ordered released on an $8,000 bond. When he could not pay the bond set for him, he filed the underlying class-action complaint and habeas petition in March 2020. After he filed suit, a community bail fund posted his bond, and he was released from DHS custody in 2020.

PRIOR PROCEEDINGS

Class Certification and Preliminary Injunction. Onosamba-Ohindo argued that the government's section 1226(a) bond-hearing procedures violate the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause. Specifically, he contended that those procedures (1) improperly place the burden of proof on noncitizens, not the government; (2) do not require the IJ to consider noncitizens' ability to pay; and (3) do not require the IJ to consider non-bond alternatives to detention.

He moved to certify a class of all individuals detained under section 1226(a) who had or would have bond hearings before the Batavia and Buffalo Immigration Courts, and he moved for a class-wide preliminary injunction requiring the government to change its bond-hearing procedures.

The district court granted the motions in part. It certified a class of individuals detained at the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility under section 1226(a) who had not yet had a bond hearing (the Pre-Hearing Class). The court found that class a proper Rule 23(b)(2) class, defined by the indivisible nature of the injunctive or declaratory remedy warranted, because Onosamba-Ohindo had demonstrated deficiencies in the procedures employed by the government that stem from central and systemic failures and apply across-the-board to each putative class member, such that the government's conduct could be enjoined or declared unlawful only as to all class members or as to none of them. The court denied the motion to certify a class of individuals who already had bond hearings, reasoning that those detainees would have to make individualized showings of prejudice. The court allowed Onosamba-Ohindo to proceed as a class representative notwithstanding his release from custody because his claims were inherently transitory.

Having certified the Pre-Hearing Class, the district court issued a preliminary injunction as to that class. The injunction ordered that all members of the Pre-Hearing Class must receive a bond hearing wherein the government bears the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that the individual is a danger to the community or flight risk, and where the IJ must consider non-bond alternatives to detention or, if setting a bond, ability to pay.

The parties cross-appealed the order. In the meantime, the government complied with the injunction and instructed IJs in the Batavia and Buffalo Immigration Courts to change their bond-hearing procedures. Those revised procedures remained in effect for nearly two years, from September 2021 until August 2023, while the cross-appeals were pending.

Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez. While the cross-appeals were pending, the Supreme Court decided Aleman Gonzalez, holding that 8 U.S.C. section 1252(f)(1) strips lower courts of jurisdiction to issue class-wide injunctive relief affecting, among other provisions, section 1226(a). The parties then stipulated that section 1252(f)(1) barred the class-wide preliminary injunction the district court had entered. Onosamba-Ohindo moved to vacate the preliminary injunction, dismiss the pending interlocutory appeals, and remand to the district court for further proceedings, and the motion was granted.

POSTURE ON REMAND

On remand, Onosamba-Ohindo moved for summary judgment on his claim for class-wide declaratory relief. He proposed a declaration stating that the Due Process Clause requires that people detained under 8 U.S.C. section 1226(a) receive custody hearings in which the government bears the burden to justify continued detention by clear and convincing evidence that the detainee is a danger to others or a flight risk, and even if they are, that no condition or combination of conditions will reasonably assure the detainee's future appearance and the safety of the community, and which includes consideration of the detained person's ability to pay in selecting the amount of any bond and suitability for release on alternative conditions of supervision.

The government cross-moved to decertify the class and to dismiss.

The district court concluded that section 1252(f)(1) did not strip it of jurisdiction to enter class-wide declaratory relief. It stated that it continues to be of the view that the Due Process Clause requires that individuals detained under section 1226(a) be provided a bond hearing at which the government bears the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that the individual is either a danger to the community or a flight risk. Nevertheless, the district court granted the government's motion to decertify the class, denied Onosamba-Ohindo's motion for summary judgment as moot, and dismissed the case. The court reasoned that class-wide injunctive relief is not available post-Aleman Gonzalez, that this is not a case in which issuance of a declaratory judgment would be appropriate, and that, as a result, certification under Rule 23(b)(2) is no longer appropriate.

seed.consideration: Whether the Rule 23(b)(2) certification inquiry should be confined to asking if a single declaratory judgment would provide indivisible relief to the whole class, rather than importing the discretionary Declaratory Judgment Act balancing factors into the certification decision.
seed.why_material: By deciding at certification whether declaratory relief would be 'appropriate' or useful under the Duane Reade/Admiral multi-factor test, the district court applied the wrong legal standard and thereby abused its discretion in decertifying the declaratory-relief class.

10936134.case_name: Keith Thaete, Steve King, Lance Thaete v. St. Luke's Magic Valley Center, Michael R. Fry, D.O
10936134.holding_quote: Although Dr. Fry was questioned during his deposition about the standard of care for nursing staff, he was never asked about the standard of care applicable to himself or board-certified internists.
10936134.situation:
PARTIES AND FORUM

Plaintiffs are Keith Thaete and Sherry Thaete (the Thaetes). Sherry Thaete is deceased. Defendants (Respondents) are Dr. Fry, the attending physician, and St. Luke's Magic Valley Medical Center, a hospital in Twin Falls, Idaho. The matter is pending in the district court.

UNDERLYING FACTS

On January 15, 2021, Keith Thaete brought his wife, Sherry Thaete, to St. Luke's Magic Valley Medical Center in Twin Falls, Idaho, because she was disoriented and unable to communicate. Mr. Thaete brought two of his wife's prescription bottles with him to the hospital: phenelzine (Nardil) and Ativan.

Mr. Thaete recalls showing the bottles to an unidentified nurse in the emergency room and later to another female nurse after his wife was admitted and transferred to an upper floor. Mr. Thaete also believed, though he could not state definitively, that he showed the prescription bottles to Dr. Fry, the attending physician.

An ER nurse, Nurse Brown, remembers Mr. Thaete providing two prescription bottles to him, and that he handed the bottles to Dr. Fry. Nurse Brown recalls Dr. Fry looking at the bottles before returning them to Mr. Thaete, but the doctor did not enter the medications into the computer system in Nurse Brown's presence.

During Mrs. Thaete's hospitalization, Dr. Fry prescribed her paroxetine (Paxil), a medication her psychiatrist had discontinued months earlier when initiating Nardil. Paxil and Nardil are contraindicated drugs and pose a significant risk when taken concurrently. There is conflicting testimony as to whether Dr. Fry was aware of Mrs. Thaete's Nardil prescription. Paxil was administered. Mrs. Thaete died two days after being admitted to the hospital.

PLEADINGS

In October 2021, the Thaetes filed a complaint and demand for jury trial against the Respondents. Although labeled as "negligence, negligence per se, and reckless conduct," the claim was brought under Idaho's Medical Malpractice Act. The Respondents filed an answer on November 19, 2021, denying all material allegations.

SCHEDULING ORDERS

The district court's original April 2022 scheduling and pretrial order required the Thaetes to disclose expert witnesses no later than 120 days before trial and the Respondents to do so no later than 75 days before trial. The order set a ten-day jury trial to begin on October 31, 2023.

The scheduling order was amended twice before discovery concluded. The first amendment required the Thaetes to disclose expert witnesses 210 days before trial and the Respondents to disclose their expert witnesses 120 days before trial. The second amendment extended the Respondents' expert disclosure deadline by 35 days to August 7, 2023, while setting the Thaetes' rebuttal deadline 21 days later, on August 28, 2023.

DISCOVERY

The parties engaged in extensive discovery. The Thaetes served written discovery on January 26, 2022, and moved to compel twice. The Thaetes' discovery requested documentation regarding the policies and practices for internists prescribing medications at St. Luke's. The Respondents objected, arguing that the request was overly broad. In response, the Thaetes narrowed their request. The Thaetes' first motion to compel was denied due to their failure to meet and confer with opposing counsel. In March, the district court partially granted the Thaetes' second motion to compel and imposed a temporal limitation on the internal policy request.

Both parties timely disclosed expert witnesses. The Thaetes deposed Dr. Fry and Nurses Victor and Brown. The Respondents produced relevant hospital policies on March 28 and April 10, 2023. The Respondents deposed the Thaetes' experts, Dr. Dodson and Dr. McIlraith. In June, the Thaetes filed a supplemental witness disclosure identifying Nurse Tripp.

MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT

On August 1, 2023, the Respondents filed a motion for summary judgment, contending that the Thaetes could not establish a prima facie case of medical malpractice against Dr. Fry or St. Luke's. They argued that Dr. McIlraith's opinions lacked foundation for a standard of care opinion against Dr. Fry; that Dr. Dodson's opinions lacked foundation for a standard of care opinion against St. Luke's; that Nurse Chisum's disclosure did not contain a breach opinion; and that Nurse Tripp's disclosure was untimely.

A hearing on the motion for summary judgment was initially scheduled for September 5, 2023. The Thaetes filed a motion to extend their August 15 response deadline. On August 17, the district court granted the motion, ordered the Thaetes' response be filed no later than August 22, and, because of its calendar, rescheduled the hearing for September 19.

The Thaetes filed a timely opposition brief on August 15. They then filed rebuttal expert declarations on August 28 and a supplemental response on August 29 — six and seven days after the August 22 deadline.

MOTION TO STRIKE

The Respondents moved to strike the Thaetes' August 28 and 29 filings.

DISTRICT COURT RULINGS

The district court granted both the Respondents' motion to strike and motion for summary judgment.

The court gave three reasons for striking the filings: untimeliness; improper rebuttal designation for a dispositive motion addressing the Thaetes' case-in-chief; and new standard-of-care opinions that would prejudice the Respondents.

The court then concluded that Dr. McIlraith's opinions were inadmissible because he failed to show actual knowledge of the community standard of care; that Nurse Chisum's disclosure did address the element of breach; and that Nurse Tripp's disclosure was untimely. Without admissible expert testimony, the court concluded that the Thaetes could not establish a prima facie medical malpractice case and entered judgment in favor of Dr. Fry and St. Luke's.

MOTION FOR RECONSIDERATION

The Thaetes moved for reconsideration, challenging the court's exclusion of all three expert witnesses. The district court denied the motion.

Regarding Nurse Chisum, the court determined that the Thaetes had not disclosed any breach of the standard of care opinion from Nurse Chisum in their initial or rebuttal expert disclosures, nor had they submitted a timely declaration to supplement the record indicating that she would testify to a breach of the standard of care by nursing staff. The court also cited representations by the Thaetes' counsel that Chisum was unwilling to testify, which contradicted their later position on reconsideration.

Regarding Nurse Tripp, the court reiterated that her disclosure was untimely, as it violated the amended scheduling order.

Regarding Dr. McIlraith, the district court maintained that he lacked the necessary foundational basis to provide opinions concerning Dr. Fry's actions. Despite recognizing that shared board certification might support familiarity with the standard of care, the court concluded that the lack of precision in Dr. Fry's deposition and the insufficient evidence regarding Dr. McIlraith's preparation did not meet the requirements under Idaho Code sections 6-1012 and 6-1013. The district court entered final judgment for the Respondents.

NOTICE OF APPEAL AND MOTION TO DISMISS

The Thaetes timely filed a notice of appeal but did not serve the notice on the Respondents. Twelve days later, the Respondents filed a motion to dismiss the appeal, arguing that both filing and service are jurisdictional requirements. The motion was denied without prejudice, and the parties were ordered to address the issue in their substantive briefing and at oral argument.

GOVERNING STANDARDS

The claim arises under Idaho's Medical Malpractice Act. Idaho Code sections 6-1012 and 6-1013 govern the foundation required for expert standard-of-care testimony. Summary judgment is governed by I.R.C.P. 56(a), which provides that summary judgment is proper if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. The admissibility of expert testimony is a threshold question separate from whether the testimony creates a genuine issue of material fact; in determining admissibility, the standard of liberal construction does not apply. Evidentiary rulings, including a grant of a motion to strike, are governed by an abuse-of-discretion standard, evaluated under the four-part Lunneborg test.

RELIEF SOUGHT

The Thaetes seek reversal of the orders striking their filings, excluding their experts, and granting summary judgment. Both parties seek attorney fees.

10936547.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
10936547.holding_quote: We conclude that the trial court erred by categorically excluding evidence of Allen's rehabilitation from its eligibility analysis.
10936547.situation:
This is a compassionate release matter under D.C. Code § 24-403.04(a), pending in the trial court on Henry Allen's motion to modify his sentence.

UNDERLYING CONVICTION AND SENTENCE

Henry Allen was convicted in 2003 of first-degree murder and related offenses. He was sentenced to forty-five years in prison. At the time of the present motion, Allen has served more than twenty years of that sentence.

THE MOTION

In 2023, after serving more than twenty years, Allen moved for compassionate release under D.C. Code § 24-403.04(a). Allen acknowledges that he does not satisfy either of the statute's categorical eligibility criteria: he does not have a terminal illness under § 24-403.04(a)(1), and he is several years short of sixty years old for purposes of § 24-403.04(a)(2). At the time of the motion, Allen was fifty-six years old.

Allen instead relies on the catch-all provision, § 24-403.04(a)(3). He argues that his age (fifty-six at the time), his length of incarceration, his medical conditions, his vulnerability to COVID-19, and his degree of rehabilitation combine to form "[o]ther extraordinary and compelling reasons" warranting his release under the catch-all provision. He presents his rehabilitation evidence "as evidence both of his lack of dangerousness and of the extraordinary and compelling circumstances justifying release."

GOVERNING STATUTE

D.C. Code § 24-403.04(a) provides that, notwithstanding any other provision of law, the court shall modify a term of imprisonment imposed upon a defendant if it determines the defendant is not a danger to the safety of any other person or the community, pursuant to the factors in 18 U.S.C. §§ 3142(g) and 3553(a) and evidence of the defendant's rehabilitation while incarcerated, and: (1) the defendant has a terminal illness meaning a disease or condition with an end-of-life trajectory; (2) the defendant is 60 years of age or older and has served at least 20 years in prison; or (3) other extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant such a modification, including: (A) a debilitating medical condition involving an incurable illness, or a debilitating injury from which the defendant will not recover; (B) elderly age, defined as a defendant who is 60 years of age or older, has served the lesser of 15 years or 75% of the sentence, and suffers from a chronic or serious medical condition related to the aging process or that causes an acute vulnerability to severe medical complications or death as a result of COVID-19; (C) death or incapacitation of the family member caregiver of the defendant's children; or (D) incapacitation of a spouse or domestic partner when the defendant would be the only available caregiver.

The statute imposes two requirements: (1) non-dangerousness, captured by the statute's opening sentence; and (2) eligibility, captured by the remainder of the statute at (a)(1)-(3). To be eligible, a movant must demonstrate "extraordinary and compelling reasons" warranting a sentence modification. Subsections (a)(1)-(2) provide two primary examples, and (a)(3) provides a catch-all with four non-exhaustive, illustrative examples.

The District's compassionate release statute was enacted in April 2020, prompted by the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, through temporary emergency legislation (D.C. Act 23-286), and later permanently codified with changes (D.C. Law 23-274), most notably making sentence modifications mandatory rather than discretionary if the movant satisfies the statutory requirements. The statute was modeled after and intended to align with the federal compassionate release statute, 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), which permits a district court to reduce a sentence upon finding extraordinary and compelling reasons consistent with applicable Sentencing Commission policy statements. The federal scheme provides, per 28 U.S.C. § 994(t), that rehabilitation of the defendant alone shall not be considered an extraordinary and compelling reason.

The District's statute differs from the federal counterpart: it reduces the age and time-served requirements for categorical eligibility from seventy years old and thirty years served to sixty years old and twenty years served; it makes reductions mandatory ("shall modify") rather than discretionary ("may reduce"); it directs courts to consider rehabilitation as part of the non-dangerousness inquiry; and it does not contain the federal provision that rehabilitation alone cannot amount to an extraordinary and compelling reason.

EVIDENCE PRESENTED

To substantiate his rehabilitation, Allen submitted letters from eight men who attested that he often resolved conflicts and served as a mentor in prison, one referring to him as a "shining beacon of hope for redemption." Allen's supervisor at the National Association for the Advancement of Returning Citizens described his involvement with the organization and wrote that Allen's mentorship "had such an impact on some of our participants that they gave up the street life." The supervisor stated, "In my unwavering opinion, I strongly believe that without Mr. Allen's involvement with our youth mentorship program, and sharing his inspiring story of redemption and reform, there would be a lot more of our youth incarcerated or deceased." The supervisor further predicted Allen "would be a great asset to our organization," and indicated the organization would employ him as an "Outreach Specialist" if released.

At a hearing, Allen expressed remorse for the murder he committed in 2003, recounted his experiences in federal prison, and described his rehabilitation and how he hoped to use it to help young men in his community. Allen submitted an affidavit from a registered nurse, who opined that Allen had seven comorbidities that put him at "more than an above average risk for severe COVID-19 outcomes." The court heard from a former inmate and a friend of Allen's who spoke about the violent conditions in prison to provide context for Allen's infractions for possessing a weapon while imprisoned. The court also considered victim-impact statements from the brother, mother, and daughter of the murder victim, all of whom opposed Allen's release.

TRIAL COURT RULING

The trial court denied Allen's compassionate release motion in a written order. The court found that Allen was no longer dangerous, satisfying the non-dangerousness requirement. It concluded, however, that he failed to demonstrate extraordinary and compelling reasons that would render him eligible for release under § 24-403.04(a)(3).

On eligibility, the court first found that Allen failed to show an acute vulnerability to severe illness from COVID-19. The court then disagreed with Allen's argument that his age and time served should be considered together with other factors for eligibility purposes, reasoning that the statute "sets an explicit age limit for eligibility" at sixty. Finally, the court declined to consider Allen's rehabilitation in its eligibility analysis, concluding that rehabilitation is relevant only "to the question of dangerousness."

ISSUES RAISED

Allen contends the trial court erred (1) by concluding it could not consider evidence of his rehabilitation when evaluating whether he had demonstrated extraordinary and compelling reasons rendering him eligible for release; and (2) by reviewing the reasons supporting his release piecemeal, assessing whether any one of them was individually extraordinary and compelling, rather than evaluating whether the factors cleared that bar when viewed collectively.

RELIEF SOUGHT

Allen seeks a modification of his sentence under D.C. Code § 24-403.04(a), the eligibility component being the sole matter in dispute, as the trial court's finding that Allen satisfied the non-dangerousness requirement is not challenged.

10936593.situation:
CASE FILE: Qoye v. United States

I. PARTIES AND OVERVIEW

Claimant is Mr. Qoye, a former enlisted member of the United States Navy. The opposing party is the United States (the government). This file concerns Mr. Qoye's efforts to have his service records corrected to reflect medical disability retirement for narcolepsy, related monetary relief, and correction of the characterization surrounding removal of his Navy Enlisted Classification (NEC).

II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

A. Service and Assignment

Mr. Qoye originally enlisted in the Navy on June 17, 2003. He signed a reenlistment contract on November 10, 2006, for a period of six years, expiring November 9, 2012. Under the reenlistment contract, he was to receive a total reenlistment bonus of $38,458.19, which could be "recouped" if he was "no longer classified in [his] rating/NEC" or did not "serve the entire period of reenlistment."

Mr. Qoye served in the United States Navy from November 2004 to September 2011. In 2008, he began a tour aboard the USS Eisenhower, a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, serving as a nuclear machinist mate.

B. Sleep-Related Symptoms and Medical Treatment

During his assignment aboard the USS Eisenhower, Mr. Qoye struggled to stay awake. Fellow service members described him as "consistently falling asleep in the middle of whatever it was that he was doing," including while standing watch or performing maintenance. His performance evaluations did not reflect any interference of fatigue with his duties.

Mr. Qoye sought medical treatment from the Navy for his sleep issues in November 2009, and again in June and July of 2010. In September 2010, the Navy conducted a sleep study of Mr. Qoye. The study revealed that Mr. Qoye snored and possibly had sleep apnea. The study did not test for narcolepsy, and the Navy did not perform a separate test for narcolepsy.

C. Misconduct and NEC Removal

In December 2010, Mr. Qoye was charged with failure to obey a lawful order and making a false official statement for falsifying a shipboard maintenance log. He received non-judicial punishment (NJP) for this misconduct in January 2011. Following his NJP, Mr. Qoye's supervisor requested removal of his NEC as a nuclear machinist mate, citing Mr. Qoye's "demonstrated unreliability and lack of integrity." Mr. Qoye alleges that the Navy removed his NEC in April 2011, although there is some dispute over whether the removal actually took place.

D. Separation

Mr. Qoye requested early separation from the Navy. In November 2011, he was honorably discharged with a narrative reason for separation of "reduction in force." The Navy sought recoupment of the reenlistment bonus because he failed to perform his duties through November 2012.

E. Post-Service VA Findings

In 2012, Mr. Qoye sought treatment for fatigue at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and underwent another sleep study. This study concluded that Mr. Qoye snored and ruled out a diagnosis of sleep apnea. Mr. Qoye also underwent a Multiple Sleep Latency Test, which showed he suffered from symptoms consistent with narcolepsy. The VA assigned him a 40 percent service-connected disability rating for narcolepsy, effective the date of his discharge, October 1, 2011. One of Mr. Qoye's VA doctors documented that he "believe[d] it is a certainty that [Mr. Qoye] developed narcolepsy, or at least had a major worsening of the condition, while he was on active duty in the Navy."

III. PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE BOARD

A. Initial Petition (June 2015)

In June 2015, Mr. Qoye petitioned the Board for correction of his service records to reflect that he was medically retired for narcolepsy and placed on the permanent disability retired list (PDRL). He also petitioned for retirement back pay, refund of his recouped enlistment bonus, and for his NEC removal characterization to be changed from misconduct to medically unfit.

The Board found that the Navy failed to properly diagnose Mr. Qoye's narcolepsy during his service and, specifically, failed to refer him to a Medical Evaluation Board (MEB) and Physical Evaluation Board (PEB) for a fitness determination. The Board forwarded Mr. Qoye's service records to an informal PEB for post hoc consideration.

B. Informal PEB (September 2017)

In September 2017, the informal PEB found Mr. Qoye fit for continued naval service, noting that there was insufficient evidence in his service records to show that his health conditions "interfered significantly with [his] ability to carry out the duties of his office, grade, rank, or rating at the time of his separation." In reaching this conclusion, the PEB initially relied on the medical records of another service member. After the error was discovered, the PEB reviewed the correct records and reached the same conclusion.

C. Request for Reconsideration (October 2018) and Denial (April 2020)

In October 2018, Mr. Qoye sought reconsideration from the Board regarding the informal PEB's determination that he was fit for service. He requested placement on the PDRL and a retroactive medical disqualification from his NEC. The Board requested comments and a recommendation from the Council of Review Boards (CORB), which issued an advisory opinion concluding the record did not support Mr. Qoye's requested relief.

In April 2020, relying on CORB's recommendation, the Board denied Mr. Qoye's request for reconsideration and upheld the informal PEB decision. The Board determined that the Navy properly removed Mr. Qoye's NEC because of misconduct, and that liberal consideration did not apply to Mr. Qoye's claim because he had been honorably discharged.

IV. FEDERAL CLAIMS COURT PROCEEDINGS AND REMAND

In October 2020, Mr. Qoye challenged the Board's April 2020 decision in the Court of Federal Claims. The Federal Claims Court granted the government's motion to remand the case to the Board and directed the Board to "address all issues and claims for relief" raised in Mr. Qoye's complaint.

On remand, the Board conducted a de novo review and issued a decision in April 2022. The Board upheld its prior determination, stating that "[t]he preponderance of the evidence simply does not establish that [Mr. Qoye was] incapable of performing the duties of [his] office, grade, rank or rating due to narcolepsy or any other condition." The Board again explained that Mr. Qoye lost his NEC because of his NJP, which was not the result of "the types of offenses which are mitigated or explained by a sleeping disorder like narcolepsy."

V. FEDERAL CLAIMS COURT DECISION (April 2024)

In April 2024, the Federal Claims Court issued an opinion and order granting the government's motion to dismiss and for judgment on the administrative record. The court affirmed the Board's decision that Mr. Qoye is not entitled to medical disability retirement as supported by substantial evidence. The court pointed to the Board's consideration of Mr. Qoye's 2010 sleep study, his application to be a military mechanic in 2015, and his final three in-service performance evaluations as substantial evidence that Mr. Qoye was not unfit for duty. The court also found that Mr. Qoye's claims for recoupment of his reenlistment bonus and for correction of his service record were time-barred.

VI. RELIEF SOUGHT

Mr. Qoye seeks: (1) correction of his service records to reflect medical retirement for narcolepsy and placement on the PDRL; (2) retirement back pay; (3) refund of his recouped reenlistment bonus; and (4) change of the characterization of his NEC removal from misconduct to medically unfit.

VII. GOVERNING STANDARDS

A Board decision is subject to being overturned if it is arbitrary, capricious, contrary to law, or unsupported by substantial evidence. A Board decision that fails to consider the relevant factors may be arbitrary and capricious. The question of whether Mr. Qoye's health conditions interfered significantly with his ability to carry out the duties of his office, grade, rank, or rating at the time of separation governs the fitness determination. The applicability of liberal consideration, the timeliness of the recoupment and record-correction claims, and the proper basis for the NEC removal are matters in dispute in the record.

10936856.holding_quote: Here, the record does not show that the Circuit Court considered less severe sanctions — nor did it state its essential findings on the record or make written findings — as required by Erum. It therefore erred in granting Century's MTD.
10936856.situation:
CASE FILE

Parties
- Plaintiff/Counterclaim-Defendant: Century Campus Housing Management, L.P. ("Century").
- Defendants/Counterclaim-Plaintiffs: EH/KAD (Elda Hana, LLC and related party, referred to collectively as "EH/KAD").

Nature of the Action
This is a breach of contract action pending in the Circuit Court. Century commenced the litigation in March 2010 by filing a complaint against EH/KAD alleging breach of contract. EH/KAD filed a counterclaim.

Procedural History Before Remand
Century filed motions for partial summary judgment as to certain counts of the counterclaim. The case was thereafter appealed and remanded to the Circuit Court. See Century Campus Hous. Mgmt., L.P. v. Elda Hana, LLC, Nos. CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX & CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX, 2018 WL 637373 (Haw. App. Jan. 31, 2018) (mem. op.).

Post-Remand Pleadings
In March 2020, following remand, EH/KAD filed an amended counterclaim (the First Amended Counterclaim). The First Amended Counterclaim was filed on March 5, 2020. Century answered.

For almost four years thereafter, there were no filings in the case other than a few notices of appearance and withdrawal of counsel.

Century's Motion to Dismiss
In January 2024, Century filed a motion to dismiss EH/KAD's amended counterclaim with prejudice pursuant to Hawaiʻi Rules of Civil Procedure (HRCP) Rule 41(b) ("Century's MTD"). The motion was filed on January 30, 2024.

The entire "Discussion" section of the memorandum in support of Century's MTD stated:

"As detailed above, since the filing of the [First Amended Counterclaim] in early March 2020, Defendants have done nothing to prosecute their claim. Defendants have not propounded any discovery, filed no motions and have failed to file a pre-trial statement. Forty-six months would certainly appear to be proof of a lack of diligence and/or failure to prosecute. It might well be deemed an abandonment of claim."

EH/KAD's Position
EH/KAD opposed Century's MTD. On March 27, 2024, EH/KAD filed its Memorandum in Opposition to Century's MTD.

Submission Without Hearing
On March 18, 2024, the Circuit Court ordered the motion to be submitted on the briefs without a hearing (Dkt. 347). The Circuit Court did not hold a hearing on Century's MTD and considered only the parties' written submissions.

The April 17, 2024 Minute Order
On April 17, 2024, the Circuit Court issued a Minute Order stating:

"4/17/24: Court's Minute Order re: [Century's MTD] having come before the court, the court ordered the motion to be submitted on the briefs without a hearing Dkt. 347 filed March 18, 2024. After consideration of [Century's MTD] and [EH/KAD's] Memorandum in Opposition to the Motion, the court rules as follows: The court will grant the motion and dismiss [EH/KAD's] First Amended Counterclaim with prejudice. The dismissal is predicated on [HRCP] Rule 41(b) for failure of [EH/KAD] to take any action for close to four years to prosecute the counterclaim. [Century's] counsel to prepare written order. Parties served via JEFS."

The Written Order
The next substantive docket entry was the proposed order, filed by Century, on January 10, 2025. The Circuit Court entered a written order on January 16, 2025, which provides in full:

"On January 30, 2024, [Century] filed its [MTD] with Prejudice [EH/KAD's] First Amended Counterclaim ('Motion'), which came before the Honorable John M. Tonaki. The Motion was filed pursuant to [HRCP] Rule 41(b). On March 18, 2024, the Court ordered the [M]otion to be submitted on the briefs without a hearing [Dkt 347]. On March 27, 2024, [EH/KAD] filed its Memorandum in Opposition to [Century's MTD] [EH/KAD's] First Amended Counterclaim Filed on March 5, 2020 [Dkt. 325].

The Court, having considered the Motion, the Opposition, and the exhibits thereto, and the arguments of counsel, and being duly advised of the record and files herein, and for good cause shown, entered its Order Granting [Century's MTD] with prejudice on April 17, 2024. The dismissal is predicated on HRCP Rule 41(b) for failure of counterclaim plaintiff to take any action for close to four (4) years to prosecute the counterclaim.

Therefore, in accordance with the Court Order IT IS HEREBY ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED that [Century's MTD] is GRANTED for the reasons set forth in the Court's minutes which are attached hereto as Exhibit A."

Judicial Officers
The Honorable John M. Tonaki and the Honorable James H. Ashford presided at various points in the matter.

Motion for Reconsideration and Judgment
EH/KAD filed a Motion for Reconsideration, which the Circuit Court denied. The Final Judgment was entered on August 20, 2025.

Governing Standard
The motion was brought and decided under HRCP Rule 41(b), on the ground of failure to prosecute the counterclaim, based on EH/KAD's asserted inaction — no discovery propounded, no motions filed, and no pre-trial statement filed — for a period of close to four years following the March 5, 2020 filing of the First Amended Counterclaim.

Relief Sought
Century sought dismissal of EH/KAD's First Amended Counterclaim with prejudice. EH/KAD opposed the dismissal and later sought reconsideration of the order granting dismissal.
