10937838.holding_quote: To the extent the court found Orchid's presentation below was sufficient to discharge its burden of proving that litigating Salamon's claims "'will not diminish in any way [his] substantive rights afforded . . . under [sections 1600 and 1601]'" (Verdugo, supra, 237 Cal.App.4th at pp. 147–148), the court erred.
10937838.situation:
PARTIES AND ENTITIES

David Salamon is a California resident and a shareholder of Orchid Global, Inc. (Orchid). He was a contractor for Orchid from 2017 to 2019. Since 2019, he has held 11.11% of Orchid's outstanding voting shares.

Orchid Global, Inc. and its subsidiary, Orchid Labs, Inc., are Delaware corporations with their principal places of business in San Francisco. Orchid Labs, Inc. is a software provider. OXT is Orchid's token, which can be used to pay for the VPN (Virtual Private Network) services Orchid offers. A VPN is a network that protects a user's privacy by routing an internet connection through a secure server, making it appear as if the user is browsing from that server's location rather than the user's actual location.

BACKGROUND FACTS

In December 2024, Orchid offered to purchase all of Salamon's shares for $1,372,880.

On April 1, 2025, Salamon's counsel sent a letter to Orchid's counsel requesting to inspect the following documents pursuant to Corporations Code sections 1600 and 1601:

1. The record of the names and addresses of all shareholders and the number of shares held by each;
2. All minutes of meetings of the shareholders, Board of Directors, and/or committees of the Board for the past five years;
3. All quarterly and annual financial statements of the Company and its subsidiaries, including income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements for the past five years;
4. All financial audits of the Company and its subsidiaries prepared by an independent auditing firm for the past five years;
5. Copies of the federal and state income tax returns for the Company and its subsidiaries, including all supporting schedules, for the past five years;
6. The current Certificate of Incorporation and Bylaws of the Company and its subsidiaries and any amendments thereto;
7. Documents sufficient to show the terms and status of any off balance sheet loans made by the Company or any of its subsidiaries;
8. Documents sufficient to show the terms and status of any loans the Company or any of its subsidiaries made to any Board member;
9. Documents sufficient to show the Company's accounting of OXT owned by, or held in the treasury of, the Company or any of its subsidiaries;
10. All documents referring or relating to complaints that Orchid Labs, Inc. violates state and/or federal gambling laws; and
11. All communications of any Board member discussing whether Orchid Labs, Inc. violates state and/or federal gambling laws.

In the letter, Salamon's counsel explained that Salamon sought these records for four stated reasons: (1) to confirm his ownership interest in the Company; (2) to determine the current and potential value of such interest; (3) to communicate with other shareholders; and (4) to investigate mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duties by the Company's management.

In a letter dated April 10, Orchid's counsel rejected Salamon's request in its entirety. Counsel wrote that the Company is a Delaware corporation and thus the demand is void ab initio as it seeks to inspect and copy the Company's books and records under an inapplicable California statute. Counsel further stated that, separate and apart from the demand being invalid under California law, under applicable Delaware law a shareholder demand to inspect books and records must be for a proper purpose, and characterized the demand as appearing to be part of a scheme to extort the Company into buying back Salamon's shares at an inflated price by leveraging what counsel described as bogus illegal gambling allegations regarding Orchid's nanopayment system.

According to Salamon, for the past five years he has not received any financial documents from Orchid and thus has not been able to evaluate the value of his shares.

GOVERNING STATUTES

Corporations Code section 1600, subdivision (a), provides in relevant part: "A shareholder . . . holding at least 5 percent in the aggregate of the outstanding voting shares of a corporation . . . shall have an absolute right to . . . inspect and copy the record of shareholders' names and addresses and shareholdings . . . ." Section 1600, subdivision (d), provides: "The rights provided in this section may not be limited by the articles or bylaws."

Corporations Code section 1601, subdivision (a), provides in relevant part: "The accounting books, records, and minutes of proceedings of the shareholders and the board and committees of the board of any domestic corporation . . . shall be open to inspection at the corporation's principal office in California . . . for a purpose reasonably related to the holder's interests as a shareholder . . . ." Section 1601, subdivision (b), provides: "The right of the shareholders to inspect the corporate records may not be limited by the articles or bylaws."

Delaware General Corporation Law section 220 (Del. Code Ann. tit. 8, § 220) permits inspection of a corporation's books by any shareholder who demands it, provided the shareholder articulates a proper purpose.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY

On April 18, 2025, Salamon filed in the San Francisco Superior Court a petition for a writ of mandate to compel Orchid to allow him to inspect and copy his requested records pursuant to sections 1600 and 1601.

On May 30, 2025, Orchid filed in the Delaware Court of Chancery a complaint for declaratory relief to enforce its rights under Section 220 of the Delaware General Corporation Law (the Delaware action). Orchid sought a declaration that Delaware law (not California law) governs the rights, if any, of minority shareholder Salamon to inspect Orchid's books and records, and that Orchid is not obligated to make its books and records available to Salamon for inspection pursuant to sections 1600 and 1601.

On that same day, Orchid filed in the superior court a motion to stay the proceedings based on a forum selection clause in its bylaws. The bylaw provides in relevant part: "Forum. Unless the corporation consents in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware shall be the sole and exclusive forum for . . . any action asserting a claim against the corporation or any director or officer or other employee of the corporation governed by the internal affairs doctrine." The bylaws contain no choice-of-law provision.

ORCHID'S POSITION ON THE MOTION

Orchid argued that under both California and Delaware law, Salamon's right to inspect Orchid's books and records is an internal affair governed by the internal affairs doctrine, which places the dispute squarely under the mandatory forum selection clause in Orchid's bylaws. Orchid asserted that the trial court should stay the action during the pendency of the Delaware action.

SALAMON'S POSITION ON THE MOTION

Salamon opposed the motion. He did not dispute Orchid's assertion that the forum selection clause was mandatory, but argued that the clause does not cover this dispute. He maintained that, contrary to Orchid's contention, California law holds that a shareholder inspection demand does not implicate the internal affairs of a Delaware corporation operating in California.

Alternatively, Salamon argued that even if the forum selection clause applies, it is unenforceable because it violates public policy. He asserted that a shareholder's right to inspect corporate records is unwaivable under sections 1600 and 1601, and that he would be deprived of such right if the forum selection clause were enforced.

ORCHID'S REPLY

Orchid reasserted that Delaware law, not California law, governed the interpretation of the forum selection clause and that, in any event, both Delaware and California law hold that a shareholder's right to inspect records is an internal affair. Orchid maintained the clause covered Salamon's inspection request. Orchid also disagreed that enforcing the clause would violate public policy, asserting that Salamon has a clear avenue to seek inspection of Orchid's books and records under Section 220 of the Delaware Code.

THE HEARING

On July 9, 2025, the court conducted a hearing on the motion, prior to which it issued a tentative ruling granting the motion. During the hearing, the court observed that neither party had addressed whether Delaware law or California law governs the interpretation of a forum selection clause in the bylaws of a Delaware corporation. The court stated that question was dispositive and asked Salamon's counsel, "What law governs how I interpret that forum selection clause?" Salamon's counsel stated that the bylaws say Delaware law applies; the bylaws in fact contain no choice-of-law provision. Counsel then argued that the court has to interpret California Corporations Code section 1600, and that whether it involves and invokes the internal affairs doctrine should be decided under California law.

The parties also addressed Salamon's argument that the forum selection clause was unenforceable as contrary to California public policy. Salamon's counsel argued that Salamon would lose unwaivable rights if the clause were enforced because of critical differences between a shareholder inspection demand made under California Corporations Code section 1600 and Section 220 of the Delaware Code. Counsel asserted that the California statute provides broader inspection rights and the Delaware statute is narrower, so that if forced to make an inspection demand under Delaware law, Salamon will lose valuable protections under California law and be severely limited in the financial information he can seek.

At the conclusion of the hearing, the court adopted its tentative ruling as its final order.

THE ORDER UNDER REVIEW

On July 11, 2025, the court filed its written order granting Orchid's motion to stay. The order was based on the petition, its attached exhibits, and the declarations and exhibits attached to the parties' papers in connection with the motion to stay.

The court first assessed, as a matter of contract interpretation, whether Salamon's inspection demand was covered by the forum selection clause. The court determined that Delaware law governed the interpretation of that clause. As to whether a shareholder's inspection request constituted a matter concerning a corporation's internal affairs within the meaning of the clause, the court noted that Delaware law answered that question in the affirmative and added that, in any event, California law is in accord. The court concluded that the forum selection clause covered Salamon's claims.

The court then turned to, and rejected, Salamon's argument that the court should not enforce the forum selection clause because it would vitiate his unwaivable right as a California resident shareholder to inspect Orchid's books. The court explained that Salamon cited two public policies, one of which was his unwaivable right as a shareholder to inspect Orchid's books under Corporations Code section 1601. The court stated that Delaware law allows for inspection rights of the corporation's books by any shareholder who demands it, provided the shareholder articulates a proper purpose, citing Delaware Code Annotated title 8, section 220. The court noted that the Delaware Court of Chancery recognizes that a shareholder's desire to inspect corporate books to value his shares is a proper purpose, citing Woods Trustee v. Sahara Ents., Inc. (Del. Ct. Ch. 2020) 238 A.3d 879, 891, and that this is the purpose Salamon recites here. The court therefore concluded that enforcing the forum selection clause does not offend California public policy.

RELIEF SOUGHT

Salamon seeks issuance of a writ of mandate to compel Orchid to allow him to inspect and copy the requested corporate records pursuant to Corporations Code sections 1600 and 1601. Orchid seeks a stay of the superior court proceedings during the pendency of the Delaware action based on the bylaws' forum selection clause.

RELATED DELAWARE PROCEEDINGS (MATTERS SUBJECT TO JUDICIAL NOTICE)

Salamon filed and obtained judicial notice of several filings in the Delaware action, including his motion to dismiss that action for lack of personal jurisdiction over him, his accompanying affidavit, Orchid's opposition, his reply, and his supplemental affidavit. Salamon also sought and obtained judicial notice of the transcript of the hearing on his motion to dismiss in the Delaware action and of the Delaware Court of Chancery's memorandum opinion and order granting the motion to dismiss on the ground that Orchid lacked personal jurisdiction over Salamon.

seed.consideration: Before enforcing the forum selection clause, the enforcing party must show that Delaware's inspection statute provides the same or greater rights than California's sections 1600 and 1601, or that Delaware will apply California law, so as not to diminish Salamon's unwaivable statutory rights.
seed.why_material: Because the anti-waiver provisions of sections 1600 and 1601 make the party seeking enforcement bear the burden, and the trial court's failure to compare the two statutes' scope allowed a forum selection clause to circumvent unwaivable inspection rights, violating California public policy.

10872589.situation:
CASE FILE

Parties and Charges

Defendants Joel Smith (Mr. Smith) and Amanda Smith (Mrs. Smith), husband and wife, are charged and tried together in the United States District Court following indictment by a federal grand jury on July 18, 2022. That indictment superseded an earlier indictment and is the operative charging document.

Mr. Smith is a member of the Cherokee Nation. Mrs. Smith is non-Indian. The victim, referred to as H.M. (also identified at trial as M.V. and K.B.), is Indian.

Mr. Smith is charged with one count of child abuse in Indian country in violation of Oklahoma law, OKLA. STAT. tit. 21, § 843.5(A), and one count of child neglect in Indian country in violation of OKLA. STAT. tit. 21, § 843.5(C). Because Mr. Smith is Indian and the offenses occurred in Indian country, the government proceeds under the Major Crimes Act (MCA), 18 U.S.C. § 1153.

Mrs. Smith is charged with one count of child abuse and one count of child neglect under the same Oklahoma statutes. Because Mrs. Smith is not Indian, her victim is Indian, and the offenses occurred in Indian country, the government proceeds under the Assimilative Crimes Act (ACA), 18 U.S.C. § 13, as applied to Indian country through the General Crimes Act (GCA), 18 U.S.C. § 1152.

The indictment further charges each defendant with aiding and abetting the other in the commission of these offenses.

Factual Background

In 2014, Mr. Smith's then five-year-old niece, H.M., moved in with Mr. and Mrs. Smith. On April 5, 2019, H.M. ran away to a neighbor's home. She appeared malnourished and unwashed, was extremely hungry, wore a diaper, smelled of urine and feces, and showed signs of physical abuse. The neighbor called police. H.M. was hospitalized for a week to treat infections and malnutrition.

An investigation indicated H.M. experienced severe neglect and abuse while she lived with the Smiths. According to that investigation, H.M. was deprived of food, forced to perform manual labor outside, beaten frequently with a belt and a livestock whip, handcuffed at night, and made to wear a diaper. When found, H.M. was nine years old and weighed 42 pounds—eight pounds less than when she entered the Smiths' care.

Pleas and Trial

The Smiths pleaded not guilty. Their joint jury trial began on June 20, 2023, and lasted three days. Mrs. Smith testified; Mr. Smith did not. The jury also heard testimony from H.M. and from Mrs. Smith's daughter, Allison Smith.

Mr. Smith's primary defense was that he did not abuse or neglect H.M. Mrs. Smith's primary defense was that H.M. had challenging medical needs and that, given those circumstances, the government had not carried its burden of showing criminal misconduct.

Aiding-and-Abetting Objection

Near the end of trial, Mrs. Smith objected to the government's proposed jury instruction on aiding and abetting and asked to be dismissed from the indictment. She argued the MCA applies only to an Indian defendant, so the statute cannot be used to prosecute her, a non-Indian, as an aider or abettor. See 18 U.S.C. § 1153(a). Mr. Smith joined the objection. He argued that, because he is Indian, he cannot be found guilty of aiding and abetting under the GCA, which does not apply to offenses committed by one Indian against the person or property of another Indian. See 18 U.S.C. § 1152.

The district court denied the motions and instructed the jury on aiding and abetting.

Verdict

On June 23, 2023, the jury found each defendant guilty on one count of child abuse and one count of child neglect.

Post-Trial Motions (Mrs. Smith)

Mrs. Smith moved for a judgment of acquittal under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 29 and a new trial under Rule 33. As relevant here, she argued her convictions should be dismissed because, after Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. 629 (2022), a federal court would lack subject-matter jurisdiction over her offenses. The district court denied the motion.

Sentencing

A probation officer prepared a presentence investigation report (PSR) for Mr. Smith. In calculating the advisory Guidelines range, the PSR stated that no analogous guideline exists for a violation of child abuse in Indian country or child neglect in Indian country. The PSR explained that when no sufficiently analogous guideline exists, the provisions of 18 U.S.C. § 3553 control. The PSR concluded the Guidelines range is up to life imprisonment per count.

Mr. Smith objected, arguing the district court should use U.S.S.G. § 2A2.2, the federal sentencing guideline for aggravated assault, when calculating his advisory range. In his calculation, use of U.S.S.G. § 2A2.2 as a starting point would have yielded an advisory range of 46–57 months in prison. Before sentencing, all agreed there is no expressly promulgated guideline for child abuse by injury.

Governing sentencing framework: every federal sentencing proceeding begins with determining the guideline section applicable to the offense of conviction under U.S.S.G. § 1B1.2(a). Where no guideline has been promulgated for the offense, the court must apply the most analogous offense guideline under U.S.S.G. § 2X5.1.

At sentencing, the district court rejected Mr. Smith's argument to apply U.S.S.G. § 2A2.2 and instead followed the PSR's approach, concluding Mr. Smith could be sentenced to any number of years up to life imprisonment. The court applied the factors under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) and imposed a total term of 180 months of imprisonment, with the sentences on the two counts to run concurrently.

The district court sentenced Mrs. Smith to concurrent terms of 240 months of imprisonment, applying the § 3553(a) factors.

Victim-Impact Letters

Approximately 22 hours before the sentencing, the government submitted four letters, described as victim-impact statements, to the district court. The Smiths requested more time to review the letters or to quash them. The district court refused the request.

Mrs. Smith's Second Post-Trial Motion

Almost two weeks after sentencing, Mrs. Smith filed an amended second motion for judgment of acquittal, new trial, or correction of sentence under Rules 29 and 33. The district court denied the motion, concluding Mrs. Smith filed it too late.

Relief Sought

Mr. Smith seeks resentencing on the ground that the district court miscalculated his advisory Guidelines range and imposed a procedurally unreasonable sentence by concluding there is no sufficiently analogous guideline for his child abuse conviction under OKLA. STAT. tit. 21, § 843.5(A), and by declining to apply U.S.S.G. § 2A2.2.

The Smiths jointly contend the district court erroneously refused to consider their objection to the aiding-and-abetting jury instruction.

Mrs. Smith contends the district court erred in denying her motion to dismiss the indictment for lack of jurisdiction under Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. 629 (2022).

Mrs. Smith contends the district court erroneously determined her second motion for a new trial and judgment of acquittal was untimely.

Mrs. Smith seeks resentencing, contending the district court improperly considered the letters submitted by the government on the eve of sentencing, arguing they were written by individuals who do not count as victims under 18 U.S.C. § 3771(e)(2).

Applicable Authorities Invoked

OKLA. STAT. tit. 21, § 843.5(A) and (C); 18 U.S.C. § 1153 (Major Crimes Act); 18 U.S.C. § 13 (Assimilative Crimes Act); 18 U.S.C. § 1152 (General Crimes Act); U.S.S.G. §§ 1B1.2(a), 2X5.1, and 2A2.2; 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a); 18 U.S.C. § 3771(e)(2); Fed. R. Crim. P. 29 and 33; Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. 629 (2022).

10873243.holding_quote: The juvenile court did not resolve the foundational legal question of whether the investigatory stop was lawful and did not determine whether Davis provided credible information to support Fehrman's reasonable suspicion.
10873243.situation:
This is a juvenile delinquency matter in the Hamilton County Juvenile Court involving the respondent K.J. The State filed delinquency complaints and a traffic citation arising from events on September 11, 2024. The matter reaches the posture of the juvenile court's rulings on K.J.'s motion to suppress and its adjudications following an evidentiary hearing and adjudication hearing.

CHARGES: On September 11, 2024, the State filed delinquency complaints against K.J. alleging acts that, if committed by an adult, would constitute: (1) carrying a concealed weapon in violation of R.C. 2923.12, a third-degree felony; (2) tampering with evidence in violation of R.C. 2921.12(A)(1), a third-degree felony; and (3) obstructing official business in violation of R.C. 2921.31, a second-degree misdemeanor. K.J. was also cited for a jaywalking violation under Cincinnati Municipal Code (CMC) 506.46. The initial jaywalking citation was filed September 11, 2024, then dismissed and refiled by the State on December 19, 2024. K.J. was also charged with burglary and receiving stolen property, but those charges were dismissed.

GENERAL FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS: The complaints, taken together, allege that K.J. jaywalked outside of a marked crosswalk, then ran from police who attempted to investigate. When police searched an apartment K.J. entered after fleeing, they found a firearm hidden in a closet. The State charged K.J. with concealing the weapon on his person and then tampering with it to prevent police from finding it. K.J. was arrested and taken into custody after he came out of the apartment.

MOTION TO SUPPRESS: On January 7, 2025, K.J. filed a motion to suppress evidence, arguing that police lacked both reasonable suspicion for the initial stop and probable cause for the arrest. The juvenile court held an evidentiary hearing at which three Cincinnati Police Department (CPD) witnesses testified: Sergeant James Davis, Officer Zachary Kress, and Officer Cameron Fehrman.

Suppression hearing testimony -- Sergeant Davis: Davis had been with CPD for 27 years and was assigned to the Crime Gun Intelligence Unit (CGIU), where he had worked since 2018. On September 11, 2024, his unit was conducting surveillance in the Village of Roll Hill by the Fay Apartments, a neighborhood he described as a 'high crime area.' Davis was in plain clothes but supported by uniformed officers, and observed from his car parked on President Drive. From that vantage point, Davis saw K.J., who was wearing a crossbody bag, and two other young men cross from Baltimore to President Drive without using either of the two crosswalks available at the intersection. Davis radioed ahead to another officer closer to the boys' location to report what he had seen. On cross-examination, Davis was questioned about a possible discrepancy between CPD's investigation report and the jaywalking citations. He acknowledged the investigation report indicated the offense location was 3732 President Drive, the original jaywalking citation alleged 3700 President Drive, and the refiled citation stated 3601 President Drive. Davis admitted none of these addresses matched the location where he saw the boys jaywalk. He explained that he did not create the investigation report or either citation and was unaware the State had dismissed and refiled the jaywalking citation. He pointed out that the incident occurred in several locations -- including where K.J. jaywalked and the apartment K.J. entered -- but the investigation report and citation forms provide space for only one address.

Suppression hearing testimony -- Officer Kress: Kress had been with CPD for eight years and assigned to the CGIU since 2021. On September 11, 2024, he went to the Village of Roll Hill apartments to follow up on ShotSpotter alerts (a technological system that alerts police to gunshots in real time). While conducting surveillance in an unmarked car near 3708 or 3710 President Drive, Kress heard Davis report over the radio that he saw three individuals commit a jaywalking violation and the direction the suspected jaywalkers were headed. The boys soon walked past Kress's car. Kress observed one of the young men, C.H., with his 'arm pinned against his hip' with 'no arm swing,' while his other arm swung normally; Kress said this could be indicative of holding a firearm to prevent it from falling. Kress also noticed K.J. wearing a crossbody bag, which he said could be used to carry a firearm. Kress then told uniformed officers by radio to conduct an investigative stop for the jaywalking violations. He watched officers approach the boys, who immediately started running.

Suppression hearing testimony -- Officer Fehrman: Fehrman, a CPD officer, was working in uniform on September 11, 2024 when he received a dispatch from Kress to stop the boys regarding the jaywalking incident. Kress relayed that C.H. was holding onto his waist and that K.J. had a crossbody bag. Fehrman testified that over his years on the force he has found multiple firearms and drugs in crossbody bags. In a police cruiser, Fehrman approached the boys from behind, got out, and attempted to stop them to discuss the jaywalking. According to Fehrman, when K.J. and C.H. saw him, they began running, which prevented him from fully conducting the stop. Fehrman told them to stop, threatened to tase them, and chased them to a building where K.J. went into the back door of an apartment. Fehrman then left K.J. and continued chasing C.H.

RULING ON SUPPRESSION: Following the hearing, the juvenile court denied K.J.'s suppression motion. The court held that officers had probable cause to arrest K.J. for obstruction of official business because he ran from police. The court stated: 'This is not a Terry stop. This is a probable cause stop for an obstruction of official business. . . . In this case, before being able to be stopped for what might have been an illegal Terry respond or might not have been an illegal Terry respond, two of the three took off running. . . . So the Court is making a delineation between a Terry stop and a reasonable suspicion and probable cause caused by further running by a kid or kids when they saw a police officer, which Ohio Supreme Court law supports.'

ADJUDICATION HEARING: On June 16, 2025, the juvenile court conducted an adjudication hearing. Davis and Fehrman both testified as they had at the suppression hearing. Fehrman also testified about the results of a search of the apartment conducted after K.J. was in custody. Fehrman found a loaded gun in a lunch box hidden on the floor of a utility closet. Police also found the crossbody bag K.J. had been wearing on a bed in the apartment. Marijuana was near the bag on the bed. Fehrman never saw what, if anything, was inside the bag.

Officer Chris Vogelpohl, a CPD officer assigned to the CGIU, testified that he collected the gun from the apartment on September 11, 2024. It was loaded with nine bullets, one in the chamber. Vogelpohl test-fired the gun twice, confirming operability. He also swabbed the gun for DNA.

Kress testified that he waited with other officers for about 20 or 30 minutes before K.J. exited the apartment. Kress saw the gun when it was hidden inside the closet but never saw the contents of K.J.'s crossbody bag. He also collected K.J.'s DNA.

Officer Nick Clark of CPD questioned K.J. at the police department after his arrest. K.J. said that on September 11, 2024, he spent the day with his girlfriend at The Fay and met up with a friend (described by Clark as C.H., K.J.'s codefendant, the other person who ran). K.J. admitted that a person who lives at The Fay gave him the gun. When asked where he hid the gun, K.J. said he did not remember. On cross-examination, Clark acknowledged that the offense addresses on the investigation report and both jaywalking citations were inconsistent, explaining that the offenses occurred in several different locations. Although Clark filled out part of the citation, he admitted he did not personally observe K.J. jaywalking.

ADJUDICATIONS: After the adjudication hearing, the juvenile court adjudicated K.J. delinquent of obstructing official business, carrying a concealed deadly weapon, and tampering with evidence, and adjudged him a juvenile traffic offender for the jaywalking offense. The court continued the matter for disposition.

DISPOSITION: At the disposition hearing, the juvenile court ordered K.J. committed to the permanent custody of the Ohio Department of Youth Services until age 21 for carrying a concealed weapon and tampering with evidence, but suspended the commitment on the condition that K.J. engage in treatment and complete the recommendations of his probation officer. For the obstructing adjudication, the court ordered K.J. to stay away from 2204 Williamsburg Drive until August 15, 2029. As to the obstructing and jaywalking adjudications, the court remitted court costs due to K.J.'s indigence.

ISSUES RAISED BY K.J.: K.J. contends the trial court erred in failing to suppress evidence obtained after he ran from what he contends was an unreasonable police encounter. He challenges the sufficiency of the evidence supporting his adjudications for carrying a concealed deadly weapon, tampering with evidence, and obstructing official business. He argues that his adjudication for jaywalking was against the manifest weight of the evidence.

10876644.holding_quote: Based on the foregoing, we find that the ICA was correct when it concluded that the circuit court failed to consider the relevant HAWJIC 3.19A factors and the effect of suggestiveness in finding CW's identification sufficiently reliable.
10876644.situation:
PARTIES AND CHARGE

Respondent/Defendant-Appellant Silber M. Jercy (Jercy) is charged with assault in the second degree, in violation of Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes (HRS) § 707-711(1)(m) (Supp. 2021). The matter proceeds in the Circuit Court, the Honorable Rowena A. Somerville presiding.

FACTS FROM TRIAL TESTIMONY

On March 22, 2022, the complaining witness (CW), sixty-nine years old at the time, was hanging laundry at her Halawa home when a man she had never seen before attacked her by hitting her several times around her head. The man ran off, and two of CW's neighbors separately chased after him.

One neighbor, C. Hernandez (Hernandez), testified that he went after the man on his moped but lost sight of the man for ten to fifteen seconds during the chase. The other neighbor, J. Wainit (Wainit), drove off in a car with his "friend" but admitted that he did not get a "clear view" of the assailant. The record does not identify Wainit's "friend."

The neighbors subsequently saw Jercy sitting at a nearby bus stop, which Hernandez testified was approximately one to two minutes away by moped. Believing that Jercy was the man who had hit CW, the neighbors detained Jercy and called the police. Honolulu Police Department (HPD) Officer Alayna Benton (Officer Benton) arrived at the bus stop and handcuffed Jercy.

Back at CW's home, CW, whose primary language is Chuukese, verbally provided HPD with a brief description of the assailant. CW's granddaughter was present to interpret between Chuukese and English, but HPD did not obtain a written statement from CW at the time because of the language barrier. According to HPD Officer Jon Tomishima, a Chuukese translator was not available at the time.

CW was told that HPD "had a male in custody" and that she "would identify him before [going] to the hospital." CW was then placed in an ambulance for transport to the hospital without her granddaughter or a Chuukese interpreter. The ambulance was rerouted to the nearby bus stop to have CW identify her attacker. Officer Tomishima testified that although HPD wanted to instruct CW that the perpetrator may or may not be present in the show-up, he was unable to provide that instruction due to the language barrier.

After the ambulance arrived near the bus stop, CW, who was sitting on a gurney in the back of the ambulance, was able to view Jercy through the rear windows. During this field show-up, Jercy stood alone and remained handcuffed, with his hands behind his back and an HPD officer standing behind him. No other persons were shown to CW.

CW identified Jercy as her attacker. CW testified that she based her identification on Jercy's face.

SUPPRESSION MOTION

Prior to his jury trial, Jercy moves to suppress CW's field show-up identification, arguing that the show-up was so suggestive that it was unreliable for presentation at trial.

The governing authority is State v. Kaneaiakala, 145 Hawaiʻi 231, 450 P.3d 761 (2019). The applicable factors are set out in Hawaiʻi Pattern Jury Instructions--Criminal (HAWJIC) 3.19 and HAWJIC 3.19A.

HAWJIC 3.19 (Eyewitness Testimony) provides that the burden of proof is on the prosecution as to every element, including proof beyond a reasonable doubt of the identity of the defendant as the person responsible for the crime, and directs the factfinder to decide whether an eyewitness gave accurate identification testimony. In evaluating identification testimony, the factfinder may consider: the opportunity of the witness to observe the person involved in the alleged criminal act; the stress, if any, to which the witness was subject at the time of observation; the witness's ability, following the observation, to provide a description of the person; the extent to which the defendant fits or does not fit the description previously given; the cross-racial or ethnic nature of the identification; the witness's capacity to make an identification; evidence relating to the witness's ability to identify other participants; whether the witness was able to identify the person in a photographic or physical lineup; the period of time between the alleged criminal act and the identification; whether the witness had prior contacts with the person; the extent to which the witness is certain or uncertain and whether assertions of certainty or uncertainty are well-founded; whether the identification is in fact the product of the witness's own recollection; and any other evidence relating to the witness's ability to make an identification.

HAWJIC 3.19A addresses identifications made at police show-ups. It states that while show-ups are permissible, they are inherently suggestive police procedures, and that in determining the reliability and accuracy of an identification made at a show-up, the totality of the circumstances must be considered, which may include: whether the identification was the result of a suggestive procedure, including actions taken or words spoken by police or anyone else before, during, or after the identification process; whether the police indicated to the witness that a suspect was present or failed to warn the witness that the perpetrator may or may not be in the procedure; and whether the defendant was required to wear distinctive clothing the perpetrator allegedly wore, or was handcuffed or otherwise appeared to be in police custody.

Relying on Kaneaiakala, the circuit court analyzes the facts in light of the relevant factors listed in HAWJIC 3.19 and determines that CW's identification is sufficiently reliable notwithstanding the suggestiveness of the field show-up. The circuit court denies Jercy's suppression motion.

TRIAL RESULT

The jury finds Jercy guilty as charged. An Amended Judgment of Conviction is entered.

PROCEEDINGS ON APPEAL AND CERTIORARI

On appeal, the Intermediate Court of Appeals (ICA) vacates the circuit court's judgment and remands for a new trial. Applying Kaneaiakala, the ICA finds that the circuit court erroneously failed to consider the relevant factors listed in HAWJIC 3.19A and the effect of the suggestiveness of the show-up on the reliability of CW's identification. The ICA does not indicate whether CW's identification would be admissible or was suppressed upon remand.

The State applies for certiorari, presenting four questions: (1) whether the ICA erred or acted inconsistently with prior decisions by requiring the circuit court to expressly address the factors in HAWJIC 3.19A in its admissibility determination; (2) whether the ICA erred or acted inconsistently with prior decisions in vacating the circuit court's decision even though the circuit court did in fact consider the relevant factors regarding suggestiveness; (3) whether the ICA erred or acted inconsistently with prior decisions in vacating the circuit court's decision based on the suggestiveness of the show-up when the real issue was whether the identification was reliable notwithstanding suggestiveness; and (4) whether the ICA erred or acted inconsistently with prior decisions in vacating the Amended Judgment of Conviction even though any errors in the identification constituted harmless error. The application was granted on April 29, 2026.

seed.why_material: Because these considerations, not addressed below, determined whether the identification evidence should be suppressed rather than left for the jury to weigh.

10879164.situation:
CASE FILE — State v. Kayne (bench trial, criminal)

CHARGES
The state charges defendant with two counts of maintaining a dangerous dog under ORS chapter 609. The charges arise from an incident involving defendant's two dogs, Moki and Gyptian, and a dog named Baby Girl owned by another person, Gaul.

GOVERNING LAW
The prosecution proceeds under ORS 609.035. (After defendant's conviction, the legislature amended ORS 609.035 by Or Laws 2025, ch 170, § 1; the parties and court work from the version in effect at trial.) The offense as argued turns on whether defendant's dogs caused physical injury to a domestic animal without provocation, at a location where defendant has no lawful right to exclude others. Criminal negligence is defined by ORS 161.085(10) as a failure to be aware of a substantial and unjustifiable risk that a specified result will occur or that a specified circumstance exists, where the risk is of such nature and degree that the failure to be aware of it constitutes a gross deviation from the standard of care that a reasonable person would observe in the situation.

POSTURE AND WAIVERS
Defendant appears pro se. Defendant waived a jury and proceeded to a bench trial before the trial court.

THE STATE'S THEORY (OPENING)
The state argued that the evidence would show that defendant had previously been convicted of maintaining two dogs — Moki and Gyptian — as a nuisance, and that the two dogs broke through defendant's fence and pulled Baby Girl into defendant's yard.

DEFENDANT'S THEORY (OPENING)
Defendant argued that the evidence would show that Baby Girl bit her small dog, Zorro, through the fence; that Gyptian and Moki had been provoked when Zorro yelped; and that Baby Girl was 'stuck in [her] broken fence' on defendant's private property when Moki and Gyptian grabbed her.

STATE'S EVIDENCE
Gaul testified that he was walking Baby Girl on a public path past defendant's house, on the outside of a picket fence that surrounded defendant's yard. Gaul saw a small barking dog, Zorro, in defendant's front yard. Baby Girl did not bark at Zorro or try to push her nose through the fence. As they walked by, two large dogs, Moki and Gyptian, broke through a 'makeshift' barrier on defendant's porch, charged toward the picket fence, and broke a board off the fence. One of the dogs reached through the broken fence, grabbed Baby Girl, and dragged her through the fence into defendant's yard, where both dogs 'started mauling her' until Gaul went into the yard and defendant came out of her house to intervene.

Shoesmith testified that she was driving past defendant's house and saw defendant's two dogs break the fence and pull Baby Girl into the yard, and that Baby Girl did not 'initiate the physical alteration.'

The state presented photos of injuries on Baby Girl's chest, back, and underarm, and photos of the fence showing a board that had been replaced in the location where Gaul and Shoesmith testified the dogs had broken through.

The state also presented evidence that defendant had previously been convicted of two counts of maintaining a potentially dangerous dog as a public nuisance after Moki and Gyptian attacked another dog at a campground.

DEFENDANT'S EVIDENCE
Defendant called her neighbor, McCrery, who testified that as Gaul and Baby Girl walked by the fence, Baby Girl was barking and nipping at Zorro through the fence. McCrery testified that Baby Girl pushed her head through the fence and bit Zorro, and that Moki and Gyptian grabbed Baby Girl's head when it was sticking through the fence and pulled her farther into the yard.

Defendant offered photos of a small, decorative fence in her yard that had been knocked over, and argued that the direction in which the small fence was knocked over rebutted the state's theory that her dogs charged at and broke the larger fence.

STATE'S CLOSING
The state argued that defendant should be found guilty because her dogs 'caused physical injury to a domestic animal without provocation and on a location where [defendant] has no lawful right to exclude another.' The state pointed to Gaul and Shoesmith's testimony that defendant's dogs charged at the fence, broke a fence board, grabbed Baby Girl, dragged her into defendant's yard, and attacked her, causing injuries. The state argued that McCrery's testimony was not credible, that Baby Girl did not provoke the dogs by barking at or biting Zorro, and that Baby Girl was dragged from public property onto defendant's property.

DEFENDANT'S CLOSING
Defendant argued that Baby Girl provoked her dogs by nipping at Zorro through the fence and that Baby Girl 'somehow * * * got through the boards and was a sitting duck on [defendant's] private property.' Defendant argued that 'for the first time in three years' her 'big dogs' got the gate open on her porch to 'go save * * * Zorro' and that she 'reacted as quickly as possible.'

THE TRIAL COURT'S RULING
Before announcing its verdict, the trial court explained that 'the state bears the burden of proving each and every issue, or element, beyond a reasonable doubt.' The court found certain elements not in dispute: that defendant is a keeper of Moki and Gyptian; that there is a previous conviction for those dogs as a public nuisance; and that the two dogs inflicted physical injury on Baby Girl. The court stated that what was in dispute was whether there was provocation by Baby Girl and whether the incident occurred or began on premises from which defendant could lawfully exclude others.

The court found defendant guilty of two counts of maintaining a dangerous dog. It found Gaul's and Shoesmith's testimony credible, found that the area in which the incident began was premises that defendant could not lawfully exclude others from, and found that Moki and Gyptian were not provoked.

seed.consideration: Whether defendant failed to be aware of a substantial and unjustifiable risk that her dogs would injure another animal, constituting a gross deviation from a reasonable standard of care.
seed.why_material: Criminal negligence is a required element the state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt, and convicting without finding it omits an essential element of the offense.

10880488.situation:
PARTIES AND NATURE OF PROCEEDING

This matter involves cross-petitions for domestic violence restraining orders (DVROs) between R.M. (former boyfriend) and A.G. (former girlfriend), each seeking a DVRO against the other under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (DVPA) (Fam. Code, § 6200 et seq.). The court conducted a combined evidentiary hearing on both petitions on September 10, 2024. R.M. was represented by counsel; A.G. represented herself.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND

A.G. and R.M. met in May 2022 at Pasadena City College (PCC), where they took classes and R.M. worked. By October 2022, they were a couple. R.M. was 20 years old; A.G. was 34 years old. In 2023, they lived together for six to eight months. In September 2023, R.M. moved back into his mother's home. The parties broke up in November 2023 (according to A.G.) or December 2023 (according to R.M.). They agree they saw each other at least twice in December 2023.

Both parties claim the other physically, verbally, and emotionally abused them during the relationship. A.G. claims R.M. sexually assaulted her; R.M. claims A.G. falsely accused him of rape. According to A.G., their final in-person confrontation occurred on December 17, 2023, when R.M. broke into A.G.'s home and assaulted her. The next day, A.G. filed a police report. The police photographed bruises on A.G.'s neck, arms, and legs. A.G. later recanted her statement to the police.

There was evidence both parties used drugs during their relationship. Between December 28, 2023 and February 13, 2024, R.M. attended a drug and alcohol abuse rehabilitation program and did not see A.G. in person. Around that same time, A.G. attempted to communicate with R.M. over one thousand times by phone, text, or social media direct messages. In the early morning hours of February 12, 2024, A.G. appeared outside of R.M.'s mother's home. R.M. considered these attempted contacts to be harassment. During this same time, R.M. made various disparaging posts on social media about A.G.

A.G. alleges that on January 2, 2024, she obtained a temporary restraining order (TRO) against R.M. but did not serve it. On January 18, 2024, the court dismissed the case, purportedly at A.G.'s request.

On January 30, 2024, R.M.'s attorney sent a cease-and-desist letter to A.G. directing her to stop communicating with R.M. and to stop making defamatory statements about him to others.

On February 6, 2024, PCC notified R.M. that, at A.G.'s request, the college had instituted "a non-punitive, non-disciplinary" mutual no-contact order. That order prohibited both direct and indirect contact, including through social media, between the parties. After this no-contact order, A.G. texted R.M. multiple times and showed up at his house, and R.M. indirectly contacted A.G. repeatedly through social media.

R.M.'S PETITION FOR A DVRO

On April 26, 2024, R.M. petitioned for a DVRO against A.G. to protect himself and certain members of his family. R.M. averred that on or about August 20 and 31, 2023, A.G. scratched R.M.'s face and neck when she yelled at him and acted erratically because she wanted him to leave their home. The petition provided evidence of repeated and unwanted contact from A.G. following the December 2023 break-up, including that A.G. went to his mother's home "many times" and attempted to contact him repeatedly through email and social media. R.M. claimed A.G. falsely accused him of rape, for which the police declined to bring charges. R.M. explained that A.G. had a history of mental health issues and was suicidal. He also asserted that because of his difficulties with A.G., he had to work remotely, although he was not sure if A.G. still attended PCC.

R.M. attached several exhibits to his petition, including the cease-and-desist letter to A.G., the notice from PCC of the mutual no-contact order, photographs of R.M.'s face and neck with scratch marks, photographs from February 12, 2024 at approximately 1:45 a.m. showing A.G. at a door, and hundreds of pages of screen shots of text or social media direct messages and missed telephone calls from A.G. to R.M. or his mother. In one undated message, A.G. stated, "Is it that you want me to harass you? Don't you have enough evidence? Yeah I did it. I continue to do it. You can block me. I admit I don't have self-control. I have admitted it to everyone." "You win . . . ." "You also have plenty evidence [sic] to file a restraining order or whatever. Just block me."

On April 26, 2024, the court granted a TRO prohibiting A.G. from abusing, contacting, or coming within 100 yards of R.M. or his mother.

A.G. filed a response to R.M.'s petition. She asserted R.M. physically abused her and that to the extent she injured him it was in self-defense. She recognized her messages to R.M. after December 18, 2023 were "incessant," "sometimes hostile," and "wrong," but said she ceased contacting him on March 29, 2024, a month before he filed his request for a DVRO. A.G. argued that if her messages to R.M. had truly disturbed his peace, he would have blocked her on social media sooner and not posted photographs on his social media to taunt her.

A.G.'S PETITION FOR A DVRO

On May 20, 2024, A.G. petitioned for a DVRO against R.M. A.G. alleged abuse by R.M. that included "harassment, humiliation, intimidation, violation of privacy, encourag[ing] suicide, [and] damag[ing] professional rep[utation]." The petition included a lengthy declaration from A.G. and numerous exhibits.

A.G. averred that between January and December 2023, R.M. physically and emotionally abused her. Her declaration detailed the alleged abuse by date. On February 25, R.M. forced A.G. to kneel on the ground, hit her on her head, screamed at her, pushed his thumbs into her eyes, pulled her hair, choked her by putting his hand and fingers into her mouth, and coerced her into having sex with him by threatening to otherwise continue to hurt her. On August 31 (one of the days R.M. claims A.G. scratched his face), R.M. attacked and choked A.G. and kicked in the locked bedroom door, breaking it. On other occasions, R.M. called A.G. degrading names, spit and urinated on her, restrained or trapped her while he screamed at her, and broke into her home. A.G. also alleged that in December 2023, after the break-up, R.M. repeatedly pressured her to have sex with him. She eventually acquiesced on December 17. She claims that later that day R.M. returned to her home, broke in, threw her to the floor and against furniture, screamed at her while he pinned her down, tore her clothing, smashed her smartphone against the wall, and strangled her.

The exhibits to A.G.'s petition included signed statements from two neighbors, who on two separate occasions heard a commotion from A.G.'s apartment due to R.M.'s alleged violence against her. The exhibits also included two declarations from A.G.'s male friend, describing that the friend got into an altercation with R.M. in late August 2023, when stopping R.M. from forcing his way into an apartment to see A.G. when she did not wish to see R.M.; shortly afterwards, R.M. sent the male friend a text stating, "Don't fuck w me boi" with a photograph of a hand holding a gun. A copy of the text and photograph are in the record.

A.G.'s petition also included screenshots of messages between the couple. In one message from September 13, 2023, R.M. apologized for hurting her "emotionally and physically," and asked, "[p]lease give me one more chance." On September 24, 2023, R.M. sent a text message to A.G. admitting to breaking into her home and smashing her phone because he "was just fed up." Photographs from December 18, 2023 showed bruises on A.G.'s neck, arms, and leg, a cellphone with a broken screen, and a broken door.

A.G. declared that in February 2024, R.M. publicly posted images and messages for her to see on his social media, including photographs of his face and neck with scratch marks, A.G.'s male friend, A.G.'s phone number, and A.G. herself (including cropped photographs of her head, face, and bare shoulder purportedly taken while she was in the bath, asleep, or engaged in oral sex). R.M. also changed his username to phrases directed at her, including "A[.]G[.]ispsycho," "ketaminewhor[e]," "pleasekillurself," and "[A.G.'s male friend's name]nevermadeucum." R.M.'s change of his username to "pleasekillurself" was made shortly after A.G. sent a message to R.M. asking him if he wanted her to kill herself. On another occasion, R.M. changed his Instagram username to be the same as the name of A.G.'s online business but ending with ".con" instead of ".com." In May 2024, he sent at least one request to a person acquainted with A.G. to follow that Instagram account. A.G. attached exhibits demonstrating these posts.

A.G. asserted that R.M. repeatedly telephoned A.G.'s mother and male friend. During one phone call, R.M. berated A.G.'s mother for being a bad parent and told her that A.G. had been a stripper.

On May 20, 2024, the court entered a TRO against R.M. prohibiting him from abusing, contacting, or coming within 100 yards of A.G.

THE EVIDENTIARY HEARING

On September 10, 2024, the court held a combined hearing on the parties' mutual DVRO requests.

R.M.'s Testimony: R.M. testified first. The court directed him and his counsel to focus on what "happened from December 2023 to today" (after the couple broke up) that "you think would make me restrain [A.G.]." The court repeatedly redirected R.M. whenever he attempted to talk about incidents during the parties' relationship. R.M. testified that the last time A.G. tried to contact him was March 29, 2024, via direct messaging on social media. Counsel elicited testimony that he sent a cease-and-desist letter to A.G. on January 30, 2024. R.M. explained, "she was incessantly reaching out to me . . . and she would make numerous [online] accounts, saying she was going to threaten me; she was going to spread false allegations to people that I knew personally." R.M. testified that he "told [A.G. he] wanted nothing to do with her. [He] blocked her, changed phone numbers, changed [his] social media accounts, changed emails, to no avail. It hasn't helped." He testified that between December 18, 2023 and March 2024, A.G. sent him over one thousand text messages or other communications and it was not until he sought a DVRO that she stopped. A.G.'s contact caused R.M. to fear for his safety and the safety of his coworkers.

A.G.'s Testimony: The court turned to A.G. and asked, "Anything you want to tell me? You can tell me anything to defend yourself on his request for a restraining order. And you can also tell me why you need one against him." A.G. responded that she wanted to start in December 2023. The court interrupted, saying, "I don't really want you to. I'm not interested. You guys had a relationship, bad or good or somewhere in between. It ended a few years ago. I'm only interested in what's going on recently, and whether I need to restrain you from him, or him from you, or both." (The court's reference to "a few years" was an inadvertent misstatement; the court elsewhere repeatedly stated the relationship ended in December 2023.) At later points, A.G. again attempted to discuss events in December 2023, and each time the court stopped her.

The court asked A.G. if she tried to contact R.M. a thousand times. She said she had. After A.G. again attempted to discuss December 2023, the court interrupted and said, "But he hasn't contacted you since. You've been trying to contact him." The court asked A.G. why she needed to talk to R.M. in February 2024. A.G. responded that she contacted R.M. because she "was unwell." She explained that when R.M. posted photographs of his scratched face on Instagram in February 2024, it triggered her. She also explained that R.M. called her mother a week later and told her mother that A.G. had been a stripper. The court responded that it did not sound like A.G. was done with the relationship "because of all of this contact over a year after you break up, all this contact you're trying to have with him. And the only time it stops is when he gets a temporary restraining order." A.G. denied this and said she stopped contacting R.M. about a month before he sought the DVRO. She explained she filed her request for a DVRO because he changed his Instagram profile to impersonate her business. The court responded, "Do you think it would be better for you if you would just stop looking at his social media?" A.G. agreed it would be best and that she had stopped.

THE COURT'S RULINGS

At the conclusion of the hearing, the court found there was not sufficient evidence to issue a restraining order against R.M.: "[A.G.] described a bad relationship they had, but it was back in late 2023 when it ended. He's made no attempts to contact her, although she's made—and she even agrees—a thousand attempts to contact him, along with going over to his mother's." The court granted R.M.'s request to restrain A.G., stating, "I don't think that [A.G.] will stop trying to contact him in the different ways she [has]."

RELIEF SOUGHT AND GOVERNING LAW

Each party seeks a DVRO against the other under the DVPA (Fam. Code, § 6200 et seq.). Because the parties mutually seek DVROs against each other, section 6305 governs the issuance of mutual orders and whether one or both parties acted as the primary aggressor and/or primarily in self-defense. A.G., in support of her DVRO request, contends the relevant abuse includes indirect contact from R.M. that disturbed her peace, including R.M.'s social media postings that he knew A.G. and others would see (with phrases such as "A[.]G[.]ispsycho," "ketaminewhor[e]," "pleasekillurself," and "[A.G.'s male friend's name]nevermadeucum") and uninvited phone calls to A.G.'s mother, including one in which R.M. disclosed that A.G. had worked as a stripper.

seed.consideration: Whether R.M.'s indirect contacts with A.G.—social media posts using taunting usernames and private photos, and phone calls to her mother disclosing personal information—disturbed her peace under the DVPA's broad definition of abuse.
seed.why_material: The DVPA defines disturbing the peace to include indirect conduct through third parties and electronic technologies, so ignoring this evidence caused the court to apply an incorrect legal standard when denying A.G.'s DVRO request.

10880579.holding_quote: Since the district court did not analyze the Young factors before entering an order granting the motion in limine and entering its final order dismissing Yanling's complaint with prejudice, it abused its discretion under our somewhat heightened standard of review.
10880579.situation:
PARTIES AND NATURE OF DISPUTE

Plaintiff Yanling brings this action against defendant Yanhui arising out of an alleged joint venture concerning residential real estate in Las Vegas, Nevada.

Yanling alleges that she and Yanhui formed a joint venture under which Yanling provided $200,000 to Yanhui for the purchase of four residential properties in Las Vegas, with an understanding that the two would run a rental property business together. Yanling asserts that she and Yanhui had an agreement, although unwritten, that entitled each of them to 50 percent of the properties' rental income and/or sales proceeds.

When Yanhui purchased the four properties, she titled them in her name only. Yanhui subsequently sold one of the properties and retained all of the sales proceeds. Yanling thereafter attempted to add her name to the titles through a living trust, and when that effort failed, Yanling commenced the underlying lawsuit.

CLAIMS AND RELIEF SOUGHT

Yanling's complaint asserts claims for breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, unjust enrichment, and conversion. Yanling claims entitlement to a return of her initial investment and to a 50-percent share of the rental and sale proceeds from the four houses.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Early in the litigation, after Yanhui did not timely answer the complaint, Yanling entered a default against Yanhui and filed an application for default judgment. Yanling's application included a calculation of her initial investment and claimed entitlement to a 50-percent share of rental and sale proceeds. Yanhui successfully moved to set aside the default and then answered the complaint.

A few months before the scheduled trial on Yanling's claims, and after the close of discovery, Yanhui filed a motion in limine seeking to preclude evidence of special damages. Yanhui argued that Yanling did not provide a sufficient computation of damages under NRCP 16.1(a)(1)(A)(iv).

At the hearing on the motion in limine, Yanling asserted that the computation of damages was disclosed "in the moving papers." The district court expressed concern because it did not have any such disclosures to review. Yanling had neither filed a computation of damages with the court nor attached it to her opposition to the motion in limine. Yanling was unable to inform the district court when any damages disclosure was produced, but argued that the damages in this case were straightforward. With the trial date roughly two months out, and lacking a computation from Yanling to review, the court allowed Yanling one week to provide a supplemental computation of damages.

The court held a second hearing five days after the deadline for Yanling's supplemental computation. At that hearing, Yanling acknowledged that she did not provide the supplemental computation because her expert "just didn't have enough time." The court concluded that Yanling failed to act with diligence in providing a computation of damages. The court granted Yanhui's motion in limine to preclude evidence of special damages and ordered briefing on whether there was anything left to litigate.

Without moving for reconsideration, Yanling filed a supplemental computation of damages, eight days after the court-imposed deadline for the supplement. Yanling argued that even with evidence of special damages excluded, her claims could nonetheless proceed under a "general damages" theory, because it was clear from the beginning of the litigation that the dispute concerned her $200,000 investment and the split-profit arrangement from the sale of and/or rental proceeds from the four houses.

At the final calendar call, the district court rejected Yanling's arguments. The court determined that Yanling sought to recover specific, not general, damages, and thus was required to provide a detailed computation of those alleged damages under NRCP 16.1. Because Yanling had failed to do so, the district court determined there was nothing left for trial and dismissed Yanling's complaint with prejudice.

GOVERNING STANDARD

The disclosure requirement at issue is NRCP 16.1(a)(1)(A)(iv), which concerns a party's obligation to provide a computation of damages. The district court applied NRCP 16.1 in determining that Yanling was required to disclose a computation of the damages she sought.

seed.consideration: Before imposing a sanction that bars all damages evidence and effectively terminates the case, the court should weigh the Young factors, including willfulness, prejudice, severity, availability of lesser sanctions, and the policy favoring adjudication on the merits.
seed.why_material: Because excluding damages evidence eliminated an essential element of the claims and operated as a case-ending sanction, it could not be imposed without the express Young analysis required for dismissal with prejudice.

10883043.holding_quote: The court's opinion provides scant discussion of plaintiff's diligence in securing an expert witness and fails to articulate any prejudice to defendants, particularly given that the court mistakenly believed that the discovery period had closed on July 7, 2022, when the court had, in fact, extended discovery until December 12, 2022.
10883043.situation:
PARTIES AND ROLE OF THE PRINCIPALS

Defendant Jack D. Lennox, D.O., is an orthopedic surgeon. In 2019 he performed a total knee replacement surgery on Jacqueline Harris. After the surgery, Dr. Lennox advised Harris to take aspirin. Approximately 30 days after the surgery, Harris died from an acute pulmonary embolism.

The surgery took place at Beaumont Hospital. Dr. Lennox was employed by Tri County Orthopedics, PC. Dr. Lennox and Tri County Orthopedics are collectively referred to as the Tri County defendants.

THE COMPLAINT

On behalf of Harris's estate, plaintiff filed a complaint on April 9, 2021. The complaint named as defendants Dr. Lennox, Tri County Orthopedics, PC, and Beaumont Hospital. The complaint alleged that Dr. Lennox's failure to prescribe a prescription-strength anticoagulant was malpractice that caused Harris's death from a blood clot. Plaintiff also alleged claims of vicarious liability against Tri County and Beaumont.

THE AFFIDAVIT OF MERIT

The complaint was supported by an affidavit of merit (AOM) signed by B. Sonny Bal, M.D. Dr. Bal attested that "during the relevant time period at issue in this matter, I was a licensed and practicing physician, specializing in Orthopedic Surgery, and devoting a majority of my professional time for the preceding year to[] the clinical practice of orthopedic surgery." Under MCL 600.2912d, prior to filing a medical malpractice suit, a plaintiff must obtain an affidavit of merit signed by a physician qualified to testify as to the nature of the alleged malpractice.

SCHEDULING AND WITNESS LIST

The circuit court issued an initial scheduling order on June 22, 2021. That order required the parties to name their experts and submit witness lists to opposing counsel and the court by May 6, 2022. Plaintiff timely filed a witness list on April 25, 2022, listing Dr. Bal as her sole orthopedic surgery expert, an area matching Dr. Lennox's area of practice. Discovery was originally set to close by June 7, 2022.

The parties engaged in discovery. On June 3, 2022, plaintiff's counsel provided a list of five days in August during which Dr. Bal would be available for an in-person deposition. The proposed deposition dates for Dr. Bal, as well as proposed deposition dates for defendants' expert witnesses, were, per the original scheduling order, set for after the close of discovery. On June 6, 2022, the parties agreed to schedule Dr. Bal's deposition for August 15, 2022. The next day, the circuit court entered a stipulated order extending the scheduling order dates. That order extended the discovery cutoff of June 7, 2022, to December 12, 2022, the facilitation date agreed upon by the parties. Trial was scheduled for February 7, 2023.

CANCELLED DEPOSITION AND MOTION TO COMPEL

On August 15, 2022, plaintiff's counsel informed defense counsel that Dr. Bal had an emergency and had to cancel the deposition. Plaintiff's counsel indicated that new dates would be offered. Having not received new dates, the Tri County defendants filed a motion on September 9, 2022, to compel Dr. Bal's deposition within 14 days of entry of an order granting the motion, so as to provide them sufficient time to prepare motions for summary disposition and to prepare for a "meaningful" facilitation.

AMENDED WITNESS LIST AND MOTION TO STRIKE

On September 16, 2022, plaintiff's counsel sent correspondence to defense counsel indicating that he had been attempting to reconnect with Dr. Bal to obtain new deposition dates but that "[u]nfortunately, we are having an extraordinarily difficult time doing so without success." That same day, plaintiff's counsel filed an amended witness list naming Dr. John Hall, M.D., as plaintiff's orthopedic surgery expert and removing Dr. Bal. This document was filed without permission from the circuit court.

On September 20, 2022, plaintiff's counsel provided dates for Dr. Hall's deposition to defendants, including October 14, November 4, and November 11, 2022. On September 21, 2022, the Tri County defendants filed a motion to strike the amended witness list on the basis that it was untimely filed 133 days after the expert disclosure and witness list deadlines set forth in the original scheduling order, which they contended were not modified by the amended scheduling order.

In response, plaintiff represented that Dr. Bal "has not been cooperative, and he needs to be replaced." Plaintiff asserted that Dr. Bal was an "unreliable" expert because of his lack of responsiveness and unavailability, not because of his qualifications.

OCTOBER 12, 2022 HEARING AND ORDERS

On October 12, 2022, the circuit court heard argument on the motion to compel Dr. Bal's deposition and the motion to strike plaintiff's amended witness list. Plaintiff's counsel stated that the motion to compel Dr. Bal's deposition was moot because plaintiff was withdrawing Dr. Bal as an expert. Defense counsel objected, arguing that the Tri County defendants were nevertheless entitled to depose Dr. Bal about the assertions in his AOM regarding his qualifications. The circuit court ordered plaintiff to produce Dr. Bal for a deposition in the next three weeks.

As to the amended witness list, the court chastised plaintiff's counsel for filing the amended witness list without the court's permission rather than filing a motion to amend the witness list. Plaintiff's counsel admitted he had made a mistake, stating, "I should not have done it, your Honor."

Two orders were entered that day. One granted the motion to compel and ordered that Dr. Bal be deposed by November 2, 2022. The other granted the motion to strike the amended witness list and ordered that "plaintiff may file a motion to amend their witness list to be heard on a later date and time."

EMERGENCY MOTION TO AMEND WITNESS LIST

One week later, plaintiff filed an emergency motion to amend her witness list, asserting that none of the factors articulated in Dean v Tucker warranted barring plaintiff from amending her witness list as a discovery sanction. The Tri County defendants filed a response addressing the Dean factors and highlighting the prejudice that would result to them if plaintiff were allowed either to voluntarily dismiss the case without prejudice or to substitute a new expert, when, in their view, dismissal was warranted based on Dr. Bal's lack of qualifications to sign the AOM.

The Tri County defendants also argued that plaintiff's proffered "good cause" for substituting Dr. Bal—his failure to communicate—was shown to be false by the fact that plaintiff's counsel had communicated with Dr. Bal on the date of his scheduled deposition and then reached out to Dr. Hall only two days later. They argued plaintiff never submitted any evidence of attempts to contact Dr. Bal that went unanswered, and that plaintiff did not respond to defendants' request for new deposition dates for Dr. Bal until the day she named Dr. Hall as her new expert. Defendants surmised that the real reason plaintiff wanted to substitute her experts was because Dr. Bal was not qualified to sign the AOM, not because he was an uncooperative witness.

ATTEMPTS AT VOLUNTARY DISMISSAL

On October 26, 2022, plaintiff filed an "Order of Voluntary Dismissal of All Defendants" purporting to dismiss all defendants without prejudice. MCR 2.504(A) requires a voluntary dismissal to be filed either before the defendant answers the complaint or pursuant to a stipulation of dismissal signed by all the parties. The circuit court rejected plaintiff's attempt to dismiss. Plaintiff responded by filing a motion for voluntary dismissal on November 1, 2022, one day before the court-ordered deadline to take Dr. Bal's deposition.

The Tri County defendants filed responses to this renewed attempt at voluntary dismissal, and the motion was noticed for hearing the same day as plaintiff's emergency motion to amend the witness list.

MOTIONS FOR SUMMARY DISPOSITION

Several days before the emergency motion was scheduled to be heard, both sets of defendants filed motions for summary disposition to dismiss the complaint due to the invalid AOM. The motions referred to defendants' recent discovery of trial and deposition transcripts from a separate case, in which Dr. Bal had testified that he had retired from practicing and teaching medicine in 2017, and a copy of Dr. Bal's LinkedIn profile confirming the same.

NOVEMBER 14, 2022 ORDER

On November 14, 2022, the circuit court issued an order and opinion denying plaintiff's motion for voluntary dismissal without prejudice and plaintiff's motion for leave to file an amended witness list. The order stated: "This matter was filed on April 9, 2021. Witness lists in this matter were due by May 6, 2022, with discovery closing on June 7, 2022. Trial in this matter is currently set for February 7, 2023. Allowing an amended witness list at this late stage is also highly prejudicial."

MOTION FOR RECONSIDERATION

Plaintiff moved for reconsideration of the November 14, 2022 order and opinion and also filed a response to defendants' motions for summary disposition. On December 8, 2022, the circuit court issued an order and opinion denying reconsideration. The court explained that plaintiff again argued Dr. Bal was "uncooperative" and that the court had abused its discretion in denying her motion. The court disagreed, noting that Dr. Bal signed plaintiff's affidavit of merit and that, pursuant to MCL 600.2912d, a plaintiff must obtain an affidavit of merit signed by a qualified physician at the outset of every medical malpractice suit. The court noted plaintiff filed her complaint and affidavit of merit on April 9, 2021, that discovery was open until June 7, 2022, and that plaintiff had over one year to sort out any issues with her experts. The court stated that had plaintiff diligently prosecuted her case, she would have realized Dr. Bal was uncooperative and/or unqualified to testify much sooner than November 2022, and that at that stage a voluntary dismissal without prejudice or leave to file an amended witness list was inappropriate. The court found no palpable error and denied the motion.

DECEMBER 14, 2022 ORDER GRANTING SUMMARY DISPOSITION

The circuit court issued another order and opinion on December 14, 2022, granting Beaumont's motion for summary disposition and closing the case. The court recited that, according to Beaumont, Dr. Bal ceased practice in November 2017 and that the care at issue occurred on May 29, 2019. The court noted that plaintiff had not produced Dr. Bal for deposition, violating the court's order to produce him. The court noted that Dr. Bal's LinkedIn page stated he retired from the clinical practice of medicine in November 2017, and that he retired from serving as an adjunct professor at the Missouri University of Science and Technology and as a professor of orthopedic surgery at the University of Missouri Health Care in November 2017. The court noted that in September 2020 Dr. Bal was deposed in a separate matter and testified he had been winding down his practice since 2015, and that Beaumont attached sworn trial testimony in another matter in which Dr. Bal confirmed he retired in November 2017.

The court recited plaintiff's response: that the court should not dismiss because plaintiff's counsel need only a "reasonable" belief that the physician signing the affidavit is qualified at the time of signing, and that the motion was merely an "unfettered attack upon the credibility of Dr. Bal, which is not a proper basis for summary disposition." Plaintiff argued the court should not rely on outside deposition or trial testimony, but rely only on the affidavit of merit itself, in which Dr. Bal swears he is qualified to sign.

The court found it troubling that plaintiff cautioned against reliance on deposition and trial testimony from other cases when plaintiff could not produce any evidence from her own witness to refute what Beaumont was arguing. The court noted the case was filed in April 2021, that plaintiff retained Dr. Bal prior to that date because he signed the affidavit of merit, and that plaintiff had over one year to work out any issues with her experts. The court agreed that plaintiff's counsel may reasonably rely on the statements of experts, but noted discovery ended in June 2022, over one year after the complaint was filed, that Dr. Bal was the expert relied upon to file the claim, that he had not been produced for deposition, and that plaintiff had not attached any evidence indicating he was in fact qualified to sign the affidavit of merit.

The court stated that plaintiff merely pointed to the affidavit of merit itself, but that the affidavit was being directly challenged, and that it was plaintiff's burden to produce evidence creating a genuine issue of material fact as to the validity of the affidavit. The court cited Pena v Ingham County Road Com'n, 255 Mich App 299, for the proposition that once discovery is closed the summary disposition hearing becomes the "put up or shut up" stage of the proceeding, and if there is no factual support for a claim it will not continue. The court found that Beaumont provided sworn testimony suggesting the statements in plaintiff's affidavit surrounding Dr. Bal's qualifications—namely, that he was engaged in practice or teaching in the one-year period prior to the alleged conduct—were untrue, and that plaintiff had not come forward with any evidence to suggest otherwise. The court granted the motion, found plaintiff's affidavit of merit invalid, stated that absent a valid affidavit of merit a complaint for medical malpractice fails as a matter of law, and stated that the order was final and closed the case.

Plaintiff filed a motion for reconsideration, which was denied.

RELIEF SOUGHT AND GOVERNING STANDARDS

Plaintiff's pending requests before the circuit court include leave to amend her witness list to substitute Dr. Hall for Dr. Bal, and voluntary dismissal without prejudice. Plaintiff invokes the Dean v Tucker factors governing whether the barring of a witness or the effective dismissal of a claim is an appropriate discovery sanction, and MCR 2.401(I)(2) governing amendment of witness lists. Defendants seek summary disposition on the ground that the affidavit of merit is invalid because Dr. Bal was not qualified under MCL 600.2912d to sign it, and oppose amendment and voluntary dismissal, asserting prejudice given the timing relative to the witness list deadline, close of discovery, and the February 7, 2023 trial date. MCR 2.504(A) governs the requirements for voluntary dismissal.
