10918688.case_name: Shane Roy Needham v. Janet Lea Needham
10918688.holding_quote: But it did not consider whether compelling Mr. Needham to execute the BSA Waiver in his capacity as a corporate fiduciary comported with the duties of care and loyalty he owes Alturas and its shareholders.
10918688.situation:
PARTIES AND BACKGROUND

Shane Needham and Janet Needham married in August 1991. Ms. Needham earned a degree from Washington State University in 1993. During the marriage, she was a homemaker and cared for the couple's four children, all now adults. Mr. Needham earned a doctorate in chemistry and, along with Robin Woods and Michael Pearson, founded Alturas Analytics, Inc. ("Alturas") in 2000.

Alturas operates as a contract research organization, providing outsourced research services to pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies developing new drugs. Mr. Needham holds 70,000 shares, representing 50% of the company's equity. Mr. Pearson and Ms. Woods each hold 35,000 shares, or 25% apiece. Mr. Needham, Ms. Woods, and Mr. Pearson all serve as directors of the corporation. Ms. Woods also serves as president.

THE BUY-SELL AGREEMENT

In April 2005, the three shareholders and the corporation executed a Buy-Sell Agreement ("BSA") governing the transferability of Alturas shares. The BSA provides, in relevant part:

2. Right to Purchase.
(a) If the holder of any shares which are subject to this Agreement desires to sell, assign or transfer any of the shares of the Corporation, such Shareholder shall give notice in writing to the Secretary of the Corporation, with copies to each individual Shareholder, setting forth the number of shares the Shareholder desires to sell, assign or transfer. The Corporation shall have the right and obligation to purchase the shares proposed to be sold, assigned or transferred.
(b) This right and obligation to purchase shall also apply to any involuntary sale, transfer by operation of law, court decree or foreclosure of a security interest.

The BSA provides that the purchase price for shares transferred pursuant to its terms is their book value. Ms. Needham accepted the terms of the BSA, stating: "I, Janet Needham, wife of Shane Needham acknowledge and agree that sufficient consideration exists based upon my community property interest in any agreement Shane Needham has with Alturas and I agree to be bound by the terms and conditions of this agreement." Her signature appears on the document and was acknowledged by a Notary Public.

MR. NEEDHAM'S TERMINATION AND SUBSEQUENT EVENTS

In addition to being a co-founder, Mr. Needham served as Alturas's chief scientist until his termination in 2020 amidst allegations of misconduct that included performing research without Alturas's approval and refusing to remove Alturas's name from that research. Following his termination, Mr. Needham founded a new company, Veloxity, which appears to compete with Alturas. He then brought an unsuccessful lawsuit against Mr. Pearson and Ms. Woods seeking control of Alturas by contending that he was the sole director. By the magistrate court's account, since then "Alturas has been at a deadlock on nearly every decision."

DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS AND RESERVATION OF THE SHARES ISSUE

Mr. Needham filed for divorce in 2018. In 2021, the parties stipulated to entry of a divorce decree dissolving the marriage, which the magistrate court entered with an effective date of January 25, 2021. The magistrate court reserved jurisdiction over the disposition of the community Alturas shares for determination at a later date.

In May 2023, Ms. Needham filed a motion seeking an order awarding her one-half of the community Alturas shares and compelling Mr. Needham to execute a Waiver and Consent to Transfer Agreement. Ms. Needham claimed the Waiver would exempt the transfer of 35,000 shares of Alturas stock from Mr. Needham to her from the terms of the BSA (the "BSA Waiver"). The BSA Waiver submitted required the signature of Alturas's president and all three shareholders and was unsigned at that time. The magistrate court declined to rule on the motion, reserving disposition of the shares for trial.

In late March 2024, about three weeks prior to trial, during a meeting of the Alturas board of directors, Mr. Pearson and Ms. Woods assented to the BSA Waiver. Mr. Needham did not.

THE TRIAL AND VALUATION EVIDENCE

The magistrate court held a two-day trial in April 2024 to adjudicate the disposition of the Alturas shares. At trial, Mr. Needham's expert estimated the fair market value of the shares to be $16,320,000 as of June 30, 2023, while the book value on that same date would be $10,250,000. From the entry of the divorce decree to the time of trial, Mr. Needham's shares yielded $6,140,346 in dividends, half of which he remitted to Ms. Needham in accordance with the stipulated divorce decree.

THE PARTIES' POSITIONS AT TRIAL

Neither party requested an unequal division of property, but they wished for the interest to be divided differently. Ms. Needham asked the magistrate court to divide the shares equally in-kind, allowing her to become an Alturas shareholder. In the alternative, Ms. Needham proposed that Mr. Needham hold the shares in trust for her benefit. Mr. Needham asked the magistrate court to fashion a monetary award for Ms. Needham reflecting the value of her community interest in the Alturas shares and to allow him to satisfy the award in installments over four to nine years.

THE MAGISTRATE COURT'S RULING

Considering both Idaho Code section 32-712(1)(b) and "the need to disentangle the parties," the magistrate court concluded that "dividing the shares equally and awarding each party their respective one-half interest, or 35,000 shares, with each named as a shareholder is the most equitable and appropriate disposition of the community property." The magistrate court noted this arrangement would "give each spouse sole and immediate control of their respective share" of the community shares, allowing Ms. Needham to personally control her interest in Alturas and ensure that it continues to provide her with dividends.

The magistrate court found that, "[d]ue to Mr. Needham's lawsuit against the other shareholders, Alturas has been at a deadlock on nearly every decision" and that awarding Ms. Needham an ownership interest with attendant voting rights would break this "deadlock" and "effectuate moving the company forward." The court concluded that Alturas "would be more successful without Mr. Needham" as a controlling shareholder, which justified awarding the shares to Ms. Needham rather than issuing the monetary award Mr. Needham proposed.

The magistrate court observed that the Alturas shares had "increased significantly in value, nearly doubled, since the [divorce] [d]ecree was entered." In its view, "valuing the shares as of the entry of [d]ecree does not provide a substantially equal division of the parties' community interest as it would allow Mr. Needham to receive the benefit of natural enhancement that Ms. Needham would not receive." The magistrate court declined to value the Alturas shares and instead divided them evenly between the parties, deeming that "the most fair and equitable resolution" in lieu of conferring a windfall on Mr. Needham. It entered judgment awarding Ms. Needham 50% of Mr. Needham's interest in Alturas, or 35,000 shares, and ordered Mr. Needham to execute the BSA Waiver to effectuate the division.

APPEAL TO THE DISTRICT COURT

Mr. Needham appealed to the district court. He argued that the magistrate court abused its discretion by declining to determine the fair market value of Ms. Needham's "interest in the Alturas shares as of the date of divorce" and by refusing to allow him to "buy [Ms. Needham] out over a period of four-to-nine years" based on that valuation. In Mr. Needham's view, the division of the Alturas shares was unequal, diminished the value of his stake by stripping him of voting power, jeopardized his seat on the board, and was inconsistent with "Idaho precedent in community property cases requiring the trial [c]ourt to maintain the value of both parties' interest in community property." He also asserted that the magistrate court's ruling left him "entangled" with Ms. Needham.

The district court rejected these arguments and affirmed the magistrate court's disposition of the Alturas shares. Relying on Josephson v. Josephson, 115 Idaho 1142, 1149, 772 P.2d 1236, 1243 (Ct. App. 1989), and Lamm v. Preston, 171 Idaho 488, 522 P.3d 1246 (2023), the district court reasoned that a "simple division" of stock in a closely held corporation can be appropriate where the business depends on one spouse's ongoing involvement; where awarding that spouse majority control is required; and where the other spouse, as a minority shareholder, would have virtually no influence and the shares would have little or no marketable value. Finding none of those circumstances present, the district court concluded that "there is nothing in either case that states stock in a closely held corporation can never be divided," and was satisfied that the magistrate court's in-kind award was consistent with applicable Idaho caselaw.

The district court noted that the magistrate court's division was informed by "the factors set forth in Idaho Code [section] 32-712, including the parties' decades long marriage, the parties' respective incomes, the fact [that Ms. Needham] has not been employed for a number of years because of her role as a stay at home mom, the lack of spousal maintenance awarded to [Ms. Needham], and the parties' overall needs and history of using the Alturas dividends to fund their family and lifestyle."

The district court was unpersuaded by Mr. Needham's contention that dividing the Alturas shares would impair their value, concluding that "[t]he value of [Mr. Needham's] shares does not change simply because half of those shares are transferred into [Ms. Needham's] name. Instead, by dividing the shares each party is tasked with managing their own shares to maximize the value of those shares and Alturas as a whole." Agreeing with the magistrate court's finding that Alturas was "hopelessly deadlocked at the shareholder level," the district court viewed the in-kind division as an effective means to break the deadlock and maximize both parties' interest in Alturas.

The district court rejected Mr. Needham's argument that the magistrate court lacked authority to compel him to sign the BSA Waiver necessary to effectuate the transfer without triggering the BSA. Citing the principle that "[t]he divorce court's plenary and equitable power include[s] the authority 'to order the parties to execute various documents of significance such as deeds, assignment[s] of interest in stocks and bonds, insurance policies, bills of sale, and numerous other documents during the divorce process,'" (quoting Rohr v. Rohr, 118 Idaho 689, 697, 800 P.2d 85, 93 (1990)), the district court concluded that the BSA Waiver was precisely such a document. It further determined that the BSA Waiver did not "amend or alter" the BSA but merely ensured that the community property could be divided without forcing a repurchase of Ms. Needham's shares at book value rather than fair market value.

Based on this analysis, the district court concluded that the magistrate court did not abuse its discretion and affirmed its disposition of the Alturas shares. The district court also awarded attorney fees against Mr. Needham, deeming his appeal of the magistrate court's order "frivolous, unreasonable, and without foundation." Mr. Needham timely appealed.

seed.consideration: Whether compelling Mr. Needham to execute the BSA Waiver would require him to act in his capacity as a corporate director/fiduciary, and whether that waiver represented a sound business decision consistent with the duties he owes Alturas.
seed.why_material: A magistrate court lacks authority in a divorce proceeding to compel a party to act in a corporate-fiduciary role over property that is not entirely their own, so ignoring this exceeds the court's equitable-distribution power.

10920237.situation:
This is a prisoner civil-rights action brought by plaintiff Roberts, an inmate at Red Onion State Prison ("Red Onion"), operated by the Virginia Department of Corrections ("VDOC"). Roberts has been incarcerated at Red Onion since 2005. He filed suit in August 2020, proceeding pro se, against various VDOC officials in their individual and official capacities, alleging that the defendants failed to accommodate his religious dietary requirements. The record recited here is viewed in the light most favorable to Roberts as the nonmoving party on the defendants' motion for summary judgment.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND

VDOC food service operations. A VDOC dietician crafts meal plans consistent with nationally recommended allowances for basic nutrition and established basic daily servings. VDOC must comply with state safety regulations, including processes to reduce foodborne illness, acceptable cooking and storage methods, and timing for serving.

Religious dietary accommodations. VDOC offers the Common Fare menu, which it asserts was designed to comply with Jewish and Muslim dietary laws. In response to litigation from a different prisoner, VDOC developed a separate Orthodox Jewish Kosher Diet ("OJKD") for Jewish inmates whose beliefs require that, without the active supervision of an Orthodox Rabbi, the food cannot be Kashrut.

Fasting accommodations. VDOC allows prisoners to fast in observation of Ramadan or the Nation of Islam Month of Fasting. Under the VDOC Food Service Manual in effect for 2020, Red Onion accommodated such fasts by preparing four menus: a Ramadan menu, a Common Fare Ramadan menu, a Month of Fast menu, and a Common Fare Month of Fast menu. These fasting menus offered non-OJKD meals served and eaten before dawn and after sunset. Fasting inmates also received a bagged meal they could keep in their living quarters after their evening meal, but to avoid spoilage, inmates had to agree to consume or discard that meal within four hours of receiving it and to complete a Four-Hour Rule Agreement to participate.

Roberts's beliefs. Roberts is a Sunni Muslim. He believes that Islamic Dietary Laws are analogous with Orthodox Jewish requirements of the Kashrut, and it is his sincerely held religious belief that his faith requires him to follow the Kashrut, which he further believes requires an Orthodox Rabbi to be actively supervising all aspects of the Kosher diet. The defendants do not dispute the sincerity of Roberts's beliefs. His faith also requires that he fast during Ramadan, which includes fasting from sunrise to sunset, meaning meals must be consumed before sunrise and after sunset every day for a month.

Roberts's dietary history. Roberts originally chose to participate in the Common Fare program under the belief that its menu aligned with his faith. He was able to receive a modified version of the Common Fare menu that allowed him to fast during Ramadan during the first several years of his confinement. In June 2019, Roberts requested to switch to the OJKD after hearing through the prison's grapevine that the OJKD had been developed in response to litigation alleging that the Common Fare diet was not strictly following Kashrut law. His request did not include any reference to additional accommodations for Ramadan. Red Onion approved his request to switch to the OJKD on July 10, 2019.

The 2020 Ramadan request. On March 10, 2020, Red Onion sent inmates a memorandum announcing that Ramadan was estimated to start on April 23, 2020, and reminding inmates that they needed to complete the Four-Hour Agreement by March 24 to participate in the fast. The same day, Roberts returned the Four-Hour Agreement but included a handwritten note stating that he wished to receive his OJKD meal during Ramadan.

VDOC's response. VDOC states that it was not prepared to provide an OJKD menu that also accommodated Ramadan because doing so would have required careful planning to ensure an additional OJKD meal could be bagged and consumed safely within four hours. VDOC also states that such a change required consulting with the Muslim Chaplain Service of Virginia and allowing time for ordering and purchasing the necessary food items, a process for which the VDOC Food Service Manual allots up to 90 days. VDOC informed Roberts that it would not be able to accommodate his request. It offered Roberts a choice: he could remain on the OJKD without fasting, or he could switch back to the Common Fare diet and observe Ramadan. If Roberts opted to receive the Common Fare diet during Ramadan, he would not be permitted to switch back to the OJKD diet for at least six months.

Roberts declined both options and instead attempted a third course by saving his OJKD meals during the daylight hours until sunset in an effort to fast. Because the food had been sitting out for hours before he could consume it, this made him ill. On three separate occasions he developed food poisoning and needed to be treated by the prison medical team.

Subsequent developments. Months later, in anticipation of the 2021 Ramadan observance, VDOC developed a new variation of the OJKD that could accommodate Ramadan fasting. Since 2021, Roberts has been able to observe Ramadan's fasting requirement while on the OJKD.

PARTIES

The original complaint named as defendants Mark Engelke, Director of Food Service of VDOC; Jeffery Kiser, Red Onion's warden; Shannon Fuller, Red Onion's assistant warden; Harold Clarke, Director of VDOC; Keith Almarode, Red Onion's Food Service Manager; and John Gibson, Counselor of VDOC. Joseph Walters has since been substituted for Clarke as the Director of VDOC, though Clarke remains party to the suit in his individual capacity. The defendants are sued in their individual and official capacities.

CLAIMS AND RELIEF SOUGHT

Roberts alleges that, by failing to accommodate his religious dietary requirements, the defendants violated the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act ("RLUIPA"), the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, and the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. In April 2021, Roberts amended his complaint to add an Establishment Clause claim under the First Amendment and to verify the complaint. The amended complaint seeks: (1) a declaratory judgment that the defendants violated his rights under the First Amendment and RLUIPA by forcing him to choose between following the precepts of his religious beliefs and forfeiting governmental benefits; (2) injunctive relief to make permanent his ability to participate in Ramadan fasting while on the OJKD; and (3) compensatory and punitive damages.

PROCEEDINGS TO DATE

During discovery, Roberts moved to compel the disclosure of certain VDOC Food Manual documents. The magistrate judge denied that motion.

The defendants moved for summary judgment on all claims. The district court granted the motion in full. The court first determined that the defendants were protected by Eleventh Amendment immunity for all damages claims brought against them in their official capacities. It next found that Roberts was barred from recovering monetary damages at all under RLUIPA. It further found that Roberts was barred from injunctive relief because VDOC's creation of a new Ramadan-compliant OJKD diet beginning in 2021 rendered his claims moot.

That left Roberts's request for damages on his constitutional claims against the defendants in their individual capacities. On those, the district court found the defendants entitled to qualified immunity: on the First Amendment Free Exercise claim, because it was not clearly established that a Sunni Muslim inmate's beliefs would require him to receive meals supervised by an Orthodox Jewish Rabbi as part of his Muslim Ramadan observance; and on the First Amendment Establishment Clause and Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause claims, because there was no constitutional violation. These rulings are reported at Roberts v. Engelke, No. 7:20-cv-484, 2022 WL 791653 (W.D. Va. Mar. 14, 2022).

10868283.situation:
CASE FILE

Parties and Charge

Defendant: Timothy LaRue Sheffield. Victim: Edith Sheffield, the defendant's wife of almost 30 years. The charge is malice murder arising from the shooting death of Edith Sheffield.

Procedural Posture

Edith Sheffield was killed in January 2013. In October 2018, a Coffee County grand jury indicted Sheffield for malice murder. Law enforcement arrested Sheffield in December 2018, after almost six years of investigation. A jury trial was held in October 2021, and the jury found Sheffield guilty of malice murder. Sheffield was sentenced to serve life in prison.

Sheffield timely filed a motion for new trial in November 2021. He amended the motion with new counsel in November 2023 and April 2024. After evidentiary hearings, the trial court denied Sheffield's motion for new trial in July 2025. Sheffield filed a timely notice of appeal.

Among the matters presented is Sheffield's motion to dismiss on the ground that his constitutional right to a speedy trial was violated. The trial court denied that motion. Sheffield also challenges the sufficiency of the evidence supporting his conviction. This file is prepared at the posture of the trial court's rulings on those matters, on the trial record.

Governing Standards

The sufficiency challenge is assessed by viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the verdict. The speedy-trial claim is a constitutional claim raised in a motion to dismiss and addressed by the trial court.

Facts Presented at Trial (viewed in the light most favorable to the verdict)

At 6:04 p.m. on January 18, 2013, Edith, who was on her way home from work, called her cousin, and they spoke briefly. Based on Edith's location when she made the call, she would have arrived home by 6:19 or 6:20 p.m. The cousin called Edith back at 6:30 p.m.; Edith did not answer. At no later than 6:36 p.m., two people driving by Edith and Sheffield's house saw that the house was on fire. They stopped and called 911. When they went into the carport, they saw Edith's keys in the door that opened from the carport into the kitchen. They did not hear anyone in the house.

At the time of the fire, Edith and Sheffield's next-door neighbor, who was Sheffield's mother, and their "across the road" neighbors, who were Sheffield's sister and brother-in-law, were vacationing in Hawaii. Two other neighbors, who lived two houses down from the Sheffields, saw the fire and came to the house. Those neighbors looked into the back window of the house and could see "the entire bottom floor of the house." They did not see anyone or anything "out of place" or "messed up." Eventually, 25 to 30 people gathered at the house while the fire was burning; no one went inside the house. At least two men the neighbors did not know stopped after seeing the fire. There were "multiple people in the woods behind the property" at the time of the fire.

The first neighbor on the scene called Sheffield, who said he had been doing sheetrock work at the mobile home he and Edith had on their property, which was about 450 feet away from the house, connected by a dirt path through woods. The neighbor told Sheffield that his house was on fire, and "immediately" thereafter, Sheffield "rolled out of the woods," driving his truck "real slow." Sheffield then got out, "knelt down" or "leaned on the hood" of the truck, and "lit a cigarette." Sheffield did not ask about Edith upon his arrival.

The gathered witnesses asked Sheffield where Edith was, and he said he did not know. They told Sheffield to call Edith. Sheffield "turned his back" to the group of neighbors, walked "four or five feet" away, and made a call. Although one of the neighbors heard him "mumbl[ing]" on the phone, when he hung up and the group asked what Edith said, Sheffield said that Edith did not answer and he did not know where she was. Sheffield did not say anything more but continued to stand by his truck. After emergency services arrived, Sheffield was taken into the back of the ambulance and treated for "extremely high blood pressure," which the treating doctor said could be caused by "extreme stress" or "emotional pain."

The fire in the house caused the second floor to collapse onto the first floor. The fire chief could not determine if an accelerant was used to set the fire, but he explained that the fire "consumed more in the time frame" than ordinarily would be expected, which is evidence of an accelerant "the majority of the time." Sheffield and Edith kept a gas can in the carport for their lawn mower.

Once firefighters got the fire under control and were able to enter the house, they began to search the debris, which was "a foot to eighteen inches" deep. During the search, Sheffield asked a GBI agent about "[a] jewelry box located in the residence, a fireproof gun safe that was in the residence, and a jug ... of coins," wanting "to see if anything had been moved or taken." Sheffield did not ask the agent about Edith.

The day after the fire, Edith's burned body was found in the carport. The two witnesses who had been in the carport at the beginning of the fire had not seen a body. Edith was still wearing her jewelry -- a necklace, earrings, and three rings -- and her purse, with $1463.71 inside, was found under her body. Edith had "four pieces of ... plastic straws," the kind used "for soft drinks and things of that sort," "grasped" in her left hand.

A later autopsy showed that Edith had been shot three times by a 12-gauge shotgun: once in her hand, arm, and the front of her chest at a "more distant-range" and twice at "close range" in the back of her head and neck. The head shots "would have caused her to die immediately." Based on the lack of smoke in her lungs, the medical examiner determined that Edith died before being burned in the fire.

The burned "barrel" and "receiver" of a 12-gauge shotgun were found in the debris in "the general area" between the kitchen and the living room. Edith and Sheffield kept a shotgun in their bedroom. Because the recovered shotgun was so badly damaged, it could not be determined through testing if it was the murder weapon or was the Sheffields' shotgun. No other shotgun was found in the debris in the house. Sheffield told a GBI investigator that he kept a .32-caliber weapon in his nightstand; this gun was not found. Other guns were kept in a gun safe in the Sheffields' son's room. According to the Sheffields' son, after the fire, the safe was located "about six to eight feet from where it should have been."

Evidence Regarding Amy Stephens

Evidence was presented that at some point between the summer of 2008 and the summer of 2009, Sheffield had an extra-marital affair with Amy Stephens. Stephens testified that their sexual relationship happened "one time" and was "a mistake," but after that, she and Sheffield remained good friends. Although she moved away from Georgia in the summer of 2009, she remained in contact with Sheffield, calling him for help with a "car problem" or "a project or something like that." Sheffield sent Stephens money on a "few occasions," including $500 one time. Sheffield and Stephens would tell each other they loved each other, and "at times" Stephens "got the feeling" that Sheffield wanted a romantic relationship with her, but she "would just always reassure him ... this was a friendship."

Sometime during 2009 or 2010, after she had moved away from Georgia, Sheffield "requested" that Stephens send him photographs that were "sexual in nature" for his birthday. Stephens "reluctantly sent them." These photographs were recovered from a cell phone that was found in Sheffield's truck and admitted into evidence. The parties stipulated that Sheffield had not used this phone since September 2011 and at that point had transferred his number to a different phone.

Before Edith's death, Sheffield would talk to Stephens "about his marriage," and at some point, Sheffield told Stephens that he and Edith "had talked about" getting a divorce; that Edith did not "believe[] in" divorce; and that he was "afraid" that if he got a divorce, Edith would "take everything."

The week before Edith's death on January 18, Sheffield and Stephens exchanged two phone calls, speaking for 14 minutes on January 14 and 8 minutes on January 16. Stephens testified that she did not remember the topic of those phone calls.

After Edith's death, Stephens saw Sheffield on two occasions, both "probably" in 2014. On one occasion, Stephens stopped in Georgia on her way to her daughter's home in Alabama. In Georgia, Sheffield went with Stephens to her high school reunion and then they traveled together to Alabama to work on her daughter's house. They worked on the house for about two days, but they did not sleep together. On another occasion, Sheffield, who bought a Mustang convertible in 2014, drove the car to Colorado, where Stephens was living at the time. He did not stay with her, but he visited and gave Stephens a ring he bought for her on his recent vacation to the Caribbean, and he gave her son a rifle scope. Additionally, at some point after Stephens moved to Colorado in 2010, Sheffield asked Stephens, "What if I move out there, could we do a business together, would you move in with me? Would you be interested?" Stephens answered, "No, of course not."

The Parties' Positions at Trial

The State argued that Sheffield killed Edith so he could be with Stephens because, although Stephens thought the sexual relationship between her and Sheffield was over, to Sheffield, Stephens was "the trophy person he wanted to build a life with" and their continued communication made Sheffield "think he had a chance."

Sheffield argued that the murder was the result of Edith surprising burglars, contending that the burglars did not steal Edith's jewelry and purse because they "got out of there as quickly as they c[ould]" after shooting her and setting the fire to cover it up.

The jury found Sheffield guilty of malice murder.

Relief Sought / Issues Before the Court

Sheffield contends the evidence was insufficient to support his conviction and that his case should have been dismissed on the ground that his constitutional right to a speedy trial was violated. He also raised several other claims. The trial court denied the motion to dismiss and denied the motion for new trial.

10868664.holding_quote: Because the BIA committed reversible error by mistakenly treating Alvarado-Paz's PSG Salvadoran women as having been raised for the first time before it and then declining to consider the merits of her arguments as a consequence, we will grant her petition for review as to this issue only, vacate the final order of removal, and remand for further proceedings.
10868664.situation:
CASE FILE

Matter of Alvarado-Paz; derivative applicant J.P.A.

PARTIES AND ORIGIN

The principal applicant, Alvarado-Paz, is a native and citizen of El Salvador. Her minor relative, J.P.A., is named as a derivative asylum applicant, whose application depends on the principal applicant's. Both entered the United States without inspection, were charged as removable, and were ordered to appear for related proceedings.

Alvarado-Paz concedes removability. She applies for asylum and withholding of removal under the INA, and withholding of removal under the CAT.

FACTUAL RECORD DEVELOPED BEFORE THE IMMIGRATION JUDGE

Alvarado-Paz fled to the United States in 2016 after her father, Fabian Alvarado Parada ("Fabian"), threatened to kill her.

Alvarado-Paz testifies that Fabian is extremely violent, having physically and psychologically abused her and her immediate family, which included her mother, Porfiria Paz Martinez ("Porfiria"), and six siblings. Fabian was especially violent toward Porfiria, beating her regularly and putting a machete to her throat as he threatened to kill her and her children. After Porfiria inherited land from her family, Fabian threatened more violence to secure her agreement to deed the property to him. Porfiria also witnessed Fabian kill his stepfather with a machete, after which he threatened to kill her if she told anyone.

In June 2016, Fabian's foster brother murdered Porfiria, shooting her at her home while she was caring for J.P.A. and another child. When Alvarado-Paz learned of her mother's death, she went to Porfiria's home, where law enforcement and Fabian were already on scene. Alvarado-Paz accused Fabian of ordering his foster brother to kill her mother. Fabian told her to be quiet and grabbed his machete, which Alvarado-Paz understood to mean that he was capable of killing her at that moment even though there were a lot of police present.

In the days following her mother's death, Alvarado-Paz and her siblings told law enforcement about Fabian's history of abuse and violence, as well as their mutual belief that he was responsible for Porfiria's murder. J.P.A., who was four years old when she witnessed the murder, identified Fabian's foster brother as the person who murdered Porfiria in a photo lineup, but the police informed Alvarado-Paz that they couldn't rely on that identification because of J.P.A.'s age. Despite these repeated accusations against Fabian and his foster brother, law enforcement didn't formally interview either man about Porfiria's murder.

About two weeks after her mother's death, Alvarado-Paz was approached by two unknown masked men as she was traveling to visit her mother's grave. The men threatened to kill Alvarado-Paz if she continued investigating her mother's death. Although she couldn't recognize the men, she believed they were connected to her father because he always said that he had a lot of friends, and that for $20 they would do whatever he wanted.

Feeling trapped and fearing her father's threats, Alvarado-Paz fled El Salvador with J.P.A.

GROUNDS ASSERTED FOR RELIEF

Alvarado-Paz claims eligibility for asylum and withholding under the INA based on her past persecution and fear of future persecution arising from both her political opinion (opposition to violence in favor of the rule of law in El Salvador) and her membership in four alleged particular social groups (PSGs): (1) females viewed as property by virtue of their status in a family relationship; (2) Salvadoran women; (3) nuclear family of Porfiria Paz; and (4) family members of prosecutorial witnesses.

Her request for relief under the CAT rests on the death threats she received following her mother's murder.

HEARING AND IMMIGRATION JUDGE'S DECISION

After a hearing at which Alvarado-Paz testified and submitted documentary evidence in support of her claims, the IJ found Alvarado-Paz to be credible and accepted the above-recounted facts as true. The IJ denied all forms of relief.

Political opinion. The IJ found that even if opposing violence in favor of the rule of law qualifies as a protected political opinion, Alvarado-Paz failed to establish she holds such a political opinion. The IJ found that seeking police intervention related to the death of her mother didn't establish that she holds an anti-violence, pro-rule of law political opinion. The IJ further determined that there was no evidence that Fabian would target her on account of that political opinion because his motives were personal—to avoid being implicated in Porfiria's murder—not political.

PSGs "females viewed as property" and "Salvadoran women." The IJ concluded that Alvarado-Paz hadn't established a nexus between any persecution and membership in the groups "females viewed as property by virtue of their status in the family relationship" and "Salvadoran women." It determined that the record didn't establish persecution on account of her gender at all. It noted that Fabian had been abusive toward both male and female members of his family, as evidenced by Alvarado-Paz's testimony that Fabian had been particularly brutal toward her brother. The IJ further observed that Alvarado-Paz had testified that her father's death threats occurred because she'd accused him of murdering her mother and because she was related to him, not because she was a female or a female viewed as property by virtue of her status in the family.

PSG "nuclear family of Porfiria Paz." The IJ concluded that the record didn't demonstrate a nexus between membership in that group and any persecution. Pointing to caselaw from the Court and the BIA, the IJ observed that a nexus requires more than the existence of the named group and harm; rather, it requires proof that the persecutor targeted the applicant on account of the protected characteristic. The IJ determined that the record suggested Fabian used violence to exert extreme control over his entire family—not that he did so to inflict harm on Porfiria, noting that although despicable, his abuse of his children did not appear to be an explicit attempt to inflict further psychological violence against Porfiria. The IJ found that Alvarado-Paz hadn't shown that her familial relationship to her mother would be at least one central reason her father would subject her to future persecution if she returned to El Salvador. The IJ concluded that, based on the record, the sole reason Alvarado-Paz had been threatened appeared to be her public accusations that her father killed her mother—that revenge, rather than her relationship to her mother, motivated her father to target her. The IJ concluded that the record didn't demonstrate the requisite nexus to support this claim.

PSG "family members of prosecutorial witnesses." The IJ determined that Alvarado-Paz couldn't base her claims on this proposed PSG because neither she nor J.P.A. had ever acted as a prosecutorial witness against Porfiria's murderer. Although J.P.A. identified Fabian's foster brother as the murderer in a photo lineup, police indicated they couldn't use those statements because J.P.A. was too young. The record indicated that police didn't view that man as a suspect and had never arrested him nor prosecuted him for the offense. The IJ determined that Alvarado-Paz simply wasn't a member of this proposed PSG.

Because Alvarado-Paz couldn't show persecution on account of a protected ground, the IJ denied her applications for asylum and withholding of removal under the INA.

CAT. The IJ reviewed and denied Alvarado-Paz's application for relief under the CAT based on its determination that she hadn't shown government acquiescence to her feared torture. The IJ didn't view law enforcement's failure to prosecute anyone for Porfiria's murder as sufficient proof that Salvadoran public officials would acquiesce to Alvarado-Paz's feared torture. It noted that the investigation remained open and that officials had pursued some investigative steps after the murder. Because Alvarado-Paz pointed to no other basis for establishing her claim, the IJ denied relief.

PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE BIA

Alvarado-Paz appealed to the BIA. In a single-judge decision, the BIA dismissed the appeal. The BIA stated that it adopted and affirmed the IJ's decision to deny Alvarado-Paz's applications, and indicated it was not persuaded by her arguments that the IJ misapplied the law or ignored evidence supporting her applications.

With respect to her PSG claims, the BIA stated that Alvarado-Paz challenged the IJ's decision to reject her claims based on membership in three proposed social groups, to which she additionally added on appeal "Salvadoran woman" and "family members of witnesses to crime." The BIA agreed that Alvarado-Paz hadn't shown reversible error on the requisite nexus between her past persecution or fear of future persecution and her preserved PSGs. The BIA also found no reason to address the merits of the two PSGs it determined Alvarado-Paz was asserting on appeal in the first instance because she hadn't pursued those claims before the IJ.

The BIA rejected Alvarado-Paz's arguments with respect to her CAT claim, concluding that the record showed no reversible error in the IJ's determination that she didn't meet her burden with respect to the Salvadoran government instigating, consenting, or acquiescing to her being tortured.

POSTURE

Alvarado-Paz petitioned for review of the agency's final order of removal. Jurisdiction is asserted under 8 U.S.C. § 1252. J.P.A.'s application depends on the principal applicant's under 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(3)(A).

10869728.situation:
PARTIES AND FORUM

Applicant/Respondent: Muchiri, a native of Kenya, in removal proceedings before the Immigration Court in Chelmsford, Massachusetts, and thereafter before the Board of Immigration Appeals ("BIA").

Government: U.S. Department of Homeland Security ("DHS").

ORIGIN OF PROCEEDINGS

On May 3, 2024, DHS served Muchiri with a notice to appear at removal proceedings. The notice to appear charges Muchiri with being subject to removal under § 237(a)(1)(B) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. § 1227(a)(1)(B)) for overstaying his visa. Muchiri was ordered to appear at removal proceedings in Chelmsford, Massachusetts, on June 3, 2024.

APPLICATIONS FOR RELIEF

Muchiri applied for asylum, humanitarian asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture ("CAT").

GOVERNING STANDARDS AS INVOKED

Asylum: An applicant must show he is unable or unwilling to return to, or avail himself of the protection of, his own country because of past persecution or a well-founded fear of future persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion. See 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A). The applicant must establish either past persecution (which creates a rebuttable presumption of future persecution) or a well-founded fear of future persecution.

Rebuttal of presumption: The presumption of a well-founded fear of future persecution can be rebutted by a showing that conditions in the applicant's native country have so changed that he no longer has a well-founded fear of future persecution, in which case the presumption disappears and the applicant is not entitled to asylum. Absent past persecution giving rise to the presumption, an applicant may show an independent likelihood of future persecution.

Humanitarian asylum: An applicant who has shown past persecution but failed to show a well-founded fear of future persecution may nonetheless be eligible for humanitarian asylum. To qualify, the applicant must show either compelling reasons for being unwilling or unable to return to the country arising out of the severity of the past persecution, or a reasonable possibility that he may suffer other serious harm upon removal. See 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(1)(iii)(A)-(B).

Withholding of removal: An applicant must show a clear probability that, if returned to his homeland, he will be persecuted on account of a statutorily protected ground. This is a more demanding standard than the well-founded fear standard applicable to asylum.

CAT: An applicant must demonstrate that he is more likely than not to be tortured by or with the acquiescence of public officials.

PROCEEDINGS AND DECISION BEFORE THE IMMIGRATION JUDGE

On September 11, 2024, the Immigration Judge ("IJ") assigned to Muchiri's case held removal proceedings to consider Muchiri's application for asylum, humanitarian asylum, withholding of removal, and CAT protection. The IJ denied the application in full in an oral decision.

Factual findings by the IJ: The IJ found Muchiri credible. The IJ found that Muchiri had successfully established that he suffered past persecution "on account of family." This finding rested on evidence Muchiri put forward that, while in Kenya, he suffered abuse at the hands of his father, who is "a Mungiki." The Mungiki is described throughout the record as a movement, cult, tribe, gang, clan, and minority religion.

Asylum ruling: The IJ found that the government had overcome the presumption of a well-founded fear of future persecution. The IJ based this on evidence that Muchiri is an adult no longer subject to his father's control and that country conditions in Kenya have changed, such that the police are now making an effort to combat the Mungiki group.

Humanitarian asylum ruling: The IJ denied the claim on the ground that Muchiri failed to show the required severity of past harm or a reasonable possibility of other serious harm to warrant humanitarian asylum. The IJ further stated that, even if Muchiri were eligible for asylum and humanitarian asylum, he would have been denied such relief on discretionary grounds due to his past encounters with law enforcement in the United States.

Withholding of removal ruling: The IJ determined that Muchiri's failure to establish eligibility for asylum necessarily precluded him from meeting the higher standard for withholding of removal. The IJ noted that, in any event, Muchiri failed to make the required showing "with respect to," in the IJ's words, "government unwilling and unable for future harm."

APPEAL TO THE BIA

On October 7, 2024, Muchiri, represented by new counsel, appealed the IJ's order to the BIA. In his brief to the BIA, Muchiri requested that the BIA reverse the IJ's decision denying his various claims or remand for further proceedings if necessary. On March 7, 2025, the BIA dismissed the appeal.

MOTION FOR RECONSIDERATION AND REQUEST FOR STAY

On March 12, 2025, Muchiri filed a motion for reconsideration of the BIA's March 7 decision and a request for an emergency stay of removal. On April 7, 2025, before the BIA ruled on the motion for reconsideration, Muchiri filed a petition for review of the BIA's March order (docketed as No. 25-1340).

BIA RULING ON RECONSIDERATION

On June 4, 2025, the BIA granted Muchiri's motion for reconsideration but again dismissed the appeal. The BIA explained that it had erred in finding that Muchiri had only been harmed by his father, "as the record shows [Muchiri] also suffered harm from other members of the Mungiki movement." The BIA determined, however, that all the incidents in which Muchiri had been subjected to harm while in Kenya occurred when he was a child. The BIA thus determined that these incidents did not undermine its original decision affirming the IJ's ruling, based on its "ultimate determination" that Muchiri's age and the country conditions "support a fundamental change in circumstances rebutting his well-founded fear of future persecution."

In ruling on the motion for reconsideration, the BIA also declined to disturb its prior rulings affirming the IJ's denial of Muchiri's claims for humanitarian asylum and CAT protection. The BIA explained that, although Muchiri had suffered harm from his father, "age mates" (whom Muchiri defined as people his age who had already joined the Mungiki), and "other Mungiki members," he had not established compelling reasons relating to this past harm or a reasonable possibility of other serious harm warranting a grant of humanitarian asylum. (Citing Matter of L-S-, 25 I. & N. Dec. 705, 710-14 (BIA 2012).) The BIA found that Muchiri had failed to explain how the sources of past harm the BIA had overlooked in its first decision—such as other Mungiki members and Muchiri's age mates—made him eligible for CAT protection, because he still had not demonstrated that he was more likely than not to be tortured by or with the acquiescence of public officials.

SUBSEQUENT PETITION

The same day the BIA issued its order granting reconsideration but dismissing the appeal, Muchiri petitioned for review of that order (docketed as No. 25-1544). Two petitions for review were then pending: the first concerning the BIA's initial ruling dismissing his appeal, and the second concerning the BIA's ruling granting reconsideration but again dismissing the appeal. On June 25, 2025, the two petitions were consolidated.

RELIEF SOUGHT

Muchiri seeks reversal of the denial of his claims for asylum, humanitarian asylum, withholding of removal, and CAT protection, or a remand for further proceedings.

10869844.situation:
CASE FILE

Parties
- Petitioner: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS).
- Respondent: mother of the minor children at issue.
- The oldest child's biological father is a placement caregiver.

Children and Placements
This matter concerns minor children of respondent. Three children were initially involved. The third, middle child was removed from these proceedings in accordance with the Indian Child Welfare Act, 25 USC 1901 et seq. The proceedings addressed here concern the oldest child and the youngest child.

- The youngest child was placed in licensed foster care.
- The oldest child remained in the care of her biological father, with whom she already was staying at the time of the proceedings.
- Both children remained in these respective placements for the duration of the case.

Initiation of Proceedings
DHHS filed a petition for jurisdiction over the minor children under MCL 712A.2(b)(1) and (2). The petition followed an investigation that confirmed medical neglect of the youngest child. The youngest child had been admitted to the hospital for weight concerns and received a diagnosis of "failure to thrive."

Preliminary Hearing
At the preliminary hearing, petitioner testified that it was contrary to the welfare of the children to remain in respondent's care and custody because respondent was unable to provide the necessary medical attention to keep the youngest child safe in light of his medical issues. The trial court agreed and placed the children in the care and supervision of petitioner.

Plea and Initial Disposition
Respondent pleaded no contest to the petition. The trial court ordered her to participate in, and show benefit from, the services recommended by petitioner. These services included:
- maintenance of housing and employment;
- undergoing a psychological evaluation and following up with its recommendations;
- completing parenting classes; and
- participating in anything else that might be added to the Parent Agency Treatment Plan (PATP) as the case evolved.

Amendment of the Service Plan
Soon after initial disposition, petitioner became aware of respondent's use of methamphetamine. Her service plan was amended to include participation in and benefit from substance use disorder (SUD) treatment as well as submission to periodic drug screening.

SUD Treatment History
- Respondent was referred to Recovery Pathways, an outpatient treatment provider. She failed to consistently engage with the provider and was discharged.
- She was later referred to another outpatient provider, Wellspring Lutheran Services, and was ultimately also discharged for inconsistent engagement, despite her representations to petitioner that she was making progress in the program.
- Throughout the case, respondent's drug screens consistently returned positive for methamphetamine use.

Psychological Evaluation
Respondent failed to appear for the psychological evaluation that petitioner scheduled for her early in the case and eventually was assessed months later. The evaluation reflected a need for continued mental-health interventions and inpatient drug treatment services.

Parenting Time and Parenting Education
- Respondent attended parenting times inconsistently.
- She received a parenting education certificate from Catholic Charities.
- Both the caseworker and the doctor who prepared her psychological evaluation found that she did not exhibit a benefit from that education.

Income
As of the termination hearing, respondent had not found a continued source of verifiable legal income beyond receiving government assistance.

Housing
The viability and stability of respondent's housing was the subject of some dispute between petitioner and respondent. Respondent had been living with an elderly woman for the majority of the case. Petitioner eventually found that living situation to be unstable because it was unclear whether respondent's lease agreement was enforceable.

Termination
The trial court terminated respondent's rights to both children, citing:
- respondent's inability to consistently engage with SUD treatment;
- inability to abstain from drugs; and
- inconsistency in addressing her service plan.

The statutory ground referenced was MCL 712A.19b(3)(c). Although the trial court only referred to MCL 712A.19b(3)(c), the parties agree that the trial court relied upon sub-division (c)(i), not (c)(ii).

Issue Presented for Review
Among the matters at issue is whether reasonable efforts were made.

10874475.holding_quote: Given the court’s failure to expressly consider JS’s relative placement as weighing against termination, as well as various other factors that may be relevant to its best-interests determination, we must vacate the trial court’s best-interests determination and remand for the trial court to conduct a new best-interests hearing.
10874475.situation:
CASE FILE

Parties and Roles:
- Petitioner: Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS).
- Respondent: the individual whose parental rights to JS are at issue. Respondent is not JS's custodial parent; JS lived with her mother and visited respondent almost daily.
- JS: a four-year-old child (at the time of the allegations) who is the subject of the proceedings.
- JS's mother: not a respondent in these proceedings and not a party to any appeal.
- JS's half-sister: the mother's minor daughter, who turned 18 at some point during the proceedings.

Origin of the Case:
DHHS became involved in January 2025 after Children's Protective Services (CPS) received allegations of sexual abuse of then-four-year-old JS by respondent. At that time, JS was living with her mother but visiting respondent almost daily.

Investigation Findings:
DHHS investigated the allegations. During a medical examination by a sexual assault nurse examiner (SANE), JS disclosed that respondent bathed her every visit and always used his bare hands, rather than a washcloth, to clean her genital area. JS demonstrated how respondent touched her genital area during the baths and, while doing so, pointed to her clitoral area and stated that respondent placed his fingers on that area and "wiggle[d]" them. JS tested positive for a urinary tract infection.

JS's mother informed CPS investigators that in the few weeks prior, JS had demonstrated significant behavioral changes, including night terrors, sleepwalking, and constant complaints that her vaginal area was irritated and itchy. According to JS's mother, JS had also "been more shut down and scared," and she started refusing to visit respondent. JS's mother became particularly concerned because these behaviors began shortly after respondent had started sending JS home with no underwear on and after respondent had repeatedly expressed that he was sexually attracted to the mother's minor daughter (JS's half-sister) and wished that he could have had a sexual relationship with her.

Respondent was interviewed by CPS investigators and police. He denied sexually abusing JS, but admitted to touching JS's genital area with his bare hands while bathing JS. He admitted that he had expressed that he was sexually attracted to JS's half-sister and wished that he had had a sexual relationship with her.

Petition and Relief Sought:
DHHS filed a petition requesting that the trial court remove JS from respondent's care, take jurisdiction over JS, and terminate respondent's parental rights at initial disposition.

Preliminary Hearing:
Following a preliminary hearing, the trial court authorized the petition, instructed that JS remain out of respondent's care and in the care of her mother under the supervision of DHHS, and suspended respondent's parenting time.

Adjudication:
Following an adjudication bench trial in April 2025, the court assumed jurisdiction. At that trial, the court received documentary evidence and testimony from JS's mother, a CPS investigator, an investigating officer, and the SANE who performed JS's medical examination.

Dispositional/Termination Hearing:
The trial court conducted a two-day initial dispositional hearing, which also acted as a termination hearing because DHHS had petitioned for termination at initial disposition. The first day occurred in July 2025 and the second occurred in September 2025. During the hearing, the court received additional testimony from respondent and two of his siblings.

Respondent's siblings both testified that JS and respondent appeared to have a strong bond and that they believed JS's allegations of sexual abuse were simply based on JS's misunderstanding of the situation.

Respondent testified. He admitted to touching JS in the way she described to the SANE but denied ever doing so for a sexual purpose or in such a way that penetrated her vagina. He asserted that he bathed JS so frequently because JS had bathroom-related accidents and he wanted to ensure her genital area was thoroughly cleaned, and he believed JS simply misunderstood what was going on during the baths. Respondent also acknowledged that he had admitted to others that he had sexual feelings for JS's half-sister and had wanted to have a sexual relationship with her.

Governing Standards Invoked:
Statutory grounds for termination under MCL 712A.19b(3)(b)(i) and (k)(ii), to be established by clear and convincing evidence; and the best-interests determination, to be established by a preponderance of the evidence.

Trial Court's Findings and Ruling:
At the conclusion of the hearing, after considering all the evidence, testimony, and arguments provided by the parties, the trial court found that statutory grounds for termination under MCL 712A.19b(3)(b)(i) and (k)(ii) had been established by clear and convincing evidence. The court also found, by a preponderance of the evidence, that termination of respondent's parental rights was in JS's best interests. The trial court subsequently issued an order terminating respondent's parental rights.

seed.consideration: Whether the child's placement with a relative (her mother) weighs against terminating the parent's rights.
seed.why_material: A trial court is required to expressly consider relative placement as a factor weighing against termination, and failure to do so renders the best-interests record inadequate and requires reversal.

10877182.holding_quote: Accordingly, we vacate Hampton's sentence and remand for resentencing based on the trial court's failure to make the proportionality finding required to impose consecutive sentences.
10877182.situation:
PARTIES AND CASES

Defendant: Hampton. Prosecuting authority: the State (Cuyahoga County). Two cases, consolidated for trial, are before the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas.

Case 695982 (Cuyahoga C.P. No. CR-24-695982-A)

On October 22, 2024, a Cuyahoga County Grand Jury indicts Hampton on two counts of failure to comply with an order or signal of a police officer in violation of R.C. 2921.331(B) and one count of having weapons while under disability in violation of R.C. 2923.13(A)(1). Each failure-to-comply count carries one- and six-year firearm specifications. All three counts carry forfeiture specifications.

The charges arise from an August 26, 2024 incident in which Hampton is involved in a police chase. Hampton ultimately runs from the vehicle he had been driving. A 3-D-printed firearm with a switch attachment -- making the firearm a dangerous ordnance -- is found on the driver's seat.

Case 698386 (Cuyahoga C.P. No. CR-25-698386-A)

On January 9, 2025, a Cuyahoga County Grand Jury indicts Hampton on: one count of involuntary manslaughter in violation of R.C. 2903.04(A) with the underlying felony of receiving stolen property; one count of involuntary manslaughter in violation of R.C. 2903.04(A) with the underlying felony of vehicular assault; two counts of failure to stop after an accident in violation of R.C. 4549.02(A)(1)(a); one count of aggravated vehicular homicide in violation of R.C. 2903.06(A)(2)(a); two counts of vehicular assault in violation of R.C. 2903.08(A)(2)(b); and one count of receiving stolen property in violation of R.C. 2913.51(A).

The charges arise from a July 21, 2024 car accident in which Hampton is driving a stolen Dodge Durango in Cleveland, Ohio and strikes a pole. Two people are thrown from the vehicle; one is hospitalized with serious injuries, and the other is pronounced dead on the scene. The other individuals in the vehicle, including Hampton, flee the scene. Hampton is identified as the driver because his DNA is found on the driver's side airbag.

Though Case 698386 is initiated several months after Case 695982, the incident underlying Case 698386 (July 21, 2024) occurred approximately one month before the incident underlying Case 695982 (August 26, 2024).

PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Hampton originally pleads not guilty to all charges in both cases.

On April 29, 2025, the State moves to consolidate the cases for trial. On June 2, 2025, the court grants the motion and the cases are consolidated.

CHANGE-OF-PLEA HEARING (June 16, 2025)

In Case 695982, Hampton pleads guilty to: one count of failure to comply with a six-year firearm specification and a forfeiture specification; one count of receiving stolen property; one count of unlawful possession of a dangerous ordnance with a six-year firearm specification; and one count of obstructing official business. The remaining counts and specifications in that case are dismissed.

In Case 698386, Hampton pleads guilty to: one count of involuntary manslaughter; one count of failure to stop after an accident; one count of aggravated vehicular homicide; two counts of vehicular assault; and one count of receiving stolen property. The remaining counts and specifications are dismissed.

SENTENCING HEARING (July 30, 2025)

The court states that it has reviewed the presentence-investigation report. A family member of one of the victims addresses the court, along with the assistant prosecuting attorney, defense counsel, Hampton's mother, and Hampton.

In Case 695982, the court sentences Hampton to: nine months' imprisonment for failure to comply, to be served consecutively to the remaining charges; 12 months for receiving stolen property; six months for unlawful possession of a dangerous ordnance, together with six years for the attendant firearm specification to be served consecutively; and 12 months for obstructing official business. With the exception of the firearm specification and the failure-to-comply sentence, the sentences are ordered to be served concurrently, for a prison sentence of seven years and three months.

In Case 698386, the court sentences Hampton to: 36 months' imprisonment for involuntary manslaughter; 36 months for failure to stop after an accident; 12 months for aggravated vehicular homicide; and 12 months for receiving stolen property. The court orders the sentence for aggravated vehicular homicide to be served consecutively to the remaining sentences, for a total prison sentence of four years.

The sentences in Cases 698386 and 695982 are ordered to be served concurrently.

ISSUE PRESENTED

Hampton contends that his rights under the Fifth, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution, and under Article I, Sections 9 and 16 of the Ohio Constitution, were violated by the trial court's imposition of sentences that were contrary to law.

10877255.case_name: Hey Listen Mandyhan, L.L.C. v. Trody
10877255.holding_quote: There is no indication that the trial court considered the evidence in the record regarding the current status of the property and whether it now contained a dwelling despite its past commercial use.
10877255.situation:
PARTIES AND PROPERTY

Plaintiff Mandyhan is the owner of a parcel of land in Toledo, Lucas County, Ohio. The parcel contains a single structure—a garage that was previously used as an auto repair business. Defendant Rick Trody occupies the parcel.

The property is zoned "commercial," specifically "neighborhood commercial" (CN). Mandyhan's exhibits define the CN zoning district as one "intended to accommodate pedestrian oriented small-scale retail and service businesses that serve nearby residential areas."

THE AGREEMENTS

Mandyhan executed the agreements at issue on December 14, 2021. The parties agree the agreements were executed "simultaneously" and assign Trody's signature date of January 4, 2022, as the date they became effective.

The first agreement is titled "Residential Real Estate Lease Agreement." It obligates Trody to pay monthly rent of $459.10 on or before the first day of each month, and requires a security deposit of $3,000. The lease contains an integration clause stating that the lease is the entire agreement between the parties.

The second agreement is titled "Residential Real Estate Purchase Agreement." Its terms include a down payment of $3,000, a purchase price of $35,000, and seller financing of $32,000. The purchase agreement includes a term requiring Trody to pay the taxes and "assessments" on the property.

Mandyhan's representative testified that although the lease stated a rent price of $459.10, Trody actually paid $570 per month (elsewhere described as $574), with the additional funds allocated toward taxes and insurance on the property.

MARK GRABOW is identified as the Mandyhan representative who executed the agreement.

PAYMENT HISTORY AND NOTICE

It is undisputed that Trody paid the monthly rent through March 2025. Trody did not make the rent payments in April and May 2025. Mandyhan's representative described the delinquency as running since March 1, 2025.

On May 2, 2025, Garrison Hill, an associate of Mandyhan, posted a three-day notice at the property ordering Trody to vacate. The notice did not provide Trody with ten days to vacate the premises or to cure. Trody attempted to make the delinquent payments after receiving the notice; Mandyhan declined them. Trody did not vacate the property.

PROCEDURAL POSTURE

On May 28, 2025, Mandyhan filed a complaint for forcible entry and detainer of the parcel pursuant to R.C. Chapter 1923. Attached to the complaint were a copy of the "Residential Real Estate Lease Agreement" (Exhibit B), the three-day notice to vacate (Exhibit C), and zoning materials.

The matter proceeded to a hearing before a magistrate on July 8, 2025.

OPENING STATEMENTS

Trody informed the court that he intended to show that the parties had contemporaneously entered into both the lease and a purchase agreement for the property, and that these agreements together constituted a land installment contract pursuant to R.C. 5313.02. He stated that if the parties had entered into a land installment contract, he was entitled to a ten-day period to repay the arrearage, and that because he had already paid more than 20 percent of the purchase price, any proceedings to forfeit his interest and evict him had to proceed through foreclosure rather than through a forcible entry and detainer action. Mandyhan declined to make an opening statement.

TESTIMONY OF JENNIFER MARIE

Jennifer Marie testified that she is a representative for Mandyhan whose responsibilities include collecting rent from tenants and paying taxes and insurance on the properties. She confirmed Mandyhan is the owner of the disputed property. She identified Exhibit B as the lease agreement, which required monthly rent of $459.10, and testified Trody had been delinquent since March 1, 2025. She identified Exhibit C as the three-day notice to vacate posted by Garrison Hill on May 2, 2025, and stated Trody attempted to make the delinquent payments after receiving it and Mandyhan declined them.

On cross-examination, she described the lease's $3,000 security deposit requirement. She denied knowledge of another agreement titled "Residential Real Estate Purchase Agreement." After being presented with a copy, she confirmed its basic terms—$3,000 down payment, $35,000 purchase price, and $32,000 seller financing. She stated Trody actually paid $570 per month, with additional funds allocated to taxes and insurance, and acknowledged the purchase agreement required Trody to pay taxes and assessments.

Trody introduced a payment ledger prepared by Mandyhan reflecting his rent payments. Marie could not calculate the total amounts paid according to the ledger or the remaining purchase-price balance assuming the sales agreement was valid. She confirmed she did not provide Trody with a ten-day notice to make the delinquent payments.

On redirect, Marie testified the property was zoned commercial, identified the zoning as "neighborhood commercial," and identified the definition of that district. Over Trody's objection, she testified she did not believe the zoning permitted residential structures. She recognized the lease's inclusion of a "purchase portion" but stated that if Trody defaulted on rent, the purchase portion would be terminated.

On recross, she could not recall whether there were other residential properties in the area and denied knowledge that Trody was residing at the property under the lease. On additional redirect, she stated the parties had not entered into a land installment contract.

TESTIMONY OF GARRISON HILL

Hill testified that he posted the three-day notice at the property on May 2, 2025. On cross-examination, he confirmed the notice did not provide Trody ten days to vacate the premises.

MOTION FOR JUDGMENT

At the conclusion of Hill's testimony, Trody moved for judgment in his favor, arguing that the preponderance of the evidence showed the parties had entered into a land installment contract, and therefore that Mandyhan could not proceed with an eviction providing only a three-day notice to vacate rather than the ten-day notice to cure required under R.C. 5313.06. He further argued that because he had paid more than 20 percent of the purchase price through prior rent payments, Mandyhan had to proceed through a foreclosure action rather than an eviction pursuant to R.C. 5313.07. The court took the motion under advisement, and Trody proceeded with his defense.

TESTIMONY OF RICK TRODY

Trody testified that he entered into an agreement with Mandyhan to purchase the property in November 2021, and that this was Mandyhan's understanding based on representations its representatives made to him at that time. He described improvements he made with Mandyhan's approval, including dividing a portion of the former auto repair business to establish a residential apartment for his use. He stated that Mark Grabow, the Mandyhan representative who executed the agreement, provided him with materials and paint for the renovation. Trody has lived at the property since making the renovations, and Mandyhan never objected to his residing there.

Trody addressed the ledger he received from Mandyhan, confirming he had made $21,543 in total payments under the agreement, with $12,399 going toward interest on the financing. After dispute over what the ledger showed, the court questioned Trody directly, and he confirmed he paid a monthly fee of $574 to Mandyhan.

On cross-examination, Trody stated he had previously run a commercial auto repair business at the property. He was unaware of any requested variances from the commercial zoning restriction to allow residential use. He described the property as a garage with a small entry area leading into the apartment he created, which had a couch, television, bed, kitchen, and bathroom.

JUDICIAL NOTICE REQUESTS

Trody requested that the court take judicial notice of the ledger calculations and other calculations referenced during the hearing. The court did not explicitly rule on these requests, instructing Trody to "proceed."

CLOSING ARGUMENTS

Mandyhan argued the parties entered into a lease agreement in late 2021 or early 2022; that the property was zoned for commercial purposes and Trody's conversion of it into a residence did not render it residential property subject to a land installment contract; and that the purchase agreement was an option to purchase separate from the lease, effective only upon Trody's completion of his lease obligations. Because Trody failed to make the March and April 2025 payments, Mandyhan argued he could not exercise the purchase option, had violated the lease, and was subject to the forcible entry and detainer action.

Trody argued the parties entered into a land installment contract for residential property, entitling him to the protections of R.C. Chapter 5313—including a ten-day notice to make delinquent payments before forfeiting rights, and the requirement that any adverse action proceed through foreclosure. He further argued that if the agreement did not meet the statutory requirements of R.C. 5313.02, the purchase agreement substantially complied with the statute and was enforceable.

MAGISTRATE'S DECISION

The magistrate issued a decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law on July 17, 2025. It determined there was no residential dwelling on the property—a predicate for application of R.C. Chapter 5313—and that the agreement did not meet the statutory requirements for a land installment contract under R.C. 5313.02. The magistrate found the parties' agreement ambiguous, requiring a determination of the parties' intent, and held that the parties intended a lease agreement with a separate purchase option to be executed at the conclusion of the lease. It found Trody was not entitled to the protections of R.C. Chapter 5313 and ordered the tenancy terminated with possession returned to Mandyhan.

TRODY'S OBJECTIONS AND THE TRIAL COURT'S JUDGMENT

Trody filed objections on July 31, 2025, arguing that the magistrate (1) incorrectly found the property's commercial zoning precluded the premises from being considered a dwelling; (2) failed to consider whether the agreements substantially complied with the requirements of a valid land installment contract; and (3) erroneously interpreted the parties' intent as executing a lease with a purchase option after finding the agreements ambiguous.

The trial court overruled the objections. It found the magistrate had not relied on the commercial zoning in finding no dwelling on the property, but rather that "the stated purpose of the occupied structure at the time of its building was non-residential." Noting that R.C. 5313.01(B) defines property subject to a land installment contract as "real property located in this state improved by virtue of a dwelling having been erected on the real property," the court concluded that Trody's failure to erect a new dwelling on the property precluded the existing building from being considered a dwelling. Because the property lacked a dwelling and was therefore not subject to a land installment contract, the court found the magistrate's alleged failure to consider substantial compliance moot. The court found the magistrate correctly resolved the ambiguities because it found Mandyhan's witness more credible when she denied the parties had entered into a land installment contract. Because the lease included an integration clause stating the lease was the entire agreement between the parties, the court found the purchase agreement could not alter its terms, and that the magistrate properly found the parties' intent was to execute a lease with an option to purchase at the conclusion of that lease.

The trial court's judgment was memorialized on August 14, 2025.

GOVERNING PROVISIONS INVOKED

R.C. Chapter 1923 (forcible entry and detainer); R.C. 5313.01(B) (definition of property subject to a land installment contract); R.C. 5313.02 (requirements of a land installment contract); R.C. 5313.06 (notice to cure); R.C. 5313.07 (foreclosure where 20 percent of purchase price paid).
