10878135.situation:
CASE FILE — Vora v. Vora (Divorce), Warren County Domestic Relations Court

PARTIES AND FAMILY BACKGROUND

Mahendra Vora (plaintiff) and Sangita Vora (defendant) married in India on May 6, 1986. Shortly after the marriage they moved to Michigan, where Mahendra had previously lived and attended school. In 1988 they moved to Cincinnati. Two daughters were born of the marriage: Priyanka in 1989 and Anushree in 1995. Both daughters are now adults.

During the marriage, Sangita was not employed outside the home. She managed the household, including child-rearing. Due in part to Sangita's efforts at home, Mahendra was able to focus on work and on an entrepreneurial career developing and selling multiple technology-focused companies. Beginning the marriage with essentially no assets, the parties now hold assets in both the United States and India valued at well over $100 million. The most significant of these assets is the family business, Vora Ventures, LLC, a holding company that acquires or develops technology companies with the aim of turning them into profitable businesses and/or acquisition targets.

SEPARATION AND FILING

In August 2018, problems arose in the marriage. Sangita left the marital home but eventually returned. The parties separated again in April 2019. For two years, the parties attempted to resolve their issues through mediation, without success. In February 2022, Mahendra filed for divorce.

PRE-TRIAL STIPULATIONS AND NOTICES

Prior to trial, the parties entered into stipulations. Among them, the parties stipulated that Vora Ventures was valued at $96 million. Prior to trial, Mahendra also filed a notice, pursuant to Civ.R. 44.1, that he would raise and rely on foreign law with respect to a 'Hindu Undivided Family' trust.

THE CONTESTED HEARING

In June 2023, the domestic relations court held a 10-day trial on all contested matters. Numerous witnesses testified and a large number of exhibits were introduced. The contested matters relevant to this file were: (1) whether a series of charitable transfers of shares of Vora Ventures to the parties' daughters were legitimate transfers, and, if not, whether the court should make an unequal division of marital assets to compensate Sangita for the transfer of these shares; (2) the value of the parties' vacation home in India; (3) the value of an investment in a plot of vacant land in India; and (4) whether certain marital assets were placed into Mahendra's Hindu Undivided Family trust, and, if so, whether those assets remained marital property.

AnuPriya (Indian Vacation Home)

In 2006, Mahendra purchased a 2.5-acre vacant plot of land in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India, with a plan to build the family's Indian vacation home. Planning and discussions lasted two or three years. Construction began in 2014 and was completed in 2018. The home is approximately 21,000 square feet on the first and second floors alone. The parties named the home 'AnuPriya,' a combination of their daughters' names. There is no dispute that AnuPriya (the land and the building) was purchased and built entirely with marital funds.

The parties disagreed about the value of AnuPriya and presented competing expert reports and testimony. Mahendra obtained a valuation from an appraisal firm named 'JLL,' which valued AnuPriya at 1,375,341,000 Indian rupees. Sangita obtained a valuation from another appraisal firm, 'Colliers,' which valued AnuPriya at 1,848,000,000 Indian rupees. The expert valuations differed by about $6 million (using an exchange rate of 82.65 Indian rupees per U.S. Dollar drawn from the Colliers report).

SGV and the SGV Plot

The parties also disagreed about the value of another marital asset in India: a plot of undeveloped land in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India. Around 2007 or 2008, Mahendra entered into a joint venture with two business partners, named 'SGV.' SGV's only asset is a 16-acre plot of undeveloped land (the 'SGV Plot'). At the onset, Mahendra owned one-third of the shares in SGV. Over time he sold part of his interest to his partners and held a 15% share in SGV at the relevant time.

Because the SGV Plot was SGV's only holding, the parties presented competing expert testimony and reports concerning the value of the SGV Plot and Mahendra's 15% interest in SGV. JLL valued Mahendra's 15% interest at 844,917,900 Indian rupees. Colliers valued Mahendra's 15% interest at 1,095,000,000 Indian rupees. The competing opinions differed by about $3 million.

Mahendra testified that he owed a debt to his two SGV business partners for amounts they had spent maintaining the property. He identified an exhibit indicating that as of April 2023 he owed them 87,472,943 rupees. Mahendra asked that this debt be considered in the overall valuation of his interest in SGV.

Vora Ventures, LLC

In 2006, Mahendra formed Vora Ventures, a holding company for various technology companies he either built from the ground up or acquired. For the most part, the companies owned by Vora Ventures operate in a negative-cash-flow environment for years before they may or may not begin producing positive cash flow. Mahendra would often obtain bank loans or extend personal loans to these companies to keep them operating. One company owned by Vora Ventures, which contributed a great portion to its paper value, had been operating at a monthly loss of $1.1 million for three years, between 2019 and 2022; it continued to operate, relying on loans from Vora Ventures and a $30 million bank loan. Vora Ventures profits when one of these businesses is sold or starts turning a profit.

Vora Ventures' initial operating agreement provided that Mahendra had a 99% controlling interest and Sangita had a 1% interest.

Beginning in May 2017, Mahendra and Sangita began transferring shares of Vora Ventures to their daughters. Mahendra, Priyanka, and Anushree described this as an intentional estate planning strategy: to make tax-advantaged gift transfers of Vora Ventures shares to Priyanka and Anushree at a time when the relative valuation of Vora Ventures was low, and shares could be transferred without exceeding the then $5 million estate and gift tax limitation. Mahendra, Priyanka, and Anushree testified that the family, including Sangita, had numerous and extensive discussions about making these transfers, starting in 2016.

Between May 2017 and January 2019, the parties signed revised operating agreements that ultimately resulted in Mahendra holding 51% of the shares, Sangita holding 11%, and Priyanka and Anushree each holding 19%. Later, both Priyanka and Anushree assigned their shares to non-marital trusts. Mahendra explained this was done immediately before Priyanka married, to safeguard their interests in Vora Ventures, and because pre-nuptial agreements are culturally unacceptable in India.

Sangita's signature appears on all of the documents effecting these transfers, including the consent documents necessary to assign the Vora Ventures shares to the daughters' trusts. At trial, Sangita did not deny signing these documents. She claimed she essentially had no knowledge of what she was signing, that single-page documents were handed to her and she signed without question, and that she was not involved in or consulted regarding these transfers as they occurred. Sangita argued that what occurred was essentially a scheme by Mahendra to move her marital interest in Vora Ventures outside of the marital estate, noting that some of the transfers occurred after she had separated from Mahendra.

Mahendra, Priyanka, and Anushree all testified that Sangita was fully aware and actively involved in the estate planning efforts. When asked if Priyanka was lying about her being present for these family discussions, Sangita would not agree that her daughter was lying, but indicated that 'maybe her perception is that I was there, but in reality, I wasn't there.'

Sangita asked the court to award her half of the total value of Vora Ventures ($48 million), rather than half of the 62% owned by her and Mahendra ($29.76 million). She was not seeking to unwind the transactions; she asked the court to equitably grant her this amount in the overall property division.

The Mahendra Vora HUF (Hindu Undivided Family)

A 'Hindu Undivided Family,' or 'HUF,' is a legal, taxable entity recognized under Indian law, similar to an American trust. Its purpose is to place assets in a separate legal entity held for the betterment of lineal descendants. The person who forms the HUF is known as the 'Karta.' The main beneficiaries are called 'co-parceners' — generally the lineal (blood) descendants of the Karta, plus the Karta. A second class of beneficiary is called a 'member' — any person in the Karta's immediate family related only by marriage. Members have no vested interest in assets placed in the HUF. Here, Mahendra is the Karta of the Mahendra Vora HUF ('MV HUF'); Mahendra, Anushree, and Priyanka are co-parceners; and Sangita is a member.

Mahendra testified that he formed the MV HUF shortly after his marriage to Sangita and then opened a bank account with an Indian bank, the Bank of Baroda, in the name of the MV HUF. He testified that in 2006, and again in 2015, he signed formal declarations declaring AnuPriya to be part of the MV HUF. He further testified that in the beginning of 2018 he assigned his shares in SGV to the MV HUF.

THE DOMESTIC RELATIONS COURT'S DECISIONS

Following the hearing, the court issued a series of decisions: a first partial decision on October 26, 2023; a second partial decision on January 8, 2024, following briefing on the payment issue; and a 'third and final partial decision' on March 1, 2024, following requests for clarification. The court then ordered the parties to submit a proposed final decree of divorce. The parties disputed the language, and the court issued two decisions regarding the disputes. On October 3, 2024, the court issued the final decree of divorce.

First Partial Decision (October 26, 2023)

Value of the Marital Portion of Vora Ventures: The court noted that, based on the charitable transfers to the daughters, Mahendra and Sangita collectively owned 62% of Vora Ventures. Mahendra agreed this was a marital asset subject to equal division, leaving Mahendra and Sangita with $29.76 million each (based on the $96 million valuation). Sangita argued the court should disregard the charitable transfers, based on her allegedly being kept in the dark, and sought half the total value of Vora Ventures — $48 million — grounded in equity.

The court declined to disregard the charitable transfers. It noted Mahendra's argument that Sangita's own financial expert, after reviewing 'countless documents,' found that Mahendra never committed any act of financial misconduct. The court found that Vora Ventures' operating agreement and its revisions, which effected the transfers, had not been challenged in any court. Absent a successful challenge to the corporate structure, the court stated it was 'convinced that its current setup is the way the parties wanted it to be, and therefore should not be changed.' The court noted the outcome may have differed if the transfers had resulted in the daughters owning all or a vast majority of shares, leaving Sangita with only a small amount, or if Sangita had transferred her interest in return for another asset of non-comparable value. The court found the marital portion of Vora Ventures valued at $59,520,000, making Sangita's share $29,760,000.

The MV HUF and Whether Assets Were Transferred: The court summarized the expert testimony from both parties on the nature, creation, and means of transferring assets to a HUF, and Mahendra's testimony about the steps he took to create the MV HUF and transfer property, including AnuPriya and his SGV shares. The court first found Mahendra had properly created the MV HUF. As to AnuPriya, the court noted competing expert testimony as to whether Mahendra's two declarations sufficed to transfer a legal interest to the MV HUF, notwithstanding that title to AnuPriya remained solely in Mahendra's name up to trial; the court resolved that AnuPriya was not properly transferred to the MV HUF and found it a marital asset subject to equal division. As to the SGV Plot, the court noted Mahendra testified and introduced exhibits showing he transferred his SGV shares to the MV HUF in April 2018, and found Sangita 'did not contradict' that the SGV shares were properly transferred; the court found the SGV shares were in the MV HUF, and that the SGV shares were marital property subject to equal division. As to the Bank of Baroda account, the court made no findings as to whether it was in the MV HUF, instead finding it marital and subject to equal division.

Contested Values: The court found the value of AnuPriya to be that suggested by Mahendra's expert, 1,375,341,000 rupees. The court found the value of Mahendra's 15% share of SGV to be 844,917,900 rupees, and noted that value would have to be reduced by 87,473,943 rupees because of Mahendra's debt owed to his partners.

Spousal Support: Sangita requested spousal support, noting Mahendra earned a salary of $500,000 from Vora Ventures and that his income should be equalized with hers, which would result in a monthly payment of $20,833. Mahendra argued Sangita should receive no spousal support given the significant assets she would receive in the property division. The court considered all factors set forth in R.C. 3105.18, including the income of the parties, the relative earning abilities, the duration of the marriage, the contribution of each party to the education, training, and earning ability of the other, and the standard of living. The court awarded Sangita monthly spousal support of $10,000. The court continued the matter for hearing and argument on how Mahendra would pay Sangita her share of the overall property division for assets in both countries.

Second Partial Decision (January 8, 2024)

The court noted Mahendra owed Sangita $18,311,054 for assets in the United States. Mahendra asked to pay this amount over 10 years, at $1.8 million yearly, and proposed that no interest accrue for the first seven years. Mahendra's arguments for no interest were: (1) it would incentivize him to pay the total debt within the first seven years; (2) most Vora Ventures companies operated at negative cash flow and he needed liquidity to keep them operating; (3) he would have to generate significant pre-tax income to pay the annual $1.8 million; and (4) Sangita would have access to $8.7 million in marital assets immediately following the divorce. Mahendra also offered that if any Vora Ventures company were sold during the repayment plan, Sangita would receive 50% of the net post-sale proceeds, up to a maximum of $10 million in one year, which would satisfy the $1.8 million obligation for that year.

Sangita argued the payment plan was 'wholly inequitable,' noting Mahendra did not offer interest-free loans to the Vora Ventures companies to which he lent personal monies, and that an interest-free arrangement would let him invest monies owed to her and further enrich himself during the repayment period. Sangita asked the court to impose interest at 10% per annum on amounts owed.

The court ordered the payment plan suggested by Mahendra — $1.8 million per year with no interest for the first seven years — and ordered 5% interest on any unpaid balance after the first seven years, citing the reasons set forth in Mahendra's memorandum as the basis for the no-interest period. The court further ordered that Mahendra was restrained from selling, giving away, or otherwise transferring his interest in Vora Ventures until Sangita was paid her share of the property division in full.

Third Partial Decision (March 1, 2024)

The court addressed various questions posed for clarification or reconsideration from the first two partial decisions, and ordered Mahendra's attorney to prepare the final decree of divorce incorporating the decisions set forth in the three partial decisions.

Disputes over Final Decree

The parties could not agree on the language in the final decree and raised the disputed issues with the court, leading to additional briefing and two hearings. The court issued two decisions on these disputes. Sangita raised issues concerning the valuation date of certain accounts the parties held with Goldman Sachs, and issues regarding whether the parties had agreed to certain language regarding the use of a U.S.-dollar-to-Indian-rupee conversion formula. The court issued rulings on both.

On October 3, 2024, the domestic relations court issued the entry and final decree and judgment of divorce.

SANGITA'S POSITION ON THE PROPERTY DIVISION

Sangita contends the division of marital property was inequitable. Her supporting issues are whether the court failed to make an equitable division based on Mahendra's dissipation of significant marital assets, and whether the court failed to make a finding regarding Mahendra's financial misconduct. Her position is that she presented evidence Mahendra engaged in financial misconduct by orchestrating a series of transfers of Vora Ventures outside the marital estate by gifting shares to the daughters without her consent or knowledge. She asserts Mahendra presented self-serving testimony that these transfers began in 2017, prior to when she first left the marital residence, but that the first documentary evidence the transfers actually occurred was in gift tax returns executed in October 2018, after she had left the marital residence in August 2018. She argues the transfers were 'undertaken as an act of divorce planning after the parties separated in 2018,' suggesting Mahendra created a record of undated documents to make it appear that the family began planning and making charitable transfers before any signs of trouble, and that all transfers occurred after Mahendra realized the marriage was likely ending. Sangita argues the court made no specific factual findings regarding Mahendra's alleged financial misconduct and instead simply found it lacked jurisdiction to alter the corporate structure of Vora Ventures as set forth in the operating agreements.

10884052.situation:
CASE FILE

PARTIES AND BACKGROUND

Mother and Father are the parents of two minor children. The parties were never married but once lived together. During the period they lived together, Father earned approximately $160,000 a year and Mother stayed home with the children. The parties separated in 2010.

The district court docket reflects that a decree of paternity was entered in Texas and was subsequently registered as a foreign decree in Oklahoma.

THE 2021 AGREED ORDER

In 2021, the district court entered an agreed order. The order awarded Mother sole custody of the children and awarded Father supervised visitation. Under the 2021 order, Father was ordered to pay monthly child support of approximately $720, based on his then-current gross income of approximately $3,600 a month.

The 2021 order contained a provision requiring each party to notify the other within seven days if that party obtained employment earning remuneration of more than 25% of their current income. The order also included instructions for new child support guidelines to be prepared by Mother's attorney for submission to the court without requiring Mother to file another motion to modify.

THE 2022 MOTION TO MODIFY

Father did not provide the notice required by the 2021 order. In 2022, Mother filed a motion to modify, alleging Father's income had increased by more than 25% and seeking modification of child support.

A discovery dispute followed concerning Father's income. The dispute was complicated by Father frequently changing attorneys, though some of the changes resulted from his attorney becoming ill and then recovering and reentering the case.

After Mother filed her motion, Father changed jobs two times, each change increasing his income by more than 25%. Father's gross income ultimately exceeded $26,000 a month. That amount is significantly above $15,000, the maximum combined gross monthly income listed in the child support guidelines.

THE HEARING ON THE MOTION TO MODIFY

A two-day hearing on Mother's motion was held in August 2023 and December 2023.

Mother presented evidence of the children's direct and indirect monthly living expenses. She asserted that Father's percentage of these expenses was approximately $4,055 a month and requested child support in that amount. Mother testified that the standard of living she provided the children based on these expenses was in their best interests. Mother testified that her gross monthly income was approximately $4,300, and that this amount was not enough to cover her and the children's monthly expenses.

Father testified that he did not believe the children's expenses were as much as Mother asserted. He testified that he thought a reasonable amount of the children's expenses was around $1,700 a month, which is approximately the same amount he would be required to pay by applying his percentage share of the parents' combined income to the maximum combined income amount listed in the guidelines. Father did not provide a specific calculation showing how he arrived at this amount; he stated that it sounded reasonable.

The parties' testimony indicated that Father lacked personal knowledge of the children's expenses, such as their food costs, given that he had no overnight visits and had seen the children only once in the three-year period before the hearing.

Toward the end of his testimony, Father stated that he would "offer" to pay a monthly amount of $2,250.

THE CHILD SUPPORT RULING

The district court ordered Father to pay $2,250 in monthly child support, based on the amount Father volunteered to pay. The court noted that it was not following Archer v. Archer, 1991 OK CIV APP 28, 813 P.2d 1059.

THE APPLICATION FOR ATTORNEY FEES AND COSTS

Mother filed an application for attorney fees and costs seeking a total of $14,185.95, incurred during the approximately two years it took to reach a resolution on her motion to modify.

At the hearing on the application, Mother emphasized Father's delays during the pendency of the case. She noted that the litigation could have been avoided or limited if Father had complied with the provision in the 2021 order requiring him to timely notify her of a significant change to his income so that her attorney could draft a new child support calculation for submission to the court. Mother also argued that Father was the party with the greater ability to pay.

Father made various arguments against Mother's request. He argued that Mother had declined his offers to settle the case and that she could have increased her income by returning to practicing law rather than teaching school.

The district court concluded that the amount of Mother's requested fees was reasonable. However, the court stated it was awarding only the fees and costs incurred for Mother's discovery efforts, noting that the discovery "really was quite out of line from the norm." The court did not award Mother any other fees or costs and did not elaborate on the reason for that decision. The district court entered an order awarding Mother attorney fees and costs of $4,099.31.

RELIEF SOUGHT ON REVIEW

Mother challenges the order awarding her child support in the amount of $2,250 a month and the order awarding her fees and costs in the amount of $4,099.31.

GOVERNING STANDARDS

A district court's decision on a motion to modify child support will not be disturbed unless the court's decision is clearly against the weight of the evidence so as to constitute an abuse of discretion. Williamson v. Williamson, 2005 OK 6, 107 P.3d 589.

Regarding an award of attorney fees and costs, each party ordinarily bears the cost of her own legal representation, and courts are without authority to award attorney fees and costs in the absence of a specific statute or specific agreement between the parties. Metcalf v. Metcalf, 2020 OK 20, 465 P.3d 1187; see McKiddy v. Alarkon, 2011 OK CIV APP 63, 254 P.3d 141; see also Childers v. Childers, 2016 OK 95, 382 P.3d 1020; Merritt v. Merritt, 2003 OK 68, 73 P.3d 878.

When applying an abuse of discretion standard, underlying questions of law are reviewed de novo. See Shellem v. Gruneweld, 2023 OK 26, 535 P.3d 1208; Walterscheidt v. Hladik, 2022 OK 57, 512 P.3d 354.

seed.consideration: When a parent's income exceeds the maximum amount in the child support guidelines table, the court should determine the additional support by weighing the children's needs consistent with an appropriate lifestyle, the prior standard of living, and the parent's ability to pay.
seed.why_material: Ignoring these factors and instead simply accepting the payor's volunteered figure lets the high-earning parent dictate his own obligation and denies the children the benefit of his affluence.

10917121.situation:
CASE FILE — Petition for Review of EPA Risk-Management Rules for Decabromodiphenyl Ether (decaBDE) under TSCA § 6(h)

SUBJECT CHEMICAL
Decabromodiphenyl Ether ("decaBDE") is an additive flame retardant used in numerous products, including electronics, appliances, and car and airplane parts. EPA characterizes decaBDE as a highly hazardous persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic ("PBT") chemical. According to the record, decaBDE can damage the immune system, reproductive system, brain, thyroid, liver, and other organs, and has been linked to cancer, endocrine disruption, and altered gene expression. EPA states that decaBDE poses a particular danger to human and environmental health because it remains in the environment for long periods of time, can accumulate up the food chain, and has toxic attributes in small quantities. Once released, decaBDE is very persistent; its breakdown can take generations, and when it does break down it can generate even more persistent, toxic, and bioaccumulative byproducts.

STATUTORY FRAMEWORK — TSCA GENERALLY
Congress enacted the Toxic Substances Control Act ("TSCA") in 1976 to protect the public from unreasonable risks to health or the environment posed by chemicals. 15 U.S.C. § 2601. Congress found that human beings and the environment are exposed each year to a large number of chemical substances and mixtures, that some of these may present an unreasonable risk of injury to health or the environment through their manufacture, processing, distribution in commerce, use, or disposal, and that effective regulation of interstate commerce in such substances also necessitates regulation of intrastate commerce. 15 U.S.C. §§ 2601(a)(1)–(3).

When EPA determines that a use presents an unreasonable risk of injury to health or the environment, EPA must apply one or more regulatory tools under 15 U.S.C. § 2605(a) ("Section 6"): prohibiting or restricting the substance's manufacture, processing, or distribution in commerce; requiring the substance be marked with warnings and instructions for use; requiring recordkeeping by manufacturers and processors; prohibiting, limiting, or otherwise regulating the manner or method of commercial use; and prohibiting or regulating the manner or method of disposal. Section 6(b) requires EPA to conduct risk evaluations, identifying substances as "high" or "low" priority and setting standards and deadlines for the evaluation process. 15 U.S.C. § 2605(b). Where EPA determines a substance presents an unreasonable risk, § 6(c) sets forth the timeline, process, and requirements for issuing § 6(a) rules. 15 U.S.C. § 2605(c).

Before promulgating final rules, EPA is required to provide at least 30 days for public comment on proposed rules and to allow participation through submission of written data, views, or arguments. 5 U.S.C. § 553(c).

STATUTORY FRAMEWORK — TSCA § 6(h)
TSCA has been amended many times. As part of the 2016 amendments in the Frank R. Lautenberg Chemical Safety for the 21st Century Act, Congress added subsection (h), codified at 15 U.S.C. § 2605(h) ("§ 6(h)"). Section 6(h) governs risk-management rules addressing exposures to decaBDE and other substances identified in the 2014 update of the TSCA Work Plan for Chemical Assessments. It requires EPA to take expedited action on PBTs listed in the 2014 Work Plan update that EPA (1) reasonably determines to be toxic; (2) rates high for either persistence or bioaccumulation; and (3) determines are likely to generate exposure to the general population, to higher-risk subpopulations, or to the environment. 15 U.S.C. § 2605(h).

Section 6(h) directed EPA to propose risk-management rules under subsection (a) within three years of the statute's enactment (by June 22, 2019) and to promulgate final rules within 18 months of proposing such rules. 15 U.S.C. §§ 2605(h)(1), (3). Unlike the typical § 6(a) process, EPA is not required to conduct a risk evaluation under § 6(h). 15 U.S.C. § 2605(h)(2). Section 6(h)(4) provides: "In selecting among prohibitions and other restrictions promulgated in a rule under subsection (a) pursuant to paragraph (1), the Administrator shall address the risks of injury to health or the environment that the Administrator determines are presented by the chemical substance and shall reduce exposure to the substance to the extent practicable." 15 U.S.C. § 2605(h)(4).

EPA rated decaBDE "high" for hazard, exposure, persistence, and bioaccumulation. According to the 2021 Rule, exposure to decaBDE is likely under the conditions of use to the general population, to a potentially exposed or susceptible subpopulation, or the environment, and there is potential for exposure under the conditions of use at all stages of its lifecycle.

DEFINITIONS
EPA defines an "article" as "a manufactured item: (1) Which is formed to a specific shape or design during manufacture, (2) Which has end use function(s) dependent in whole or in part upon its shape or design during end use, and (3) Which has either no change of chemical composition during its end use or only those changes of composition which have no commercial purpose separate from that of the article, and that result from a chemical reaction that occurs upon end use of other chemical substances, mixtures, or articles; except that fluids and particles are not considered articles regardless of shape or design." 40 C.F.R. § 751.403.

RULEMAKING HISTORY
2021 Rule: EPA first promulgated a § 6(h) risk-management rule for decaBDE on January 6, 2021 (Decabromodiphenyl Ether (DecaBDE); Regulation of Persistent, Bioaccumulative, and Toxic Chemicals Under TSCA Section 6(h)). The rule prohibited the manufacturing, processing, and distribution of decaBDE and articles or products containing it, but permitted delayed compliance dates in specified industries. 40 C.F.R. § 751.405(a). The 2021 Rule did not regulate decaBDE exposure in: recycling of plastics containing decaBDE; manufacturing of new articles from plastic when no new decaBDE was added; disposal of decaBDE; releases of decaBDE into air, water, and soil; and decaBDE concentration in sewage sludge.

Petitioners timely petitioned for review of the 2021 Rule. EPA moved for a voluntary remand of the 2021 Rule to reconsider it. The motion was granted on June 23, 2022, by an earlier panel, and the challenge to the 2021 Rule was held in abeyance.

Reconsideration and 2024 Rule: On November 24, 2023, as part of its reconsideration, EPA solicited public comment on the 2021 Rule. Petitioners submitted comments contending that the 2021 Rule violated TSCA's mandate to address decaBDE risks and adopt all practicable exposure-reduction measures. The comment period lasted until January 8, 2024. On November 19, 2024, EPA published final amendments (Decabromodiphenyl Ether and Phenol, Isopropylated Phosphate (3:1); Revision to the Regulation of Persistent, Bioaccumulative, and Toxic Chemicals Under the Toxic Substances Control Act).

In response to Petitioners' criticism regarding the lack of decaBDE recycling regulations, EPA required the sole company owning and using plastic shipping pallets containing decaBDE to post warning signs for its workers and to require the workers' use of personal protective equipment. Specifically, EPA required that "[a]ll persons in this regulated area who recycle plastic shipping pallets that contain decaBDE are required to wear personal protective equipment, including respiratory protection that is at least as protective as a NIOSH-approved N95 respirator with an assigned protection factor (APF) of 10 and dermal protection of gloves that are chemically resistant to decaBDE." 40 C.F.R. § 751.405(d)(2).

In response to Petitioners' criticism regarding the lack of decaBDE wastewater regulation, EPA restricted decaBDE discharges to water "during manufacture, processing, and distribution in commerce of decaBDE and decaBDE-containing products." 40 C.F.R. § 751. This prohibition did not apply to articles containing decaBDE.

The 2024 Rule did not adopt any new regulations relating to decaBDE disposal or sewage sludge.

PRESENT PROCEEDING AND RELIEF SOUGHT
Petitioners filed a timely new petition for review of the 2024 Rule on December 12, 2024, which was consolidated with the pending challenge to the 2021 Rule. Petitioners seek a declaration that the 2024 Rule is unlawful based on EPA declining to regulate the following areas of decaBDE exposure:
(1) Nearly all recycling of plastics containing decaBDE and use of that plastic to produce new articles;
(2) Disposal of decaBDE and materials containing it;
(3) Wastewater discharges of decaBDE from facilities that manufacture, process, and dispose of articles containing decaBDE; and
(4) Use of decaBDE-contaminated sewage sludge as fertilizer.

Petitioners request a remand of the 2024 Rule, without vacatur, to EPA with instructions to propose within 180 days, and finalize within one year, amendments that adopt all practicable measures to reduce decaBDE exposures in the four identified areas.

EPA'S POSITION
EPA declined to further regulate decaBDE in the disputed areas. As to recyclable articles, EPA's stated rationales include the presence of "low levels" of decaBDE exposure, a high cost of implementing such regulations, and that regulating decaBDE would undermine EPA's overall goal of promoting recycling. As to disposal of waste, discharges, and sewage, EPA determined that further regulation was not practicable, invoking its compliance with the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, a statute regulating solid waste disposal, and addressing decaBDE concentration in sewage sludge by reference to a stated factor. EPA further contends, relying on Bluewater Network v. EPA, 372 F.3d 404 (D.C. Cir. 2004), that its decision not to regulate decaBDE in the disputed areas is valid because EPA may regulate in stages.

PARTIES AND COUNSEL
Petitioners include Alaska Community Action on Toxics, represented by Kelly E. Lester, Alana R. Reynolds, and Katherine K. O'Brien of Earthjustice. Respondents are the United States Environmental Protection Agency and related federal respondents, represented by Redding C. Cates and other attorneys of the U.S. Department of Justice, Environment & Natural Resources Division, and Amber Aranda and Stephanie Schwarz of EPA. Amici Curiae include Public Health Experts (Evan N. Bianchi, Spiro Harrison & Nelson LLC) and iGPS Logistics LLC (Allon Kedem, Lawrence E. Culleen, and Judah Prero, Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP).

A prior order granted Respondents' Petition for Panel Rehearing to Amend Opinion (Dkt. No. 53), with the amended opinion filed concurrently.

seed.consideration: Before deciding not to regulate, EPA should have confined its analysis to statutorily permitted factors and refrained from treating 'low levels' of decaBDE exposure as a basis for declining to regulate at all under § 6(h).
seed.why_material: Because § 6(h) chemicals are already deemed hazardous by Congress, exposure level may guide only how to regulate, not whether to regulate, so relying on it exceeded EPA's statutory authority and undermined its no-regulation decisions.

key.label: Recycling cost rationale
key.question: Was EPA's claim that regulating recyclables would be prohibitively expensive supported by studies actually addressing decaBDE testing costs?

10937255.situation:
This is a Sex Offender Registration Act (SORA) risk-level classification matter before Supreme Court concerning the defendant, who is anticipating release from incarceration.

Underlying convictions:

In May 2006, the defendant pleaded guilty in Queens County to two separate superior court informations. Those informations charged him with course of sexual conduct against a child in the first degree and course of sexual conduct against a child in the second degree.

Later in May 2006, the defendant pleaded guilty in Sullivan County to a superior court information charging him with course of sexual conduct against a child in the first degree, aggravated sexual abuse in the second degree, and use of a child in a sexual performance.

The victim in the Sullivan County action was also the victim in one of the crimes alleged in the Queens County superior court informations.

Pursuant to a global resolution, the defendant was sentenced in Sullivan County to 20 years in prison, to be followed by five years of postrelease supervision.

Board of Examiners of Sex Offenders assessment:

In anticipation of the defendant's release from incarceration, the Board of Examiners of Sex Offenders prepared a risk assessment instrument (RAI) regarding only the Sullivan County offenses. The Board presumptively classified the defendant as a risk level two sex offender, scoring 100 points, pursuant to the Sex Offender Registration Act (see Correction Law art 6-C).

The Board recommended an upward departure to risk level three, stating that "the RAI does not capture [the] totality of [defendant's] offenses that includes a second underage victim."

Proceedings and determination under review:

Following a hearing, Supreme Court found that the defendant's presumptive risk level was properly scored as a risk level two, at 100 points. Supreme Court adopted the Board's recommendation for an upward departure and classified the defendant as a risk level three sex offender without further designation.

The defendant contests the classification.

seed.consideration: Whether the defendant's advanced age and current medical conditions (elderly, legally blind, physically feeble) should be weighed as mitigating factors when deciding if an upward departure is warranted.
seed.why_material: Because an upward departure determination requires weighing aggravating against mitigating factors, and it could not be ascertained whether the court would still have departed had it considered these mitigating conditions.

10937878.holding_quote: As such, we conclude that the court erred by approving the executor's commission and attorney's fees in this case based solely on the fact that they fell within locally accepted percentage guidelines without a proper inquiry into the reasonableness of the fees based on the services actually rendered.
10937878.situation:
MATTER: Estate of Clea Andrews ("Decedent"), Orphans' Court Division, Washington County, Pennsylvania.

POSTURE OF THIS FILE: This file is prepared at the level of the Orphans' Court, which has held an evidentiary hearing on objections to the executor's first and final account and has ruled on those objections. The file states what was decided, on what record, and what the parties argue.

PARTIES AND FIDUCIARIES:
- Decedent: Clea Andrews, who died November 29, 2022.
- Original Executor: Charles Willison, nominated in the will, granted Letters Testamentary December 21, 2022. Mr. Willison died May 28, 2024.
- Successor Executor: Thomas E. Ostrowski, nominated as successor executor in the will, granted amended Letters Testamentary July 1, 2024.
- Objectants ("Appellants"): Beneficiaries under the will, among the ten named beneficiaries.
- Estate Counsel: Attorney Thomas O. Vreeland and Attorney Corey S. Young, of Bassi, Vreeland & Associates, PC.

UNDERLYING PROBATE FACTS:
Decedent's will, dated July 14, 2021, was admitted to probate on December 21, 2022. No objections to the validity of the will were raised. Notice of Estate Administration was served on the beneficiaries on January 9, 2023. The will named ten beneficiaries, including the objectants.

An inventory was filed June 27, 2023, listing:
- Cash assets totaling $103,119.71, consisting primarily of Decedent's Prudential IRA, PSERS Death Benefit, Washington Area Teachers Credit Union savings account, and Washington Financial Bank checking account.
- Stock assets totaling $1,935,486.64, consisting of 49 shares of EnPro Industries, Inc. and an account with RBC Wealth Management.
- Real estate assets totaling $243,024.54, consisting of property in South Strabane Township, Washington County, Pennsylvania, and related mineral rights and royalties.
- Total value of Decedent's personal and real property: $2,281,630.89.

An inheritance tax appraisement was filed November 29, 2023, listing a tax amount totaling $300,956.58.

THE ACCOUNT AND OBJECTIONS:
The original executor, Mr. Willison, filed an account on April 2, 2024, along with a petition for adjudication/statement of proposed distribution pursuant to Pa.O.C. Rule 2.4. The account listed:
- Two commissions paid from the Estate to Mr. Willison on February 9, 2023, and May 18, 2023, totaling $114,044.36.
- Two payments of attorney fees to Bassi, Vreeland & Associates, PC, totaling $136,853.24.
- A payment to Deverson, Tanack & Willison, CPAs, in the amount of $10,789.94.

The objectants filed objections to the petition for adjudication and first and final account on May 16, 2024, primarily objecting to the attorney fees, the executor commission, and the payment of the accounting fee to Deverson, Tanack & Willison, CPAs.

GOVERNING STANDARDS INVOKED:
- In re Trust Estate of LaRocca, 431 Pa. 542, 246 A.2d 337 (1968), invoked as the standard requiring examination of the work and services rendered to analyze the reasonableness of attorney's fees.
- In re Estate of Donofrio, No. 63-OC-2011-1359, 2015 O.C. Washington Cty. LEXIS 94 (O.C. Washington Cty. April 30, 2015). In Donofrio, the Washington County Orphans' Court revised its local guidelines regarding attorney fees and executor commissions, determining that reasonable and adequate attorney fees would be six percent, not graduated, and that reasonable and adequate executor commissions would be five percent, not graduated. The Donofrio court stated the guidelines are helpful and establish a sort of prima facie criteria: a fee charged above the guidelines operates as a red flag warranting closer review; a fee below the guidelines is not examined unless a question is raised; and the guidelines establish the appropriate maximum fee for the routine estate.

THE EVIDENTIARY HEARING (September 30, 2024):
Before testimony, the court noted that the executor's commission and attorney's fees in this case are within the guidelines practiced in Washington County, and that objectants' counsel had been quoting a much older case suggesting that the law relied on in Donofrio regarding commissions was not relevant.

Objectants' counsel stated his position that the Pennsylvania Supreme Court has held repeatedly since the 1960s through the 2020s that the standard for determining whether an executor's commission and attorney's legal fees in estate administration is a reasonableness standard determined by weighing a number of factors. Counsel argued that the flat fee of 5 percent and 6 percent referenced in Donofrio—which involved a significantly smaller estate than the present one—does not dispense with the requirement of reasonableness or the analysis required by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. The court responded that it disagreed and that it could not find research stating that after a certain amount a fee must be based on an hourly rate. Counsel stated that was not his argument. The court stated the fees fell squarely within the Donofrio opinion and Washington County practice and it had seen nothing to the contrary.

Objectants' counsel requested a continuance, stating counsel had erroneously believed the hearing was only a status hearing and not an evidentiary hearing. The court asked what evidence counsel intended to present regarding the unreasonableness of the fees.

An exchange occurred regarding burden of proof. Objectants' counsel asserted that the burden of proof as to the reasonableness of the fees rests on the executor and his counsel, not on the objectants, and that it is an initial (not a shifting) burden resting with the executor and his counsel. The court asked whether the burden was on the objector in the first instance. Counsel maintained the initial burden rests with the executor and counsel to prove the legal fees are reasonable. The court stated the Estate had met that burden by falling within the operative case law.

The court indicated it was inclined to overrule the objections and finalize the account unless objectants presented something to consider, stating the fees are within what the county has deemed reasonable for decades and most recently in Donofrio, and that Donofrio's standard of reasonableness governs the locality. Objectants' counsel elected to proceed with an evidentiary hearing rather than accept denial of the continuance.

TESTIMONY:
Objectants called Attorney Thomas O. Vreeland, counsel for the Estate (Attorney Corey S. Young participating on behalf of the Estate while Attorney Vreeland testified). Attorney Vreeland testified that he works for Bassi, Vreeland & Associates, PC; that he does not generally charge an hourly rate for estate work unless there is extensive litigation; and that he normally charges a flat fee of six percent of the inventory value of an estate, which was the rate charged here. He testified that he does not track the number of hours he and his staff work on estate cases. He described the estate as not particularly complex but noted some things that were "less than routine." He testified that the fee paid to Mr. Willison as executor was calculated as five percent of the inventory value of the Estate, and that he did not know how many hours Mr. Willison worked on the Estate.

Estate counsel sought to qualify Attorney Vreeland as an expert in estate administration based on his education, training, and 47 years of experience. Objectants objected, noting the reasonableness of Attorney Vreeland's fees was directly at issue. The court overruled the objection, stating it was taking into account that Attorney Vreeland had an obvious interest in the case and his fees, but that the fees fall within local practice and local case law and he could add to the record.

Attorney Vreeland opined that the fees charged to the Estate were reasonable. He based his opinion on experience and the history of estate administration; on the 2015 Donofrio opinion establishing a commission of 5 percent for a personal representative and 6 percent for the attorneys as acceptable in Washington County; and on his experience that every fee and commission appears on the inheritance tax return submitted to the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue for review, that he had never had a 6 percent fee or 5 percent commission rejected by the Department of Revenue in 40 years, and that the Department had never objected to such fees on his returns. When asked for his expert opinion on how much time an attorney would take on an estate like Decedent's, he replied that he did not know because he does not track his time and bills 6 percent of the inventory value.

Objectants called Thomas E. Ostrowski, the successor executor. Mr. Ostrowski testified he was aware Mr. Willison prepared a tax return for Decedent and performed accounting work related to the Estate, but he did not know the specifics of all work Mr. Willison performed or how much time Mr. Willison spent on the Estate. Estate counsel called no other witnesses.

MOTIONS AND RULINGS AT HEARING:
At the close of evidence, objectants moved for a directed verdict (nonsuit) on the ground that Attorney Vreeland and Mr. Ostrowski had not carried their burden of proof to establish the reasonableness of the legal fees and commissions. The court denied the motion, stating it was compelled to deny the request based on the case law and Washington County practice; that the fees fall within what is considered reasonable; that the burden does not switch back to the Estate; and that objectants had offered nothing to suggest the fees were unreasonable.

Objectants again sought a continuance to present their own expert. The court stated it respected objectants' proposed expert but that local practice governs; that even if the expert could analyze that the estate might have been billed less, the fee is still considered reasonable in the county and surrounding counties; and that the court cannot look only at the amount of time an attorney puts into an estate but must also consider the assets and their viability as part of what the attorney and personal representative deal with. The court overruled the objections regarding reasonableness of the fees.

WRITTEN ORDER (November 13, 2024):
The court entered an order overruling objectants' objections to the executor's commission and attorney's fees. The court found the executor commission and attorney's fees reasonable pursuant to In re Estate of Donofrio and the lay and expert testimony of Attorney Vreeland. The order stated: "There can be no doubt that the person attempting to prove an account incorrect must sustain the burden of establishing his position."

RELIEF SOUGHT BY OBJECTANTS:
Objectants seek to have the executor's commission and attorney's fees examined for reasonableness under the LaRocca factors and the actual work performed, contend that the burden of proving reasonableness rests on the executor and counsel, seek nonsuit for failure of proof of reasonableness, challenge the qualification of Estate counsel as an expert on his own fees and his client's commissions, assert the fiduciary exception to attorney-client privilege as to communications between an executor and his attorney regarding commissions and fees, and seek consideration or award of a surcharge.

SUBSEQUENT PROCEDURAL HISTORY:
Objectants filed a notice of appeal December 6, 2024. That appeal was quashed sua sponte January 13, 2025, because the November 2024 order was not a final order. The court entered a decree July 3, 2025, confirming the account and scheduling distribution of the remaining assets. Objectants filed a notice of appeal from the final order July 11, 2025. On July 22, 2025, the court ordered a concise statement of errors complained of under Pa.R.A.P. 1925(b), and objectants complied August 1, 2025.

seed.consideration: The reasonableness of executor commissions and attorney's fees must be assessed by inquiring into the actual services rendered and the LaRocca factors, rather than by presuming reasonableness because the fees fall within locally accepted percentage guidelines.
seed.why_material: Approving fees on a percentage basis without inquiry into the value of services actually rendered is egregious error, and the fee-seeking parties—not the objectors—bear the burden of proving reasonableness.

key.question: Did the objectors bear the burden of showing the fees were unreasonable?

key.question: Was the five percent executor commission reasonable and just?

key.question: Was the six percent flat attorney fee reasonable for the estate?

10938498.situation:
This matter concerns a petition for post-conviction relief filed by Mr. Johnson that relates to two separate criminal cases in which Mr. Johnson was convicted of felonies in 2023.

CASE NO. 22CRC-I0144

In Case No. 22CRC-I0144, Mr. Johnson pleaded guilty to six counts of rape. The trial court imposed a sentence of 25 years to life in prison. Mr. Johnson filed a direct appeal in which he raised challenges to his plea and sentence. During the pendency of that appeal, Mr. Johnson filed a motion to withdraw his guilty pleas. The appellate court remanded the matter, and the trial court denied the motion after a hearing. Mr. Johnson appealed from the order denying his motion. The appellate court subsequently issued a decision affirming both the judgment of conviction and the trial court's denial of Mr. Johnson's motion to withdraw his pleas. That decision is reported as State v. Johnson, 2025-Ohio-2719 (9th Dist.) ("Johnson I").

CASE NO. 22CRC-I0207

In Case No. 22CRC-I0207, Mr. Johnson pleaded no contest to one count of having weapons while under disability, together with an attendant forfeiture specification. The trial court found Mr. Johnson guilty and imposed a 12-month prison sentence. The trial court also ordered the forfeiture of a handgun.

THE PETITION FOR POST-CONVICTION RELIEF

Prior to the appellate court's decision in Johnson I, Mr. Johnson filed a petition for post-conviction relief in both Case No. 22CRC-I0144 and Case No. 22CRC-I0207. In the petition, Mr. Johnson argued that he had obtained new evidence demonstrating that trial counsel rendered ineffective assistance of counsel. The petition cited Revised Code Section 2953.21(C), which pertains to defendants who are sentenced to death.

After the appellate court decided Johnson I, the trial court issued a journal entry denying the petition for post-conviction relief. The trial court noted that Mr. Johnson had mistakenly cited Revised Code Section 2953.21(C) in support of his petition. The trial court denied the petition on the basis that the appellate court's decision in Johnson I rendered Mr. Johnson's ineffective assistance of counsel claim moot. The trial court did not hold an evidentiary hearing on the petition.

ISSUES PRESENTED

Two issues are raised with respect to the trial court's denial of the petition. The first is whether the trial court abused its discretion by not holding an evidentiary hearing to consider evidence that was not contained in the trial record. The second is whether the trial court's facts, findings, and conclusions of law are adequate under Revised Code Section 2953.21(H) and State ex rel. Penland v. Dinkelacker, 162 Ohio St.3d 59.

seed.consideration: Whether the petition was timely under R.C. 2953.21(A)(2)(a) and 2953.23(A)(1), whether the affirmance in one case reached the separate second case, and whether the attached exhibits constituted new evidence not previously available.
seed.why_material: Without addressing these threshold and evidentiary questions, the mootness ruling could not properly dispose of the petition, especially as to the case not covered by the prior appeal.

key.question: Could the trial court defer action on the petition while the direct appeal remained pending?

10945260.situation:
This is a divorce action between Jonathan Cline and Melinda Duckett in Alaska superior court. The matter is before the court following a four-day trial and post-trial motion practice concerning child support and the division of the marital estate.

BACKGROUND

Cline and Duckett married in 1997. They have four children together. They separated in April 2021.

In April 2022, the parties agreed to a bifurcated divorce. They stipulated to certain terms, including that Cline would be reimbursed for "repairs completed on marital real estate" in the amount of $61,690. The superior court issued a divorce decree at that time, reserving for later resolution the issues of Cline's child support obligation and division of the marital estate.

THE TRIAL

The parties litigated the remaining issues at a trial held over four days between March and August 2023. The issues included Cline's child support obligation, the classification of certain items as separate or marital property, and equitable division of the marital estate.

Child support testimony. The parties disputed Cline's child support obligation for their second-youngest daughter. She was an adult by the time trial began and graduated from high school during the trial. The parties testified that she has intellectual disabilities and has been living in assisted living facilities since she was thirteen.

Cline argued that neither parent should owe past or ongoing child support for her beyond the cost of her room and board, because she had been "under the care of the [S]tate" for years, with the State covering her "necessary needs." He told the court that he had not had much contact with her since he and Duckett separated, did not "see her very often," and had "probably seen her physically four or five times in the last two years."

Duckett argued that Cline should owe child support to help cover their daughter's expenses beyond the cost of room and board. She explained that although their daughter does not live with either parent, Duckett is her legal guardian and conservator; coordinates her care, education, and therapy with little involvement from Cline; and visits her at least once a week at the facility where she lives. She testified that she covers their daughter's everyday expenses such as clothing, toiletries, and spending money, spending about $1,280 per month in total. She testified that room and board comprised $600 of that amount, and that she expected room and board to be covered by Social Security once their daughter was approved for benefits.

Property classification testimony. The parties disputed whether the court should classify a certain monetary gift as separate or marital property. Cline told the court that during the marriage his mother loaned the parties $150,000 to develop one of their properties. He testified that after he paid off $100,000 of that loan, his mother decided she wanted to give each of her sons a $100,000 early inheritance gift. He testified that she forgave the $50,000 remaining on the loan and also sent him a check for $50,000. He said he was away from home when the check arrived in the mail and told Duckett to deposit it into one of their shared accounts. Cline's mother also testified about the inheritance, indicating that she intended the entire $100,000 early inheritance to go to her son, and that she did not intend the gift to go to Duckett. Duckett told the court that the $150,000 loan was marital and that she was never informed that Cline's mother was forgiving only Cline's half of the loan.

Equitable division testimony. The parties each sought a 60% portion of the marital estate, which included some real property and proceeds held in trust from properties they had already sold. They testified at length about their respective education, work history throughout the marriage, and earning capacities.

Duckett testified that she is a physical therapist, but had primarily been a homemaker during the marriage. She re-entered the full-time workforce outside the home in October 2021, and at the time of trial was earning about $55/hour with a recent tentative raise. She testified that caring for her children still limited her earning capacity.

Cline testified that in addition to working as a pilot during the marriage, he had also worked in real estate and had been licensed as a contractor. He said he expected his future sole source of income to be his job as a pilot. On the last day of trial, he informed the court that he had taken a new pilot job. He said it offered good long-term prospects, although it started with a wage decrease. Cline also testified that he had lost around a quarter of a million dollars to "a scammer" between the time of separation and the trial.

THE APRIL 2024 ORDER

The court issued an order regarding child support and division of the marital estate in April 2024.

The court rejected Cline's argument that neither party should owe child support for their adult daughter residing in the assisted living facility. It found that Cline owed past support through the date of that daughter's high school graduation pursuant to Alaska Civil Rule 90.3. For purposes of calculating Cline's support obligation, it adopted the income figure stated in Cline's proposed findings of fact, finding that his adjusted annual income was $109,249.

The court also ordered Cline to provide ongoing support for the parties' adult daughter, recognizing that courts may order post-majority support for adult children in similar contexts. It credited Duckett's testimony that she spent about $1,280 per month on their daughter's expenses. It found this amount to be "reasonable and necessary," and reasoned that the parties should split this monthly cost evenly to provide ongoing support for their daughter until she began receiving Social Security benefits. It urged the parties to continue supporting her beyond that point "as long as [they] [were] able."

The court rejected Cline's request for a $100,000 "carve out" from the value of the marital estate to reflect the inheritance gift from his mother. It found that Cline "ha[d] not proven that this portion [was] non-marital" given the parties' testimony that $50,000 had gone toward forgiving a loan on marital property and the other $50,000 had been deposited into a shared account. It observed that Cline's mother's testimony was not "informative" and did not indicate that Cline had intended to keep the inheritance as separate property when the gift was made.

The court then turned to dividing the marital estate. It noted that in fashioning an equitable overall division of the marital estate, it would consider the factors set forth in Merrill. It made findings of fact regarding many of the factors, including the age, health, financial condition, and earning capacity of each party. The court found that the Merrill factors supported awarding 55% of the estate to Duckett. It based this division primarily on "Cline's higher earning potential and [Duckett's] role" as a homemaker throughout the marriage.

MOTION FOR RECONSIDERATION

Cline moved for reconsideration, raising four challenges to the court's order.

First, he argued that the court had failed to make specific findings about whether the parties' daughter had been in either party's primary physical custody before she graduated from high school, which he argued was required for a valid award under Civil Rule 90.3. He also argued that to the extent the court had implicitly found Duckett had primary physical custody, that was legal error because their daughter had not actually lived with either parent between separation and graduation, but rather in an assisted living facility.

Second, he challenged the court's division of the marital estate, arguing that the court should have awarded Cline at least a 50% share.

Third, he argued that although he had requested credits for separate funds he used to preserve marital assets between separation and divorce, the court had failed to make any written findings on this point. He asked the court to award him $59,121.32 in post-separation credits for funds spent to preserve marital real property.

Fourth, he asked the court to issue an order dividing the capital gains taxes the parties had incurred in selling marital real estate, which the court had not addressed in its order. He argued that the parties should "use the funds held in trust to pay off any remaining capital gains liabilities, then divide the remaining funds in trust between themselves."

The court rejected all of these arguments. First, it noted that it had "expressly recognize[d] that [Duckett] had primary physical custody" of their adult daughter through her high school graduation for purposes of the child support award. Second, it reaffirmed that its division of the marital estate had been "fair and equitable." Third, it stated that Cline had "failed to establish any evidence at trial that would allow" it to award him a post-separation Ramsey credit. Fourth, the court ordered that the payment of capital gains taxes would "follow the ... overall division of the marital estate," meaning Cline is responsible for 55% of the tax liability and Duckett is responsible for the remaining 45%.

GOVERNING STANDARDS

Child support was calculated under Alaska Civil Rule 90.3. The equitable division of the marital estate was governed by the factors set forth in Merrill. The post-separation credit request was framed in terms of a Ramsey credit. Post-majority support for an adult child was addressed as a recognized category of relief.

seed.consideration: Whether the Merrill factors support assigning capital gains taxes in a way that effectively widens the disparity beyond the 55/45 property split.
seed.why_material: Because unpaid capital gains taxes are marital debt requiring their own Merrill-based findings, and mechanically following the property split alters the overall division without justification.

key.label: Post-majority disability support

key.label: Characterization of inheritance
key.question: Did the $100,000 early inheritance transmute into marital property through deposit into a joint account and forgiveness of marital debt?

key.label: Unequal 55/45 division
key.question: Did the Merrill factors, chiefly earning capacity and homemaker role, support awarding 55% of the estate to Duckett?

key.question: Did Cline establish an evidentiary basis for a credit for post-separation expenditures preserving marital property?

10947108.court: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims
10947108.holding_quote: By ignoring the citation and discussion made within the April 2015 decision, the Board misapplied § 20.1303.
10947108.situation:
This is a claim by Robert O. Edwards, a Navy veteran, for VA disability compensation based on service connection for squamous cell carcinoma of the right tonsil. Mr. Edwards was exposed to herbicides (Agent Orange) during his service in the Vietnam War. He was later diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the right tonsil, described in the medical literature as a common malignant tumor of the oropharynx.

Mr. Edwards filed a claim for that condition in November 2019, alleging that the cancer was caused by his exposure to Agent Orange. VA regulations do not permit presumptive service connection for squamous cell carcinoma under 38 C.F.R. § 3.309(e). As a result, Mr. Edwards must prove direct service connection under the elements set out in Washington v. Nicholson, 19 Vet.App. 362, 367 (2005).

The matter involves two reports of the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) concerning veterans and Agent Orange: Update 2010 and Update 2012. NAS reports relay their conclusions about diseases and herbicide exposure in terms of an association between the two and generally place diseases into one of four categories: (1) sufficient evidence of an association; (2) limited or suggestive evidence of an association; (3) inadequate or insufficient evidence to determine an association; or (4) limited or suggestive evidence of no association. Both Update 2010 and Update 2012 found that there was inadequate or insufficient evidence to determine an association between squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue (including the tonsils) and herbicide exposure.

In response to a request for medical evidence, Mr. Edwards submitted to the Agency of Original Jurisdiction (AOJ) two Board decisions from unrelated cases. Both granted service connection for squamous cell carcinoma, both featured medical exams furnished by VA for the claimants, and both relied heavily on opinions from private medical examiners.

In the first decision, dated April 2015, the Board granted service connection to another veteran for carcinoma of the tongue. It considered three medical opinions, two provided by the Agency and the third by a private examiner. The Board found that one VA exam was inconclusive and unhelpful. The Board explained that the other VA exam's explanation that Agent Orange exposure's complications did not include tongue carcinoma was probative. It then turned to the private medical examiner's opinion, which it found adequate and compelling enough to put the evidence into equipoise. In formulating that positive nexus opinion, the private examiner reviewed Update 2010 and various other studies. After reading the report, the examiner said there was a biological mechanism by which the veteran's herbicide exposure might have caused his cancer: immune alterations associated with herbicide exposure may increase susceptibility to an infection in the oral cavity and precipitate squamous cell carcinomas in that area. Based on this theory and other unenumerated studies, the examiner opined that scientifically it was more likely than not that the veteran's squamous cell cancer of the tongue was caused by or related to in-service exposure to Agent Orange.

In the second decision, from September 2015, the Board granted service connection to another veteran for carcinoma of the right forearm. There, the veteran's private examiner opined that although there was no definitive proof that herbicides cause skin cancers, it was his experience that exposure to herbicides was definitely a factor in the development of skin cancers, including the examined condition. The Board conceded that negative nexus opinions from VA exams were valueless, but noted that sun exposure is a known cause of the condition and that the claimant had reported exposure to significant sunlight while in Vietnam. It found service connection appropriate because the evidence was in equipoise as to whether the carcinoma was connected to exposure to herbicides and sun during service.

Mr. Edwards also submitted a third unrelated Board decision, from March 2018, which concerned entitlement to an earlier effective date for a compensable rating for squamous cell carcinoma. Both parties agree that this decision was correctly dismissed, as the present matter concerns the preliminary issue of entitlement to service connection.

The AOJ was unconvinced by Mr. Edwards's submission of the unrelated Board decisions. It denied service connection in a March 26, 2020, decision. That decision did not note any consideration of NAS reports in its summary of the evidence. The AOJ continued its denial in a higher-level review decision reasoning that the submitted Board decisions could not prove a connection because they were based on the medical evidence and service histories of other veterans. That decision also noted no consideration of the NAS reports in its summary of the evidence. The AOJ did not discuss the Secretary's duty to assist under 38 U.S.C. § 5103A.

Mr. Edwards appealed to the Board in May 2021. He and his representative chose to pursue an appeal decision through the direct review docket and submitted an informal presentation arguing his case.

Under the Veterans Appeals Improvement and Modernization Act of 2017 (AMA), a claimant picks one of three appellate avenues: the hearing docket, additional evidence docket, or direct review docket, per 38 U.S.C. § 7105(b)(3)(A)-(C); see Andrews v. McDonough, 34 Vet.App. 151, 157 (2021). These paths present different restrictions on the evidentiary record before the Board and the window during which claimants may submit unconsidered evidence. By electing the direct review route, Mr. Edwards restricted his evidentiary record to the evidence of record at the time of the decision of the AOJ on appeal, under 38 U.S.C. § 7113(a). As a result, the Board was limited to reviewing the evidence of record on March 26, 2020, the date of the AOJ's denial of service connection.

Mr. Edwards's informal presentation referenced Update 2012. Arguing that there is a positive nexus between herbicide exposure and squamous cell carcinoma, Mr. Edwards cited Update 2012, which repeats the biological mechanism theory also featured in Update 2010. He stated that the evidence of record reflects an infection leading to squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil. The informal presentation asserted that the Secretary should have furnished Mr. Edwards with a medical exam, contending that the theory articulated in the NAS report was sufficient to indicate a connection between the cancer and herbicide exposure, invoking 38 U.S.C. § 5103A(d)(2)(b).

The Board issued the decision on appeal on August 5, 2024. It first reasoned that the unrelated Board decisions did not obligate VA to furnish an exam because their references to separate medical opinions were too general and conclusory to indicate that there may be a nexus linking the cancer to service. The decision then turned to the merits of Mr. Edwards's theory of direct service connection.

The Board began that discussion by addressing the other Board decisions. It emphasized that such decisions could be persuasive authority only, because each case before the Board is decided on the basis of the individual facts presented, citing 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303. The Board did not share the view that these past decisions were analogous. As to the April 2015 decision, the Board found that Mr. Edwards failed to submit a private opinion, whereas that veteran submitted such an opinion; the Board read the decision but did not mention Update 2010. As to the September 2015 decision, the Board distinguished it because Mr. Edwards, unlike the claimant there, did not provide a private medical opinion, and because sunlight exposure was not alleged as a cause of the disability here while it was deemed a possible cause in that decision.

The informal presentation's reference to Update 2012 was addressed by the Board. Because the appeal arrived via the direct review pathway, the Board found that the report's contents could not be considered either as argument or evidence. The Board reasoned that to consider that report, or any such report, would be to rely on materials received by the Agency after the AOJ's decision, citing 38 U.S.C. § 7113(a).

Mr. Edwards seeks a remand requiring the Secretary to consider the NAS reports and furnish an exam. He argues that the Board was required to address Update 2012 because the Agency constructively possessed that report long before it denied the claim at the AOJ level. He also disputes the Board's reasons or bases for its determination that a medical exam was not required, particularly given that the conclusion found within Update 2010 was raised to the AOJ through the unrelated April 2015 decision.
